title: Hidāyat al-naḥw
author: attributed to Sirāj al-Dīn ʿUthmān al-Awadhī
authorArabic: مَنْسُوبٌ إِلَى سِرَاجِ الدِّينِ عُثْمَانَ الْأَوَدِيِّ
subject: nahw
summary: Hidāyat al-naḥw, “the guidance of naḥw”, is the Arabic handbook of naḥw of the Indian madrasa, read in the Dars-i Niẓāmī after Naḥw-i Mīr and before Ibn al-Ḥājib's Kāfiya. The print names no author; the book is attributed to Sirāj al-Dīn ʿUthmān al-Awadhī. Its author says he gathered the important matters of naḥw “in the order of the Kāfiya”, in clear words, with an example for every question and without the proofs and reasons that would distract a beginner. It runs from an introduction on naḥw, the word and speech, through the noun (iʿrāb and the diptote; the marfūʿ, manṣūb and majrūr; the followers; the built noun; the other rules of the noun), to the verb and the particle. The lessons follow the Kanpur lithograph of the Nawal Kishor press, 1300/1883, a few passages at a time.

parts.title: The introduction: naḥw, the word and speech

lessons.title: The book and its plan; naḥw; the three kinds of word
body: The author says plainly what kind of book this is: “a short, carefully set-down book on naḥw”, gathering its important matters “in the order of the Kāfiya”, in clear words, with an example for every question, “without going into the proofs and the reasons, lest they distract the beginner's mind”. So the Hidāya is the Kāfiya's order made plain. In the Indian madrasa it comes after the Persian Naḥw-i Mīr and before the Kāfiya itself: the rules are already known in outline, and here they are learned in Arabic, in full, with their conditions.

The introduction gives the first principles (mabādiʾ) on which the questions depend. The madrasa asks three of them of every science before it begins, and the book gives all three. The definition: naḥw is “a knowledge of rules by which are known the states of the ends of the three kinds of word, as to iʿrāb and binā, and the manner in which some of them are put together with others”. The aim: “to guard the mind from error in wording in the speech of the Arabs”. The subject: the word (kalima) and speech (kalām).

Notice the two halves of the definition. Naḥw looks at the ends of words (whether they change, iʿrāb, or stay, binā), and it looks at how words are put together. The inside of the word, its pattern and letters, belongs to ṣarf.

The word is “an utterance laid down for a single meaning”, and it is confined to three divisions. The book proves it by a division that leaves nothing out: either a word does not indicate a meaning in itself, and that is the particle; or it does, and its meaning is joined with one of the three times, and that is the verb; or it does, and its meaning is not joined with a time, and that is the noun. There is no fourth possibility, so there is no fourth kind of word.

tasks.prompt: Give the definition, the aim and the subject of naḥw as the book gives them.
tasks.answer: Definition: a knowledge of rules by which the states of the ends of the three kinds of word are known, as to iʿrāb and binā, and how words are put together. Aim: to guard the mind from error in wording in the speech of the Arabs. Subject: the word and speech.

tasks.prompt: Explain why there are only three kinds of word.
tasks.answer: A word either does not indicate a meaning in itself (the particle), or it does; and if it does, its meaning is either joined with one of the three times (the verb) or not (the noun). The division leaves no fourth case.

tasks.prompt: What does the author leave out of his book, and why?
tasks.answer: The proofs and the reasons (al-adilla wa-l-ʿilal) of the rules, lest they distract the beginner's mind from understanding the rules themselves.

text.original: بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَنِ الرَّحِيمِ. الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ رَبِّ الْعَالَمِينَ، وَالْعَاقِبَةُ لِلْمُتَّقِينَ، وَالصَّلَاةُ عَلَى رَسُولِهِ مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ وَأَصْحَابِهِ أَجْمَعِينَ. أَمَّا بَعْدُ، فَهَذَا مُخْتَصَرٌ مَضْبُوطٌ فِي النَّحْوِ، جَمَعْتُ فِيهِ مُهِمَّاتِ النَّحْوِ عَلَى تَرْتِيبِ الْكَافِيَةِ، مُبَوَّبًا وَمُفَصَّلًا، بِعِبَارَةٍ وَاضِحَةٍ، مَعَ إِيرَادِ الْأَمْثِلَةِ فِي جَمِيعِ مَسَائِلِهَا، مِنْ غَيْرِ تَعَرُّضٍ لِلْأَدِلَّةِ وَالْعِلَلِ؛ لِئَلَّا يُشَوِّشَ ذِهْنَ الْمُبْتَدِي عَنْ فَهْمِ الْمَسَائِلِ. وَسَمَّيْتُهُ بِهِدَايَةِ النَّحْوِ رَجَاءَ أَنْ يَهْدِيَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى بِهِ الطَّالِبِينَ، وَرَتَّبْتُهُ عَلَى مُقَدِّمَةٍ وَثَلَاثَةِ أَقْسَامٍ وَخَاتِمَةٍ، بِتَوْفِيقِ الْمَلِكِ الْعَزِيزِ الْعَلَّامِ.
text.en: In the name of God, the Merciful, the Compassionate. Praise be to God, Lord of the worlds; the [good] end is for the godfearing; and blessing be upon His messenger Muḥammad, and upon his family and his Companions, all of them. To proceed: this is a short, carefully set-down book on naḥw, in which I have gathered the important matters of naḥw in the order of the Kāfiya, arranged in chapters and sections, in clear wording, giving examples in all its questions, without going into the proofs and the reasons, lest they distract the beginner's mind from understanding the questions. I have named it Hidāyat al-naḥw (“The guidance of naḥw”), in the hope that God Most High will guide the students by it; and I have arranged it in an introduction, three parts and a conclusion, with the help of the King, the Mighty, the All-Knowing.

text.original: أَمَّا الْمُقَدِّمَةُ فَفِي الْمَبَادِي الَّتِي يَجِبُ تَقْدِيمُهَا لِتَوَقُّفِ الْمَسَائِلِ عَلَيْهَا، وَفِيهَا ثَلَاثَةُ فُصُولٍ. فَصْلٌ: النَّحْوُ عِلْمٌ بِأُصُولٍ يُعْرَفُ بِهَا أَحْوَالُ أَوَاخِرِ الْكَلِمِ الثَّلَاثِ مِنْ حَيْثُ الْإِعْرَابُ وَالْبِنَاءُ، وَكَيْفِيَّةُ تَرْكِيبِ بَعْضِهَا مَعَ بَعْضٍ. وَالْغَرَضُ مِنْهُ صِيَانَةُ الذِّهْنِ عَنِ الْخَطَإِ اللَّفْظِيِّ فِي كَلَامِ الْعَرَبِ، وَمَوْضُوعُهُ الْكَلِمَةُ وَالْكَلَامُ.
text.en: The introduction is on the first principles that must be put first, because the questions depend on them; it has three sections. Section. Naḥw is a knowledge of rules by which are known the states of the ends of the three [kinds of] words, as to iʿrāb and bināʾ, and the manner in which some of them are put together with others. Its aim is to guard the mind from error in wording in the speech of the Arabs; and its subject is the word (kalima) and speech (kalām).

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الْكَلِمَةُ لَفْظٌ وُضِعَ لِمَعْنًى مُفْرَدٍ، وَهِيَ مُنْحَصِرَةٌ فِي ثَلَاثَةِ أَقْسَامٍ: اسْمٍ وَفِعْلٍ وَحَرْفٍ؛ لِأَنَّهَا إِمَّا أَنْ لَا تَدُلَّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي نَفْسِهَا، وَهُوَ الْحَرْفُ، أَوْ تَدُلَّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي نَفْسِهَا وَيَقْتَرِنَ مَعْنَاهَا بِأَحَدِ الْأَزْمِنَةِ الثَّلَاثَةِ، وَهُوَ الْفِعْلُ، أَوْ تَدُلَّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي نَفْسِهَا وَلَمْ يَقْتَرِنْ مَعْنَاهَا بِهِ، وَهُوَ الِاسْمُ.
text.en: Section. The word (kalima) is an utterance laid down for a single meaning. It is confined to three divisions: noun (ism), verb (fiʿl) and particle (ḥarf); for either it does not indicate a meaning in itself, and that is the particle; or it indicates a meaning in itself and its meaning is joined with one of the three times, and that is the verb; or it indicates a meaning in itself and its meaning is not joined with one, and that is the noun.

lessons.title: The noun and the verb: definitions, signs and names
body: The noun is “a word that indicates a meaning in itself, not joined with one of the three times, the past, the present and the future”. The book's two examples, rajul, “a man”, and ʿilm, “knowledge”, show that a noun may name a thing you can see or a meaning you cannot. Its signs: it can be told about, Zaydun qāʾimun; it can be muḍāf, ghulāmu Zaydin; it takes the lām of definiteness, al-rajul; jarr and tanwīn, bi-Zaydin; the dual, the plural, the adjective (naʿt), the diminutive and the vocative. “All these are properties of the noun”: none is found in a verb or a particle, though not every noun takes every one.

“Told about” means that something is judged of it: it is a fāʿil, a mafʿūl or a mubtadaʾ. The name ism comes, the book says, from sumuww, “rising”, because the noun rises above its two fellows, “not from wasm, a mark on the meaning”. The first is the derivation of the Baṣrans, the second that of the Kūfans.

The verb is “a word that indicates a meaning in itself, with an indication joined with the time of that meaning”: ḍaraba, yaḍribu, iḍrib. Its signs: it can be told with, but not told about; it takes qad, the sīn, sawfa and jazm; it is conjugated into the past and the muḍāriʿ; it is a command or a prohibition; and it takes the visible marfūʿ pronouns, ḍarabta, the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine, ḍarabat, and the nūn of emphasis.

“Told with” means that the verb is what is judged (the musnad), never what something is judged of. The verb is called fiʿl “by the name of its origin, the maṣdar”, because the maṣdar “is in truth the fiʿl”, the act, of the doer: ḍarb is the act of hitting, and ḍaraba tells of that act in past time.

One trap: the tāʾ of the feminine is a sign of the verb only when it is quiescent, as in ḍarabat. The moving tāʾ, as in qāʾimatun, is on nouns. A sign must be looked at closely before it is used to sort a word.

tasks.prompt: Sort the words and name the sign that shows each: al-rajulu; ḍarabat; bi-Zaydin; qad qāma.
tasks.answer: Al-rajulu: a noun (the lām of definiteness). Ḍarabat: a verb (the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine). Bi-Zaydin: a noun (jarr and tanwīn). Qāma in qad qāma: a verb (qad).

tasks.prompt: What does “told about” mean, and in what roles is a noun told about?
tasks.answer: That something is judged of it. A noun is told about when it is a fāʿil, a mafʿūl or a mubtadaʾ.

tasks.prompt: Why is the verb called fiʿl?
tasks.answer: By the name of its origin, the maṣdar: the maṣdar is in truth the fiʿl, the act, of the doer, and the verb tells of that act in a time.

tasks.prompt: From what does the book derive the word ism, and from what does it not?
tasks.answer: From sumuww, “rising”, because the noun rises above the verb and the particle; not from wasm, “a mark”. The first is the Baṣran derivation, the second the Kūfan.

text.original: فَحَدُّ الِاسْمِ: كَلِمَةٌ تَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي نَفْسِهَا غَيْرِ مُقْتَرِنٍ بِأَحَدِ الْأَزْمِنَةِ الثَّلَاثَةِ، أَعْنِي الْمَاضِيَ وَالْحَالَ وَالِاسْتِقْبَالَ، كَرَجُلٍ وَعِلْمٍ. وَعَلَامَتُهُ صِحَّةُ الْإِخْبَارِ عَنْهُ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، وَالْإِضَافَةُ، نَحْوُ: غُلَامُ زَيْدٍ، وَدُخُولُ لَامِ التَّعْرِيفِ، كَالرَّجُلِ، وَالْجَرُّ وَالتَّنْوِينُ، نَحْوُ: بِزَيْدٍ، وَالتَّثْنِيَةُ وَالْجَمْعُ وَالنَّعْتُ وَالتَّصْغِيرُ وَالنِّدَاءُ؛ فَإِنَّ كُلَّ هَذِهِ خَوَاصُّ الِاسْمِ.
text.en: The definition of the noun: a word that indicates a meaning in itself, not joined with one of the three times — I mean the past, the present and the future —, as rajulin “a man” and ʿilmin “knowledge”. Its signs are that it can rightly be told about, as Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is standing”; the iḍāfa, as ghulāmu Zaydin “Zayd's servant”; the coming of the lām of definiteness, as al-rajuli “the man”; jarr and tanwīn, as bi-Zaydin “by Zayd”; and the dual, the plural, the naʿt, the diminutive and the vocative; for all these are properties of the noun.

text.original: وَمَعْنَى الْإِخْبَارِ عَنْهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَحْكُومًا عَلَيْهِ؛ لِكَوْنِهِ فَاعِلًا أَوْ مَفْعُولًا أَوْ مُبْتَدَأً. وَيُسَمَّى اسْمًا لِسُمُوِّهِ عَلَى قَسِيمَيْهِ، لَا لِكَوْنِهِ وَسْمًا عَلَى الْمَعْنَى.
text.en: The meaning of its being told about is that something is judged of it, because it is a fāʿil, a mafʿūl or a mubtadaʾ. It is called ism for its rising (sumuww) above its two fellow divisions, not for its being a mark (wasm) on the meaning.

text.original: وَحَدُّ الْفِعْلِ: كَلِمَةٌ تَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي نَفْسِهَا دَلَالَةً مُقْتَرِنَةً بِزَمَانِ ذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَى، كَضَرَبَ يَضْرِبُ اضْرِبْ. وَعَلَامَتُهُ أَنْ يَصِحَّ الْإِخْبَارُ بِهِ لَا عَنْهُ، وَدُخُولُ قَدْ وَالسِّينِ وَسَوْفَ وَالْجَزْمِ، وَالتَّصْرِيفُ إِلَى الْمَاضِي وَالْمُضَارِعِ، وَكَوْنُهُ أَمْرًا أَوْ نَهْيًا، وَاتِّصَالُ الضَّمَائِرِ الْبَارِزَةِ الْمَرْفُوعَةِ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْتَ، وَتَاءِ التَّأْنِيثِ السَّاكِنَةِ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَتْ، وَنُونِ التَّأْكِيدِ؛ فَإِنَّ كُلَّ هَذِهِ خَوَاصُّ الْفِعْلِ.
text.en: The definition of the verb: a word that indicates a meaning in itself, with an indication joined with the time of that meaning, as ḍaraba “he hit”, yaḍribu “he hits” and iḍrib “hit!”. Its signs are that it can rightly be told with, not told about; the coming of qad, the sīn, sawfa and jazm; being conjugated into the past and the muḍāriʿ; being a command or a prohibition; the joining to it of the visible marfūʿ pronouns, as ḍarabta “you hit”, of the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine, as ḍarabat “she hit”, and of the nūn of emphasis; for all these are properties of the verb.

text.original: وَمَعْنَى الْإِخْبَارِ بِهِ أَنْ يَكُونَ مَحْكُومًا بِهِ. وَيُسَمَّى فِعْلًا بِاسْمِ أَصْلِهِ، وَهُوَ الْمَصْدَرُ؛ لِأَنَّ الْمَصْدَرَ هُوَ فِعْلُ الْفَاعِلِ حَقِيقَةً.
text.en: The meaning of its being told with is that it is what is judged. It is called fiʿl by the name of its origin, the maṣdar; for the maṣdar is in truth the fiʿl (act) of the doer.

lessons.title: The particle; speech and the sentence
body: The particle is “a word that does not indicate a meaning in itself, but indicates a meaning in something else”. The book's example is min: its meaning is “beginning”, but it shows that meaning only once the place from which the beginning is made is named: sirtu mina al-baṣrati ilā al-kūfati, “I travelled from Baṣra to Kūfa”. Its sign is negative: it can be neither told about nor told with, and it takes none of the signs of the noun or the verb.

Particles do work in speech. They link two nouns, Zaydun fī al-dāri; two verbs, urīdu an taḍriba; a noun and a verb, ḍarabtu bi-l-khashabati, “I hit with the stick”; or two sentences, in jāʾanī Zaydun akramtuhu. The third part of the book takes them one by one. It is called ḥarf, “edge”, because it stands at the edge of speech, “not intended for itself, like the musnad and the musnad ilayhi”.

Speech (kalām) is “an utterance that contains two words by predication (isnād)”, and predication is relating one word to the other “so that it gives the one addressed a complete benefit on which silence may rightly follow”: Zaydun qāʾimun, qāma Zaydun. The test of speech is that the hearer is not left waiting. Ghulāmu Zaydin is two words, but it is not speech: one waits to hear what about the servant.

So speech comes about only from two nouns, Zaydun qāʾimun, a nominal sentence, or from a verb and a noun, qāma Zaydun, a verbal sentence. Only there are the musnad and the musnad ilayhi found together: a particle is neither, and a verb cannot be told about, so two verbs, or a verb and a particle, make no speech.

The book answers an objection. Yā Zaydu, “O Zayd!”, seems to be speech made of a particle and a noun. No: “the particle of the vocative stands in the place of adʿū, ‘I call’, and aṭlubu, ‘I seek’, which is the verb”, so yā Zaydu is a verb and a noun after all.

predication: relating one word to another with a complete benefit

tasks.prompt: Explain, with the book's example, how min indicates its meaning “in something else”.
tasks.answer: Min means the beginning of a journey or a distance, but it shows that meaning only when the place it begins from is named after it, here al-baṣra. Alone, min tells nothing.

tasks.prompt: Say what each particle links: Zaydun fī al-dāri; urīdu an taḍriba; in jāʾanī Zaydun akramtuhu.
tasks.arabic: زَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ — أُرِيدُ أَنْ تَضْرِبَ — إِنْ جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ أَكْرَمْتُهُ
tasks.answer: Fī links two nouns, Zayd and the house. An links two verbs, urīdu and taḍriba. In links two sentences, the condition jāʾanī Zaydun and the response akramtuhu.

tasks.prompt: Is ghulāmu Zaydin speech? Give the reason.
tasks.answer: No. It has two words, but they are joined by iḍāfa, not by predication: nothing is said of the servant, and the hearer is left waiting, so there is no complete benefit on which silence may follow.

tasks.prompt: How does the book answer one who says that yā Zaydu is speech made of a particle and a noun?
tasks.answer: The particle of the vocative stands in the place of the verb adʿū or aṭlubu, “I call”; so yā Zaydu is in truth a verb and a noun, and the rule stands.

quiz.prompt: The sign of the particle is that…
options: it takes no sign of the noun or the verb
quiz.explanation: It is neither told about nor told with.

quiz.prompt: Min means…
quiz.explanation: It shows it only with what follows.

quiz.prompt: In ḍarabtu bi-l-khashabati, the bāʾ links…
Speech must give…
options: a complete benefit on which silence may follow

quiz.prompt: Which is speech?
quiz.explanation: A verb and a noun with predication.

quiz.prompt: Speech comes only from…
options: two nouns, or a verb and a noun
quiz.explanation: Only there are the musnad and the musnad ilayhi together.

quiz.prompt: In yā Zaydu, yā stands for…
quiz.explanation: So the vocative does not break the rule.

text.original: وَحَدُّ الْحَرْفِ: كَلِمَةٌ لَا تَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي نَفْسِهَا، بَلْ تَدُلُّ عَلَى مَعْنًى فِي غَيْرِهَا، نَحْوُ: مِنْ؛ فَإِنَّ مَعْنَاهَا الِابْتِدَاءُ، وَهِيَ لَا تَدُلُّ عَلَيْهِ إِلَّا بَعْدَ ذِكْرِ مَا مِنْهُ الِابْتِدَاءُ، كَالْبَصْرَةِ وَالْكُوفَةِ مَثَلًا، تَقُولُ: سِرْتُ مِنَ الْبَصْرَةِ إِلَى الْكُوفَةِ. وَعَلَامَتُهُ أَنْ لَا يَصِحَّ الْإِخْبَارُ عَنْهُ وَلَا بِهِ، وَأَنْ لَا يَقْبَلَ عَلَامَاتِ الْأَسْمَاءِ وَلَا عَلَامَاتِ الْأَفْعَالِ.
text.en: The definition of the particle: a word that does not indicate a meaning in itself but indicates a meaning in something else, as min “from”: its meaning is the beginning, and it indicates it only after the mention of that from which the beginning is, such as Baṣra and Kūfa, for example; you say sirtu mina al-baṣrati ilā al-kūfati “I travelled from Baṣra to Kūfa”. Its sign is that it cannot rightly be told about nor told with, and that it does not accept the signs of the nouns nor the signs of the verbs.

text.original: وَلِلْحَرْفِ فِي كَلَامِ الْعَرَبِ فَوَائِدُ، كَالرَّبْطِ بَيْنَ الِاسْمَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ فِي الدَّارِ، وَالْفِعْلَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: أُرِيدُ أَنْ تَضْرِبَ، أَوِ اسْمٍ وَفِعْلٍ، كَضَرَبْتُ بِالْخَشَبَةِ، أَوِ الْجُمْلَتَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: إِنْ جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ أَكْرَمْتُهُ، وَغَيْرِ ذَلِكَ مِنَ الْفَوَائِدِ الَّتِي تَعْرِفُهَا فِي الْقِسْمِ الثَّالِثِ إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى. وَيُسَمَّى حَرْفًا لِوُقُوعِهِ فِي الْكَلَامِ حَرْفًا، أَيْ طَرَفًا؛ إِذْ لَيْسَ مَقْصُودًا بِالذَّاتِ مِثْلَ الْمُسْنَدِ وَالْمُسْنَدِ إِلَيْهِ.
text.en: The particle has uses in the speech of the Arabs, such as linking two nouns, as Zaydun fī al-dāri “Zayd is in the house”; two verbs, as urīdu an taḍriba “I want you to hit”; a noun and a verb, as ḍarabtu bi-al-khashabati “I hit with the stick”; or two sentences, as in jāʾanī Zaydun akramtuhu “if Zayd comes to me, I will honour him”; and other uses that you will learn in the third part, if God Most High wills. It is called ḥarf because it stands in speech as a ḥarf, that is, an edge; for it is not intended for itself, like the musnad and the musnad ilayhi (what is said and what it is said of).

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الْكَلَامُ لَفْظٌ تَضَمَّنَ كَلِمَتَيْنِ بِالْإِسْنَادِ، وَالْإِسْنَادُ نِسْبَةُ إِحْدَى الْكَلِمَتَيْنِ إِلَى الْأُخْرَى بِحَيْثُ تُفِيدُ الْمُخَاطَبَ فَائِدَةً تَامَّةً يَصِحُّ السُّكُوتُ عَلَيْهَا، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، وَقَامَ زَيْدٌ، وَيُسَمَّى جُمْلَةً. فَعُلِمَ أَنَّ الْكَلَامَ لَا يَحْصُلُ إِلَّا مِنِ اسْمَيْنِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، وَيُسَمَّى جُمْلَةً اسْمِيَّةً، أَوْ مِنْ فِعْلٍ وَاسْمٍ، نَحْوُ: قَامَ زَيْدٌ، وَيُسَمَّى جُمْلَةً فِعْلِيَّةً؛ إِذْ لَا يُوجَدُ الْمُسْنَدُ وَالْمُسْنَدُ إِلَيْهِ مَعًا فِي غَيْرِهِمَا، وَلَا بُدَّ لِلْكَلَامِ مِنْهُمَا.
text.en: Section. Speech (kalām) is an utterance that contains two words by predication (isnād). Predication is the relating of one of the two words to the other in such a way that it gives the one addressed a complete benefit on which silence may rightly follow, as Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is standing” and qāma Zaydun “Zayd stood”; and it is called a sentence (jumla). So it is known that speech comes about only from two nouns, as Zaydun qāʾimun, and this is called a nominal sentence (jumla ismiyya), or from a verb and a noun, as qāma Zaydun, and this is called a verbal sentence (jumla fiʿliyya); for the musnad and the musnad ilayhi are not found together in anything else, and speech cannot do without them.

text.original: فَإِنْ قِيلَ: قَدْ نُوقِضَ بِالنِّدَاءِ، نَحْوُ: يَا زَيْدُ، قُلْنَا: حَرْفُ النِّدَاءِ قَائِمٌ مَقَامَ أَدْعُو وَأَطْلُبُ، وَهُوَ الْفِعْلُ، فَلَا نَقْضَ عَلَيْهِ. وَإِذَا فَرَغْنَا مِنَ الْمُقَدِّمَةِ فَلْنَشْرَعْ فِي الْأَقْسَامِ الثَّلَاثَةِ، وَاللَّهُ الْمُوَفِّقُ وَالْمُعِينُ.
text.en: If it is said: this is broken by the vocative, as yā Zaydu “O Zayd!”, we say: the particle of the vocative stands in the place of adʿū “I call” and aṭlubu “I seek”, which is the verb; so it is not broken by it. Now that we have finished the introduction, let us begin the three parts; God is the one who grants success and help.

parts.title: The inflected noun: iʿrāb and the diptote

lessons.title: The inflected noun; iʿrāb, the governor and its place
body: The first part is on the noun, which divides into the inflected (muʿrab) and the built (mabnī). The book treats it in two chapters and a conclusion; the first chapter, on the muʿrab, has an introduction, three aims (the marfūʿ, the manṣūb and the majrūr) and a conclusion on the followers. This is the Kāfiya's plan, and it is worth learning, for it is the map of the next forty lessons.

The inflected noun is “every noun that is put together with another and does not resemble what is mabnī in origin”, which is “the particle, the imperative to the one present and the past”. Two conditions. It must stand in a construction: Zaydun counted out alone is not yet muʿrab. And it must not resemble those built words: hāʾulāʾi in qāma hāʾulāʾi is in a construction, but it resembles the particle, so it is built. Such a noun is called mutamakkin, “firmly established” in being a noun.

Its rule is “that its end differs with the difference of the governors”, either audibly, jāʾanī Zaydun, raʾaytu Zaydan, marartu bi-Zaydin, or by implication, jāʾanī Mūsā, raʾaytu Mūsā, marartu bi-Mūsā, where the alif cannot show the vowel. Iʿrāb is “that by which the end differs”: the ḍamma, fatḥa and kasra, the wāw, alif and yāʾ.

The iʿrāb of the noun is of three kinds, rafʿ, naṣb and jarr. The governor (ʿāmil) is “that by which a word is put in rafʿ, naṣb or jarr”, and the place of iʿrāb is the last letter. In qāma Zaydun the book names all four: qāma is the governor, Zaydun the inflected word, the ḍamma the iʿrāb, and the dāl the place. A student who can name these four in any sentence has learned the language of parsing.

Last, “nothing is inflected in the speech of the Arabs but the firmly established noun and the muḍāriʿ verb”. Every particle, every past verb and every imperative is built; the muḍāriʿ's iʿrāb comes in the second part.

terms.en: the firmly established noun: the muʿrab
built in origin: the particle, the imperative, the past
the governor, by which a word is put in rafʿ, naṣb or jarr
the place of iʿrāb: the last letter

examples.en: hāʾulāʾi resembles the particle: built

examples.arabic: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ، وَرَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا، وَمَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ
examples.en: the end differs audibly

examples.arabic: جَاءَنِي مُوسَى، وَرَأَيْتُ مُوسَى، وَمَرَرْتُ بِمُوسَى
examples.en: the end differs by implication
the governor, the inflected word, the iʿrāb and its place

head: Name

tasks.prompt: Why is Zaydun muʿrab in qāma Zaydun, while hāʾulāʾi in qāma hāʾulāʾi is not?
tasks.answer: Both stand in a construction. But hāʾulāʾi resembles what is built in origin (the particle), so it is built; Zaydun resembles none of them, so it is muʿrab.

tasks.prompt: Name the governor, the inflected word, the iʿrāb and its place in raʾaytu Zaydan.
tasks.answer: The governor is raʾaytu; the inflected word is Zaydan; the iʿrāb is the fatḥa (naṣb); its place is the dāl, the last letter.

tasks.prompt: In jāʾanī Mūsā, what is the iʿrāb of Mūsā and why is it not seen?
tasks.answer: Mūsā is the fāʿil, in rafʿ, but the ḍamma is implied: the word ends in an alif, which cannot carry a vowel. Its end differs by implication, not audibly.

tasks.prompt: Which two kinds of word alone are inflected in Arabic?
tasks.answer: The firmly established noun and the muḍāriʿ verb. Every other word is built.

quiz.prompt: The first chapter of the part on the noun is on…
quiz.explanation: With an introduction, three aims and a conclusion.

quiz.prompt: Which is built in origin, in this book?
quiz.explanation: With the particle and the imperative to the one present.

quiz.prompt: Zaydun, counted out alone, is…
options: not yet muʿrab: it is in no construction
quiz.explanation: The inflected noun must be put together with another word.

quiz.prompt: The muʿrab noun is also called…
In jāʾanī Mūsā the end differs…
quiz.explanation: The alif cannot show the vowel.

quiz.prompt: The place of iʿrāb in a noun is…
Which is inflected in Arabic?

text.original: وَقَدْ مَرَّ تَعْرِيفُهُ، وَهُوَ يَنْقَسِمُ إِلَى الْمُعْرَبِ وَالْمَبْنِيِّ، فَلْنَذْكُرْ أَحْكَامَهُ فِي بَابَيْنِ وَخَاتِمَةٍ. الْبَابُ الْأَوَّلُ فِي الِاسْمِ الْمُعْرَبِ، وَفِيهِ مُقَدِّمَةٌ وَثَلَاثَةُ مَقَاصِدَ وَخَاتِمَةٌ. أَمَّا الْمُقَدِّمَةُ فَفِيهَا فُصُولٌ.
text.en: Its definition has passed. It divides into the inflected (muʿrab) and the fixed (mabnī); so let us mention its rules in two chapters and a conclusion. The first chapter, on the inflected noun: it has an introduction, three aims and a conclusion. The introduction has [several] sections.

text.original: فَصْلٌ فِي تَعْرِيفِ الِاسْمِ الْمُعْرَبِ: وَهُوَ كُلُّ اسْمٍ رُكِّبَ مَعَ غَيْرِهِ وَلَا يُشْبِهُ مَبْنِيَّ الْأَصْلِ، أَعْنِي الْحَرْفَ وَالْأَمْرَ الْحَاضِرَ وَالْمَاضِيَ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ، فِي: قَامَ زَيْدٌ، لَا زَيْدٌ وَحْدَهُ لِعَدَمِ التَّرْكِيبِ، وَلَا هَؤُلَاءِ، فِي: قَامَ هَؤُلَاءِ، لِوُجُودِ الشَّبَهِ، وَيُسَمَّى مُتَمَكِّنًا.
text.en: Section on the definition of the inflected noun. It is every noun that is put together with another [word] and does not resemble what is mabnī in origin — I mean the particle, the imperative to the one present and the past —, as Zaydun in qāma Zaydun “Zayd stood”; not Zaydun alone, because there is no putting together; and not hāʾulāʾi “these” in qāma hāʾulāʾi “these stood”, because of the resemblance. It is called mutamakkin (firmly established).

text.original: فَصْلٌ: حُكْمُهُ أَنْ يَخْتَلِفَ آخِرُهُ بِاخْتِلَافِ الْعَوَامِلِ اخْتِلَافًا لَفْظِيًّا، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ، وَرَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا، وَمَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ، أَوْ تَقْدِيرِيًّا، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي مُوسَى، وَرَأَيْتُ مُوسَى، وَمَرَرْتُ بِمُوسَى. الْإِعْرَابُ مَا بِهِ يَخْتَلِفُ آخِرُ الْمُعْرَبِ، كَالضَّمَّةِ وَالْفَتْحَةِ وَالْكَسْرَةِ وَالْوَاوِ وَالْأَلِفِ وَالْيَاءِ.
text.en: Section. Its rule is that its end differs with the difference of the governors, audibly, as jāʾanī Zaydun “Zayd came to me”, raʾaytu Zaydan “I saw Zayd” and marartu bi-Zaydin “I passed by Zayd”, or by implication, as jāʾanī Mūsā “Mūsā came to me”, raʾaytu Mūsā “I saw Mūsā” and marartu bi-Mūsā “I passed by Mūsā”. Iʿrāb is that by which the end of the inflected word differs, such as the ḍamma, the fatḥa, the kasra, the wāw, the alif and the yāʾ.

text.original: وَإِعْرَابُ الِاسْمِ عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَنْوَاعٍ: رَفْعٌ وَنَصْبٌ وَجَرٌّ. وَالْعَامِلُ مَا بِهِ يُرْفَعُ أَوْ يُنْصَبُ أَوْ يُجَرُّ. وَمَحَلُّ الْإِعْرَابِ مِنَ الِاسْمِ هُوَ الْحَرْفُ الْأَخِيرُ. مِثَالُ الْكُلِّ نَحْوُ: قَامَ زَيْدٌ؛ فَقَامَ عَامِلٌ، وَزَيْدٌ مُعْرَبٌ، وَالضَّمَّةُ إِعْرَابٌ، وَالدَّالُ مَحَلُّ الْإِعْرَابِ. وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ لَا يُعْرَبُ فِي كَلَامِ الْعَرَبِ إِلَّا الِاسْمُ الْمُتَمَكِّنُ وَالْفِعْلُ الْمُضَارِعُ، وَسَيَجِيءُ حُكْمُهُ فِي الْقِسْمِ الثَّانِي إِنْ شَاءَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى.
text.en: The iʿrāb of the noun is of three kinds: rafʿ, naṣb and jarr. The governor (ʿāmil) is that by which [a word] is put in rafʿ, naṣb or jarr. The place of the iʿrāb in the noun is the last letter. An example of them all is qāma Zaydun “Zayd stood”: qāma is the governor, Zaydun the inflected word, the ḍamma the iʿrāb and the dāl the place of the iʿrāb. Know that in the speech of the Arabs nothing is inflected but the firmly established noun and the muḍāriʿ verb; its rule will come in the second part, if God Most High wills.

lessons.title: The kinds of the noun's iʿrāb, one to four
body: The noun's iʿrāb comes in nine kinds (aṣnāf): nine sets of signs, each belonging to a class of nouns. To parse a noun, a student must first know its class, and then he knows its signs. The first kind is the plainest: rafʿ by the ḍamma, naṣb by the fatḥa, jarr by the kasra. It belongs to the singular that is munṣarif and sound, “one that has no weak letter at its end”, as Zayd; to “what runs like the sound”, a word ending in wāw or yāʾ after a sukūn, as dalw, “bucket”, and ẓaby, “gazelle”; and to the munṣarif broken plural, rijāl.

Why do dalw and ẓaby take all three vowels, when a word like al-qāḍī does not? Because the wāw and yāʾ come after a sukūn: they are spoken as firmly as any consonant, and a vowel on them is not heavy. A weak letter after a vowel is another matter (lesson 6).

The second kind: rafʿ by the ḍamma, naṣb and jarr by the kasra. It belongs to the sound feminine plural: hunna muslimātun, raʾaytu muslimātin, marartu bi-muslimātin. The third: rafʿ by the ḍamma, naṣb and jarr by the fatḥa, for the diptote (ghayr al-munṣarif): jāʾanī ʿUmaru, raʾaytu ʿUmara, marartu bi-ʿUmara. Each takes only two vowels for three states, but in opposite directions.

The fourth: rafʿ by the wāw, naṣb by the alif, jarr by the yāʾ. It belongs to the six nouns, on three conditions: not diminutives, singular, and muḍāf to something other than the yāʾ of the speaker. They are akhūka, abūka, hanūka, ḥamūki (her father-in-law, which is why the kāf is feminine), fūka and dhū mālin: jāʾanī akhūka, raʾaytu akhāka, marartu bi-akhīka. Break a condition and the letters go: ubayy, a diminutive, and akhawāni, a dual, take other signs, and abī, “my father”, takes none.

terms.en: the singular, fully declined, with no weak letter at its end
what runs like the sound: wāw or yāʾ after a sukūn
the diptote: the fatḥa for naṣb and jarr
the six nouns, with wāw, alif and yāʾ

tasks.prompt: Give the class of each noun and its sign in the state shown: raʾaytu ẓabyan; marartu bi-muslimātin; raʾaytu ʿUmara; jāʾanī abūka.
tasks.arabic: رَأَيْتُ ظَبْيًا — مَرَرْتُ بِمُسْلِمَاتٍ — رَأَيْتُ عُمَرَ — جَاءَنِي أَبُوكَ
tasks.answer: Ẓabyan: runs like the sound (yāʾ after sukūn), naṣb by the fatḥa. Muslimātin: sound feminine plural, jarr by the kasra. ʿUmara: diptote, naṣb by the fatḥa. Abūka: one of the six nouns, rafʿ by the wāw.

tasks.prompt: Why does dalw take all three vowels?
tasks.answer: Its wāw comes after a sukūn, so it runs like a sound letter and a vowel on it is not heavy. Such a noun takes the first kind of iʿrāb, like Zayd.

tasks.prompt: Name the six nouns as the book gives them, and their three conditions.
tasks.answer: Akhūka, abūka, hanūka, ḥamūki, fūka and dhū mālin. They must not be diminutives, must be singular, and must be muḍāf to something other than the yāʾ of the speaker.

tasks.prompt: Compare the sound feminine plural and the diptote.
tasks.answer: Both have only two signs for three states. The sound feminine plural takes the ḍamma in rafʿ and the kasra in naṣb and jarr; the diptote takes the ḍamma in rafʿ and the fatḥa in naṣb and jarr.

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of iʿrāb of the noun does the book count?
Ẓaby takes the first kind because…
options: its yāʾ comes after a sukūn

quiz.prompt: The sound feminine plural in naṣb takes…
ʿUmar in jarr takes…
quiz.explanation: It is a diptote: marartu bi-ʿUmara.

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT one of the six nouns?
quiz.explanation: Akh, ab, han, ḥam, fam, dhū.

quiz.prompt: Ḥamūki has a feminine kāf because ḥam is…
quiz.explanation: The husband's kin of a wife.

quiz.prompt: In raʾaytu akhāka, the sign of naṣb is…
quiz.explanation: The six nouns: wāw, alif, yāʾ.

text.original: فَصْلٌ فِي أَصْنَافِ إِعْرَابِ الِاسْمِ، وَهِيَ تِسْعَةُ أَصْنَافٍ: الْأَوَّلُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّفْعُ بِالضَّمَّةِ، وَالنَّصْبُ بِالْفَتْحَةِ، وَالْجَرُّ بِالْكَسْرَةِ، وَيَخْتَصُّ بِالْمُفْرَدِ الْمُنْصَرِفِ الصَّحِيحِ، وَهُوَ عِنْدَ النُّحَاةِ مَا لَا يَكُونُ فِي آخِرِهِ حَرْفُ عِلَّةٍ، كَزَيْدٍ، وَبِالْجَارِي مَجْرَى الصَّحِيحِ، وَهُوَ مَا يَكُونُ فِي آخِرِهِ وَاوٌ أَوْ يَاءٌ مَا قَبْلَهُمَا سَاكِنٌ، كَدَلْوٍ وَظَبْيٍ، وَبِالْجَمْعِ الْمُكَسَّرِ الْمُنْصَرِفِ، كَرِجَالٍ.
text.en: Section on the kinds of the iʿrāb of the noun. They are nine kinds. The first: that rafʿ is by the ḍamma, naṣb by the fatḥa and jarr by the kasra. It belongs to the singular that is munṣarif (fully declined) and sound — which with the grammarians is one that has no weak letter at its end, as Zaydin —; to what runs like the sound, which is one that has at its end a wāw or a yāʾ with an unvowelled letter before them, as dalwin “a bucket” and ẓabyin “a gazelle”; and to the broken plural that is munṣarif, as rijālin “men”.

text.original: تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ وَدَلْوٌ وَظَبْيٌ وَرِجَالٌ، وَرَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا وَدَلْوًا وَظَبْيًا وَرِجَالًا، وَمَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ وَدَلْوٍ وَظَبْيٍ وَرِجَالٍ. الثَّانِي أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّفْعُ بِالضَّمَّةِ، وَالنَّصْبُ وَالْجَرُّ بِالْكَسْرَةِ، وَيَخْتَصُّ بِجَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ، تَقُولُ: هُنَّ مُسْلِمَاتٌ، وَرَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمَاتٍ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِمُسْلِمَاتٍ.
text.en: You say jāʾanī Zaydun wa-dalwun wa-ẓabyun wa-rijālun “Zayd, a bucket, a gazelle and men came to me”, raʾaytu Zaydan wa-dalwan wa-ẓabyan wa-rijālan “I saw Zayd, a bucket, a gazelle and men” and marartu bi-Zaydin wa-dalwin wa-ẓabyin wa-rijālin “I passed by Zayd, a bucket, a gazelle and men”. The second: that rafʿ is by the ḍamma, and naṣb and jarr by the kasra. It belongs to the sound feminine plural; you say hunna muslimātun “they are Muslim women”, raʾaytu muslimātin “I saw Muslim women” and marartu bi-muslimātin “I passed by Muslim women”.

text.original: الثَّالِثُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّفْعُ بِالضَّمَّةِ، وَالنَّصْبُ وَالْجَرُّ بِالْفَتْحَةِ، وَيَخْتَصُّ بِغَيْرِ الْمُنْصَرِفِ، كَعُمَرَ، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي عُمَرُ، وَرَأَيْتُ عُمَرَ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِعُمَرَ.
text.en: The third: that rafʿ is by the ḍamma, and naṣb and jarr by the fatḥa. It belongs to the diptote (ghayr al-munṣarif), as ʿUmara; you say jāʾanī ʿUmaru “ʿUmar came to me”, raʾaytu ʿUmara “I saw ʿUmar” and marartu bi-ʿUmara “I passed by ʿUmar”.

text.original: الرَّابِعُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّفْعُ بِالْوَاوِ، وَالنَّصْبُ بِالْأَلِفِ، وَالْجَرُّ بِالْيَاءِ، وَيَخْتَصُّ بِالْأَسْمَاءِ السِّتَّةِ مُكَبَّرَةً مُوَحَّدَةً مُضَافَةً إِلَى غَيْرِ يَاءِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ، وَهِيَ: أَخُوكَ، وَأَبُوكَ، وَهَنُوكَ، وَحَمُوكِ، وَفُوكَ، وَذُو مَالٍ، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي أَخُوكَ، وَرَأَيْتُ أَخَاكَ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِأَخِيكَ، وَكَذَلِكَ الْبَوَاقِي.
text.en: The fourth: that rafʿ is by the wāw, naṣb by the alif and jarr by the yāʾ. It belongs to the six nouns when they are not diminutives, singular, and muḍāf to something other than the yāʾ of the speaker. They are akhūka “your brother”, abūka “your father”, hanūka “your thing”, ḥamūki “your (f.) father-in-law”, fūka “your mouth” and dhū mālin “possessor of wealth”; you say jāʾanī akhūka “your brother came to me”, raʾaytu akhāka “I saw your brother” and marartu bi-akhīka “I passed by your brother”; and likewise the rest.

lessons.title: The kinds of iʿrāb, five to nine: dual, plural, implied signs
body: The fifth kind: rafʿ by the alif, naṣb and jarr by “the yāʾ with a fatḥa before it”. It belongs to the dual, to kilā muḍāf to a pronoun, and to ithnāni and ithnatāni: jāʾanī al-rajulāni kilāhumā, raʾaytu al-rajulayni kilayhimā. The sixth: rafʿ by the wāw with a ḍamma before it, naṣb and jarr by the yāʾ with a kasra before it, for the sound masculine plural, for ulū, and for ʿishrūna and its sisters: muslimūna, muslimīna. Notice how the vowel before the yāʾ tells the dual from the plural in naṣb and jarr: muslimayni, two; muslimīna, many.

The nūn of the dual “always has a kasra”, and the nūn of the sound plural “always has a fatḥa”, and both drop in iḍāfa: jāʾanī ghulāmā Zaydin, muslimū Miṣra. In an unvowelled book this is how a reader recognises a dual or plural in iḍāfa: it has lost its nūn.

The seventh kind has all its signs implied: rafʿ by an implied ḍamma, naṣb by an implied fatḥa, jarr by an implied kasra. It belongs to the maqṣūr, a noun ending in a short alif, ʿaṣan, “a stick”, and to a noun muḍāf to the yāʾ of the speaker, except the sound masculine plural: ghulāmī. Hādhā ʿaṣan wa-ghulāmī, raʾaytu ʿaṣan wa-ghulāmī, marartu bi-ʿaṣan wa-ghulāmī: the words never change.

The eighth: rafʿ and jarr implied, naṣb by the fatḥa “audibly”. It belongs to the manqūṣ, a noun ending in a yāʾ with a kasra before it: jāʾanī al-qāḍī, raʾaytu al-qāḍiya, marartu bi-l-qāḍī. The light fatḥa can be spoken on the yāʾ; the ḍamma and kasra are heavy there and are left unsaid.

The ninth: rafʿ by an implied wāw, naṣb and jarr by the yāʾ audibly, for the sound masculine plural muḍāf to the yāʾ of the speaker: jāʾanī muslimiyya. The book shows how the form came about: the origin is muslimūya; “the wāw and the yāʾ came together, the first of them unvowelled, so the wāw was turned into a yāʾ, the yāʾ was assimilated into the yāʾ, and the ḍamma was replaced by a kasra to suit the yāʾ”. This is a rule of ṣarf at work inside a rule of naḥw.

terms.en: the dual: alif in rafʿ, yāʾ with fatḥa before it in naṣb and jarr
the sound masculine plural: wāw, and yāʾ with kasra before it
a noun ending in a short alif: all signs implied
a noun ending in yāʾ after kasra: rafʿ and jarr implied

examples.en: the dual and kilā with a pronoun
the nūn dropped in iḍāfa
all signs implied

examples.arabic: جَاءَنِي الْقَاضِي، وَرَأَيْتُ الْقَاضِيَ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِالْقَاضِي
examples.en: the manqūṣ: naṣb audible
rafʿ by an implied wāw: muslimūya

tasks.prompt: Tell the dual from the plural and give the state: muslimayni; muslimīna; muslimū Miṣra.
tasks.answer: Muslimayni: dual (fatḥa before the yāʾ, kasra on the nūn), naṣb or jarr. Muslimīna: sound plural (kasra before the yāʾ, fatḥa on the nūn), naṣb or jarr. Muslimū Miṣra: sound plural in rafʿ, its nūn dropped in iḍāfa.

tasks.prompt: Give the iʿrāb of ʿaṣan in raʾaytu ʿaṣan and of al-qāḍī in raʾaytu al-qāḍiya.
tasks.answer: ʿAṣan is the object, in naṣb by an implied fatḥa: it is maqṣūr, and all its signs are implied. Al-qāḍiya is the object, in naṣb by the fatḥa spoken on the yāʾ: in the manqūṣ the naṣb is audible.

tasks.prompt: Explain, as the book does, how muslimūya became muslimiyya.
tasks.answer: The wāw (of the plural) and the yāʾ (of the speaker) met, the first unvowelled; the wāw was turned into a yāʾ and merged into the yāʾ, and the ḍamma before it became a kasra to suit the yāʾ: muslimiyya.

tasks.prompt: Why is ghulāmī the same in all three states?
tasks.answer: It is muḍāf to the yāʾ of the speaker, which needs a kasra before it. That kasra takes the place of every sign, so all three are implied: the seventh kind.

quiz.prompt: The dual in naṣb takes…
options: the yāʾ with a kasra before it
the yāʾ with a fatḥa before it

quiz.prompt: Kilā has the dual's signs when it is muḍāf to…
The nūn of the sound plural always has…
quiz.explanation: The nūn of the dual always has a kasra.

quiz.prompt: In jāʾanī ghulāmā Zaydin the nūn of the dual is…
ʿAṣan in hādhā ʿaṣan is in rafʿ by…
quiz.explanation: The maqṣūr: all its signs implied.

quiz.prompt: Which state of the manqūṣ is audible?
In jāʾanī muslimiyya the rafʿ is by…

text.original: الْخَامِسُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّفْعُ بِالْأَلِفِ، وَالنَّصْبُ وَالْجَرُّ بِالْيَاءِ الْمَفْتُوحِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، وَيَخْتَصُّ بِالْمُثَنَّى، وَكِلَا مُضَافًا إِلَى مُضْمَرٍ، وَاثْنَانِ وَاثْنَتَانِ، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي الرَّجُلَانِ كِلَاهُمَا، وَاثْنَانِ وَاثْنَتَانِ، وَرَأَيْتُ الرَّجُلَيْنِ كِلَيْهِمَا، وَاثْنَيْنِ وَاثْنَتَيْنِ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِالرَّجُلَيْنِ كِلَيْهِمَا، وَاثْنَيْنِ وَاثْنَتَيْنِ.
text.en: The fifth: that rafʿ is by the alif, and naṣb and jarr by the yāʾ with a fatḥa before it. It belongs to the dual, to kilā “both” muḍāf to a pronoun, and to ithnāni and ithnatāni “two (m., f.)”; you say jāʾanī al-rajulāni kilāhumā “the two men came to me, both of them”, and wa-ithnāni wa-ithnatāni “and two (m.) and two (f.)”; raʾaytu al-rajulayni kilayhimā “I saw the two men, both of them”, and wa-ithnayni wa-ithnatayni; and marartu bi-al-rajulayni kilayhimā “I passed by the two men, both of them”, and wa-ithnayni wa-ithnatayni.

text.original: السَّادِسُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّفْعُ بِالْوَاوِ الْمَضْمُومِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، وَالنَّصْبُ وَالْجَرُّ بِالْيَاءِ الْمَكْسُورِ مَا قَبْلَهَا، وَيَخْتَصُّ بِجَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ، نَحْوُ: مُسْلِمُونَ، وَأُولُو، وَعِشْرُونَ مَعَ أَخَوَاتِهَا، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي مُسْلِمُونَ وَعِشْرُونَ وَأُولُو مَالٍ، وَرَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمِينَ وَعِشْرِينَ وَأُولِي مَالٍ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِمُسْلِمِينَ وَعِشْرِينَ وَأُولِي مَالٍ.
text.en: The sixth: that rafʿ is by the wāw with a ḍamma before it, and naṣb and jarr by the yāʾ with a kasra before it. It belongs to the sound masculine plural, as muslimūna “Muslims”, to ulū “possessors” and to ʿishrūna “twenty” with its sisters; you say jāʾanī muslimūna wa-ʿishrūna wa-ulū mālin “Muslims, twenty [men] and men of wealth came to me”, raʾaytu muslimīna wa-ʿishrīna wa-ulī mālin “I saw Muslims, twenty [men] and men of wealth” and marartu bi-muslimīna wa-ʿishrīna wa-ulī mālin “I passed by Muslims, twenty [men] and men of wealth”.

text.original: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ نُونَ التَّثْنِيَةِ مَكْسُورَةٌ أَبَدًا، وَنُونَ جَمْعِ السَّلَامَةِ مَفْتُوحَةٌ أَبَدًا، وَكِلَاهُمَا تَسْقُطَانِ عِنْدَ الْإِضَافَةِ، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي غُلَامَا زَيْدٍ، وَمُسْلِمُو مِصْرَ.
text.en: Know that the nūn of the dual always has a kasra and the nūn of the sound plural always has a fatḥa, and both drop in iḍāfa; you say jāʾanī ghulāmā Zaydin “Zayd's two servants came to me” wa-muslimū Miṣra “and the Muslims of Egypt”.

text.original: السَّابِعُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّفْعُ بِتَقْدِيرِ الضَّمَّةِ، وَالنَّصْبُ بِتَقْدِيرِ الْفَتْحَةِ، وَالْجَرُّ بِتَقْدِيرِ الْكَسْرَةِ، وَيَخْتَصُّ بِالْمَقْصُورِ، وَهُوَ مَا فِي آخِرِهِ أَلِفٌ مَقْصُورَةٌ، كَعَصًا، وَبِالْمُضَافِ إِلَى يَاءِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ غَيْرِ جَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ، كَغُلَامِي، تَقُولُ: هَذَا عَصًا وَغُلَامِي، وَرَأَيْتُ عَصًا وَغُلَامِي، وَمَرَرْتُ بِعَصًا وَغُلَامِي.
text.en: The seventh: that rafʿ is by an implied ḍamma, naṣb by an implied fatḥa and jarr by an implied kasra. It belongs to the maqṣūr, which is one that has a short alif (alif maqṣūra) at its end, as ʿaṣan “a stick”, and to what is muḍāf to the yāʾ of the speaker, other than the sound masculine plural, as ghulāmī “my servant”; you say hādhā ʿaṣan wa-ghulāmī “this is a stick, and my servant”, raʾaytu ʿaṣan wa-ghulāmī “I saw a stick and my servant” and marartu bi-ʿaṣan wa-ghulāmī “I passed by a stick and my servant”.

text.original: الثَّامِنُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّفْعُ بِتَقْدِيرِ الضَّمَّةِ، وَالْجَرُّ بِتَقْدِيرِ الْكَسْرَةِ، وَالنَّصْبُ بِالْفَتْحَةِ لَفْظًا، وَيَخْتَصُّ بِالْمَنْقُوصِ، وَهُوَ مَا فِي آخِرِهِ يَاءٌ مَا قَبْلَهَا مَكْسُورٌ، كَالْقَاضِي، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي الْقَاضِي، وَرَأَيْتُ الْقَاضِيَ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِالْقَاضِي.
text.en: The eighth: that rafʿ is by an implied ḍamma, jarr by an implied kasra, and naṣb by the fatḥa audibly. It belongs to the manqūṣ, which is one that has at its end a yāʾ with a kasra before it, as al-qāḍī “the judge”; you say jāʾanī al-qāḍī “the judge came to me”, raʾaytu al-qāḍiya “I saw the judge” and marartu bi-al-qāḍī “I passed by the judge”.

text.original: التَّاسِعُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الرَّفْعُ بِتَقْدِيرِ الْوَاوِ، وَالنَّصْبُ وَالْجَرُّ بِالْيَاءِ لَفْظًا، وَيَخْتَصُّ بِجَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ السَّالِمِ مُضَافًا إِلَى يَاءِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي مُسْلِمِيَّ، تَقْدِيرُهُ مُسْلِمُويَ، اجْتَمَعَتِ الْوَاوُ وَالْيَاءُ وَالْأُولَى مِنْهُمَا سَاكِنَةٌ، فَقُلِبَتِ الْوَاوُ يَاءً، وَأُدْغِمَتِ الْيَاءُ فِي الْيَاءِ، وَأُبْدِلَتِ الضَّمَّةُ بِالْكَسْرَةِ لِمُنَاسَبَةِ الْيَاءِ، فَصَارَ مُسْلِمِيَّ، وَرَأَيْتُ مُسْلِمِيَّ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِمُسْلِمِيَّ.
text.en: The ninth: that rafʿ is by an implied wāw, and naṣb and jarr by the yāʾ audibly. It belongs to the sound masculine plural muḍāf to the yāʾ of the speaker; you say jāʾanī muslimiyya “my Muslims came to me”, which is in its underlying form muslimūya: the wāw and the yāʾ came together, the first of them unvowelled, so the wāw was turned into a yāʾ, the yāʾ was assimilated into the yāʾ, and the ḍamma was replaced by a kasra to suit the yāʾ, and it became muslimiyya; and raʾaytu muslimiyya “I saw my Muslims” and marartu bi-muslimiyya “I passed by my Muslims”.

lessons.title: The munṣarif and the diptote; ʿadl, the adjective, the feminine
body: The inflected noun is of two kinds. The munṣarif, fully declined, “in which there are not two of the nine causes, nor one that stands in the place of two”, as Zayd; it takes the three vowels with tanwīn. The diptote (ghayr munṣarif) has two causes, or one that stands for two; “the kasra and the tanwīn do not come into it”, and in jarr it has the fatḥa: jāʾanī Aḥmadu, raʾaytu Aḥmada, marartu bi-Aḥmada. The nine causes are ʿadl, being an adjective, the feminine, definiteness, being foreign, the plural, compounding, the added alif and nūn, and the pattern of the verb; students learn them by heart in a short verse.

ʿAdl is “the change of the word from its original form to another form, really or by supposition”. It meets being a proper name, as in ʿUmar and Zufar, and being an adjective, as in thulāth and mathlath, “three by three”, ukhar and jumaʿ; it never meets the pattern of the verb. The commentators explain “by supposition”: in ʿUmar no original form is heard, but the Arabs treat it as a diptote, so a change from ʿĀmir is supposed; in thulāth the change from thalāthatan thalāthatan is real.

Being an adjective never meets being a proper name, and it counts only if the word was an adjective “in its original laying down”. So aswad, “black”, and arqam, “speckled”, stay diptotes even when they become names for the snake, while arbaʿ in marartu bi-niswatin arbaʿin, “four women”, is declined, though it is an adjective on the verb's pattern: it was laid down as a number, not as an adjective.

The feminine with the tāʾ counts only in a proper name, as Ṭalḥa; so too the feminine by meaning, with no tāʾ written. A feminine by meaning that is triliteral, with a sukūn in the middle and not foreign, may be declined or not, “because of its lightness”: Hind. Otherwise it must be a diptote: Zaynab, with four letters; Saqar, with a vowel in the middle; Māh and Jūr, foreign names.

The feminine with an alif, short as in ḥublā or long as in ḥamrāʾ, is never declined, “because the alif stands in the place of two causes: the feminine and its being fixed to the word”. A tāʾ can be taken off (qāʾim, qāʾima); the alif of ḥublā cannot.

the change of a word from its original form
being an adjective in the original laying down

tasks.prompt: Name the two causes of each diptote: ʿUmar; Ṭalḥa; Zaynab; ukhar.
tasks.answer: ʿUmar: ʿadl and being a proper name. Ṭalḥa: the feminine (with the tāʾ) and being a proper name. Zaynab: the feminine (by meaning) and being a proper name. Ukhar: ʿadl and being an adjective.

tasks.prompt: Why is aswad a diptote even as a name for the snake, while arbaʿ in niswatin arbaʿin is declined?
tasks.answer: Aswad was laid down as an adjective, “black”, and keeps that cause with the pattern of the verb. Arbaʿ was laid down as a number; its use as an adjective is not original, so it has only one cause, the pattern, and is declined.

tasks.prompt: Why may Hind be declined, but not Saqar?
tasks.answer: Both are proper names and feminine by meaning. Hind is triliteral with a sukūn in the middle and not foreign: it is light, so either is allowed. Saqar has a vowel in the middle, so it must be a diptote.

tasks.prompt: How does one alif stand for two causes in ḥublā?
tasks.answer: The alif marks the feminine, and it is fixed to the word: it can never be taken off as a tāʾ can. The feminine and its fixedness count as two causes.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الِاسْمُ الْمُعْرَبُ عَلَى نَوْعَيْنِ: مُنْصَرِفٌ، وَهُوَ مَا لَيْسَ فِيهِ سَبَبَانِ، أَوْ وَاحِدٌ يَقُومُ مَقَامَهُمَا، مِنَ الْأَسْبَابِ التِّسْعَةِ، كَزَيْدٍ، وَيُسَمَّى الِاسْمَ الْمُتَمَكِّنَ، وَحُكْمُهُ أَنْ يَدْخُلَهُ الْحَرَكَاتُ الثَّلَاثُ مَعَ التَّنْوِينِ، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ، وَرَأَيْتُ زَيْدًا، وَمَرَرْتُ بِزَيْدٍ.
text.en: Section. The inflected noun is of two kinds. Munṣarif (fully declined), which is one in which there are not two of the nine causes, nor one that stands in the place of two, as Zaydin. It is called the firmly established noun, and its rule is that the three vowels come into it with the tanwīn; you say jāʾanī Zaydun “Zayd came to me”, raʾaytu Zaydan “I saw Zayd” and marartu bi-Zaydin “I passed by Zayd”.

text.original: وَغَيْرُ مُنْصَرِفٍ، وَهُوَ مَا فِيهِ سَبَبَانِ، أَوْ وَاحِدٌ مِنْهَا يَقُومُ مَقَامَهُمَا. وَالْأَسْبَابُ التِّسْعَةُ هِيَ: الْعَدْلُ، وَالْوَصْفُ، وَالتَّأْنِيثُ، وَالْمَعْرِفَةُ، وَالْعُجْمَةُ، وَالْجَمْعُ، وَالتَّرْكِيبُ، وَالْأَلِفُ وَالنُّونُ الزَّائِدَتَانِ، وَوَزْنُ الْفِعْلِ. وَحُكْمُهُ أَنْ لَا يَدْخُلَهُ الْكَسْرَةُ وَالتَّنْوِينُ، وَيَكُونَ فِي مَوْضِعِ الْجَرِّ مَفْتُوحًا أَبَدًا، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي أَحْمَدُ، وَرَأَيْتُ أَحْمَدَ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِأَحْمَدَ.
text.en: And ghayr munṣarif (the diptote), which is one in which there are two causes, or one of them that stands in the place of two. The nine causes are: ʿadl (change from an original form), being an adjective (waṣf), the feminine (taʾnīth), definiteness (maʿrifa), being foreign (ʿujma), the plural (jamʿ), compounding (tarkīb), the added alif and nūn, and the pattern of the verb. Its rule is that the kasra and the tanwīn do not come into it, and that in the place of jarr it always has a fatḥa; you say jāʾanī Aḥmadu “Aḥmad came to me”, raʾaytu Aḥmada “I saw Aḥmad” and marartu bi-Aḥmada “I passed by Aḥmad”.

text.original: أَمَّا الْعَدْلُ فَهُوَ تَغَيُّرُ اللَّفْظِ مِنْ صِيغَتِهِ الْأَصْلِيَّةِ إِلَى صِيغَةٍ أُخْرَى تَحْقِيقًا أَوْ تَقْدِيرًا، وَلَا يَجْتَمِعُ مَعَ وَزْنِ الْفِعْلِ أَصْلًا، وَيَجْتَمِعُ مَعَ الْعَلَمِيَّةِ، كَعُمَرَ وَزُفَرَ، وَمَعَ الْوَصْفِ، كَثُلَاثَ وَمَثْلَثَ وَأُخَرَ وَجُمَعَ.
text.en: ʿAdl is the change of the word from its original form to another form, really or by supposition. It never comes together with the pattern of the verb; it comes together with being a proper name (ʿalamiyya), as ʿUmara and Zufara, and with being an adjective, as thulātha and mathlatha “three by three”, ukhara “others” and jumaʿa “all (f. pl.)”.

text.original: أَمَّا الْوَصْفُ فَلَا يَجْتَمِعُ مَعَ الْعَلَمِيَّةِ أَصْلًا، وَشَرْطُهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ وَصْفًا فِي أَصْلِ الْوَضْعِ، فَأَسْوَدُ وَأَرْقَمُ غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِفٍ وَإِنْ صَارَا اسْمَيْنِ لِلْحَيَّةِ؛ لِأَصَالَتِهِمَا فِي الْوَصْفِيَّةِ، وَأَرْبَعٌ فِي: مَرَرْتُ بِنِسْوَةٍ أَرْبَعٍ، مُنْصَرِفٌ مَعَ أَنَّهُ صِفَةٌ وَوَزْنُ الْفِعْلِ؛ لِعَدَمِ الْأَصَالَةِ فِي الْوَصْفِيَّةِ.
text.en: Being an adjective never comes together with being a proper name. Its condition is that it is an adjective in its original laying down; so aswadu “black” and arqamu “speckled” are diptotes even though they have become two names for the snake, because they are adjectives in origin; and arbaʿin “four” in marartu bi-niswatin arbaʿin “I passed by four women” is munṣarif although it is an adjective on the pattern of the verb, because it is not an adjective in origin.

text.original: أَمَّا التَّأْنِيثُ بِالتَّاءِ فَشَرْطُهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ عَلَمًا، كَطَلْحَةَ، وَكَذَلِكَ الْمَعْنَوِيُّ. ثُمَّ الْمَعْنَوِيُّ إِنْ كَانَ ثُلَاثِيًّا سَاكِنَ الْأَوْسَطِ غَيْرَ أَعْجَمِيٍّ يَجُوزُ صَرْفُهُ وَتَرْكُهُ؛ لِأَجْلِ الْخِفَّةِ وَوُجُودِ السَّبَبَيْنِ، كَهِنْدٍ، وَإِلَّا يَجِبُ مَنْعُهُ، كَزَيْنَبَ وَسَقَرَ وَمَاهَ وَجُورَ. وَالتَّأْنِيثُ بِالْأَلِفِ الْمَقْصُورَةِ، كَحُبْلَى، وَالْمَمْدُودَةِ، كَحَمْرَاءَ، مُمْتَنِعٌ صَرْفُهُمَا الْبَتَّةَ؛ لِأَنَّ الْأَلِفَ قَائِمٌ مَقَامَ السَّبَبَيْنِ: التَّأْنِيثِ وَلُزُومِهِ.
text.en: The feminine with the tāʾ: its condition is that it is a proper name, as Ṭalḥata; and so too the feminine by meaning (maʿnawī). Then the feminine by meaning, if it is triliteral with an unvowelled middle letter and not foreign, may be munṣarif or not, because of its lightness and the presence of the two causes, as Hindin; otherwise it must be a diptote, as Zaynaba, Saqara, Māha and Jūra. The feminine with the short alif, as ḥublā “pregnant”, and with the long alif (mamdūda), as ḥamrāʾa “red (f.)”, can never be munṣarif, because the alif stands in the place of two causes: the feminine and its being fixed [to the word].

lessons.title: The other causes; when a diptote is declined
body: Of definiteness, “only being a proper name counts”, and it can join every cause except the adjective. Being foreign counts when the word was a proper name in the foreign language and has more than three letters, Ibrāhīm, or three with a vowel in the middle, Shatar. So lijām, “bridle”, is declined, being no name, and Nūḥ is declined, its middle letter having a sukūn.

The plural counts when it is on “the pattern of the furthest plural” (ṣīghat muntahā al-jumūʿ): after the alif of the plural, two letters, masājid; a doubled letter, dawābb; or three letters with a sukūn in the middle, maṣābīḥ; and it must not take the hāʾ, so farāzina is declined. This plural stands for two causes, “being a plural and its being fixed”: it can never be made a broken plural again, “so it is as if it were made plural twice”.

Compounding counts in a proper name “without iḍāfa and without predication”: Baʿlabakk. So ʿAbd Allāh, a compound by iḍāfa, is declined; Maʿdī Karib is a diptote; and Shāba qarnāhā, a name made of a whole sentence, is built. The added alif and nūn count, in a noun, when it is a proper name, ʿImrān, ʿUthmān, but not saʿdān, a plant; in an adjective, when there is no feminine on faʿlāna: sakrān is a diptote, nadmān is declined because nadmāna exists.

The pattern of the verb counts when the pattern belongs to the verb alone and is found in nouns only as carried over from the verb, as names like Shammara and Ḍuriba; or when the word begins with a prefix of the muḍāriʿ and does not take the hāʾ: Aḥmad, Yashkur, Taghlib, Narjis. Yaʿmal is declined, because it takes the hāʾ: nāqatun yaʿmalatun, “a hard-working she-camel”.

Two rules end the introduction. A diptote whose causes include being a name becomes declined when it is made indefinite: those that need the name lose all their causes, and the ʿadl name and the verb-pattern name keep one only. Jāʾanī Ṭalḥatu wa-Ṭalḥatun ākharu, “Ṭalḥa came, and another Ṭalḥa”. And every diptote takes the kasra when it is muḍāf or takes the lām: marartu bi-Aḥmadikum, wa-bi-l-aḥmadi.

tasks.prompt: Diptote or declined, and why? Ibrāhīm; lijām; Nūḥ; maṣābīḥ; farāzina.
tasks.answer: Ibrāhīm: diptote (a foreign proper name of more than three letters). Lijām: declined (foreign, but not a proper name). Nūḥ: declined (three letters with a sukūn in the middle). Maṣābīḥ: diptote (the furthest plural). Farāzina: declined (it takes the hāʾ).

tasks.prompt: Why is ʿAbd Allāh declined, while Baʿlabakk is not?
tasks.answer: Compounding counts only in a name without iḍāfa and without predication. ʿAbd Allāh is a compound by iḍāfa, so it is declined (its first part takes the iʿrāb). Baʿlabakk is two words made one with no iḍāfa: a proper name with compounding, a diptote.

tasks.prompt: Why is sakrān a diptote and nadmān declined?
tasks.answer: In an adjective the added alif and nūn count only when there is no feminine on faʿlāna. Sakrān has none (its feminine is not sakrāna); nadmān has nadmāna, so it is declined.

tasks.prompt: Explain ḍaraba Aḥmadu wa-Aḥmadun ākharu.
tasks.answer: Aḥmad as a name has two causes, the name and the pattern of the verb: a diptote. “Another Aḥmad” is indefinite: the name is gone, only the pattern is left, one cause, so it is declined with tanwīn.

text.original: أَمَّا الْمَعْرِفَةُ فَلَا يُعْتَبَرُ فِي مَنْعِ الصَّرْفِ مِنْهَا إِلَّا الْعَلَمِيَّةُ، وَتَجْتَمِعُ مَعَ غَيْرِ الْوَصْفِ. أَمَّا الْعُجْمَةُ فَشَرْطُهَا أَنْ تَكُونَ عَلَمًا فِي الْعُجْمَةِ، وَزَائِدَةً عَلَى ثَلَاثَةِ أَحْرُفٍ، كَإِبْرَاهِيمَ، أَوْ ثُلَاثِيًّا مُتَحَرِّكَ الْأَوْسَطِ، كَشَتَرَ، فَلِجَامٌ مُنْصَرِفٌ لِعَدَمِ الْعَلَمِيَّةِ، وَنُوحٌ مُنْصَرِفٌ لِسُكُونِ الْأَوْسَطِ.
text.en: Of definiteness, only being a proper name counts in making a noun a diptote, and it comes together with [every cause] other than the adjective. Being foreign: its condition is that it is a proper name in the foreign language and has more than three letters, as Ibrāhīma, or is triliteral with a vowelled middle letter, as Shatara; so lijāmun “a bridle” is munṣarif because it is not a proper name, and Nūḥun is munṣarif because its middle letter is unvowelled.

text.original: أَمَّا الْجَمْعُ فَشَرْطُهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ عَلَى صِيغَةِ مُنْتَهَى الْجُمُوعِ، وَهُوَ أَنْ يَكُونَ بَعْدَ أَلِفِ الْجَمْعِ حَرْفَانِ، كَمَسَاجِدَ، أَوْ حَرْفٌ مُشَدَّدٌ، كَدَوَابَّ، أَوْ ثَلَاثَةُ أَحْرُفٍ أَوْسَطُهَا سَاكِنٌ غَيْرُ قَابِلٍ لِلْهَاءِ، كَمَصَابِيحَ، وَفَرَازِنَةٌ مُنْصَرِفٌ لِقَبُولِهَا الْهَاءَ. وَهُوَ أَيْضًا قَائِمٌ مَقَامَ السَّبَبَيْنِ: الْجَمْعِيَّةِ، وَلُزُومِهَا، وَامْتِنَاعِ أَنْ يُجْمَعَ مَرَّةً أُخْرَى جَمْعَ التَّكْسِيرِ، فَكَأَنَّهُ جُمِعَ مَرَّتَيْنِ.
text.en: The plural: its condition is that it is on the pattern of the furthest plural (ṣīghat muntahā al-jumūʿ), which is that after the alif of the plural there are two letters, as masājida “mosques”, or a doubled letter, as dawābba “beasts”, or three letters whose middle one is unvowelled and which does not accept the hāʾ, as maṣābīḥa “lamps”; so farāzinatun “queens (of chess)” is munṣarif because it accepts the hāʾ. It too stands in the place of two causes: being a plural and its being fixed, that is, the impossibility of its being made a broken plural once more; so it is as if it were made plural twice.

text.original: أَمَّا التَّرْكِيبُ فَشَرْطُهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ عَلَمًا بِلَا إِضَافَةٍ وَلَا إِسْنَادٍ، كَبَعْلَبَكَّ، فَعَبْدُ اللَّهِ مُنْصَرِفٌ، وَمَعْدِي كَرِبَ غَيْرُ مُنْصَرِفٍ، وَشَابَ قَرْنَاهَا مَبْنِيٌّ. أَمَّا الْأَلِفُ وَالنُّونُ الزَّائِدَتَانِ إِنْ كَانَتَا فِي اسْمٍ فَشَرْطُهُ أَنْ يَكُونَ عَلَمًا، كَعِمْرَانَ وَعُثْمَانَ، وَسَعْدَانٌ اسْمَ نَبْتٍ مُنْصَرِفٌ لِعَدَمِ الْعَلَمِيَّةِ، وَإِنْ كَانَتَا فِي صِفَةٍ فَشَرْطُهُ انْتِفَاءُ فَعْلَانَةٍ، كَسَكْرَانَ، فَنَدْمَانٌ مُنْصَرِفٌ لِوُجُودِ نَدْمَانَةٍ.
text.en: Compounding: its condition is that it is a proper name without iḍāfa and without predication, as Baʿlabakka; so ʿAbdu Allāhi is munṣarif, Maʿdī Kariba is a diptote, and Shāba qarnāhā (a name: “her locks turned grey”) is mabnī. The added alif and nūn: if they are in a noun, its condition is that it is a proper name, as ʿImrāna and ʿUthmāna; so saʿdānun, the name of a plant, is munṣarif because it is not a proper name. If they are in an adjective, its condition is that there is no faʿlānatin, as sakrāna “drunk”; so nadmānun “boon companion” is munṣarif because nadmānatin exists.

text.original: أَمَّا وَزْنُ الْفِعْلِ فَشَرْطُهُ أَنْ يَخْتَصَّ بِالْفِعْلِ، وَلَا يُوجَدَ فِي الِاسْمِ إِلَّا مَنْقُولًا عَنِ الْفِعْلِ، كَشَمَّرَ وَضُرِبَ، أَوْ يَكُونَ فِي أَوَّلِهِ إِحْدَى حُرُوفِ الْمُضَارَعَةِ وَلَا يَدْخُلَهُ الْهَاءُ، كَأَحْمَدَ وَيَشْكُرَ وَتَغْلِبَ وَنَرْجِسَ، فَيَعْمَلٌ مُنْصَرِفٌ لِقَبُولِهِ الْهَاءَ، كَقَوْلِهِمْ: نَاقَةٌ يَعْمَلَةٌ.
text.en: The pattern of the verb: its condition is that it belongs to the verb only and is not found in the noun except as carried over from the verb, as Shammara and Ḍuriba; or that at its beginning there is one of the prefixes of the muḍāriʿ and the hāʾ does not come into it, as Aḥmada, Yashkura, Taghliba and Narjisa; so yaʿmalun is munṣarif because it accepts the hāʾ, as in their saying nāqatun yaʿmalatun “a hard-working she-camel”.

text.original: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ كُلَّ مَا شُرِطَ فِيهِ الْعَلَمِيَّةُ، وَهُوَ الْمُؤَنَّثُ بِالتَّاءِ وَالْمَعْنَوِيُّ وَالْعُجْمَةُ وَالتَّرْكِيبُ وَالِاسْمُ الَّذِي فِيهِ الْأَلِفُ وَالنُّونُ الزَّائِدَتَانِ، أَوْ لَمْ يُشْتَرَطْ فِيهِ ذَلِكَ وَاجْتَمَعَ مَعَ سَبَبٍ وَاحِدٍ فَقَطْ، وَهُوَ الْعَلَمُ الْمَعْدُولُ وَوَزْنُ الْفِعْلِ، إِذَا نُكِّرَ صُرِفَ؛ أَمَّا فِي الْقِسْمِ الْأَوَّلِ فَلِبَقَائِهِ بِلَا سَبَبٍ، وَأَمَّا فِي الثَّانِي فَلِبَقَائِهِ عَلَى سَبَبٍ وَاحِدٍ، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي طَلْحَةُ وَطَلْحَةٌ آخَرُ، وَقَامَ عُمَرُ وَعُمَرٌ آخَرُ، وَضَرَبَ أَحْمَدُ وَأَحْمَدٌ آخَرُ.
text.en: Know that everything in which being a proper name is a condition — the feminine with the tāʾ, the feminine by meaning, the foreign, the compound and the noun in which there are the added alif and nūn —, or in which that is not a condition but which comes together with one other cause only — the changed (maʿdūl) proper name and the pattern of the verb —, becomes munṣarif when it is made indefinite: in the first group because it remains without a cause, and in the second because it remains with one cause; you say jāʾanī Ṭalḥatu wa-Ṭalḥatun ākharu “Ṭalḥa came to me, and another Ṭalḥa”, qāma ʿUmaru wa-ʿUmarun ākharu “ʿUmar stood, and another ʿUmar” and ḍaraba Aḥmadu wa-Aḥmadun ākharu “Aḥmad hit, and another Aḥmad”.

text.original: وَكُلُّ مَا لَا يَنْصَرِفُ إِذَا أُضِيفَ أَوْ دَخَلَهُ اللَّامُ تَدْخُلُهُ الْكَسْرَةُ، نَحْوُ: مَرَرْتُ بِأَحْمَدِكُمْ، وَبِالْأَحْمَدِ.
text.en: Every diptote takes the kasra when it is made muḍāf or the lām comes into it, as marartu bi-Aḥmadikum “I passed by your Aḥmad” wa-bi-al-aḥmadi “and by the Aḥmad”.

lessons.title: The eight marfūʿ; the fāʿil and the number of its verb
body: The first aim is the marfūʿ nouns, and they are eight: the fāʿil; “the object of a verb whose doer is not named” (mafʿūl mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhu, the Kāfiya's name for what later books call the deputy of the fāʿil); the mubtadaʾ; the khabar; the khabar of inna and its sisters; the ism of kāna and its sisters; the ism of mā and lā that resemble laysa; and the khabar of the lā that denies the kind. The muḍāriʿ in rafʿ is not counted here, because this part is only on the noun.

The fāʿil is “every noun before which there is a verb or an adjective that is predicated of it, in the sense that the act stands in it, not that it falls upon it”. Each part matters. “Before which”: the fāʿil comes after its governor. “A verb or an adjective”: qāma Zaydun, and also Zaydun ḍāribun abūhu ʿAmran, where abūhu is the fāʿil of the participle ḍāribun. “Stands in it, not falls upon it”: this leaves out the deputy, as in ḍuriba Zaydun, where the hitting falls on Zayd.

Notice the third example, mā ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran, “Zayd did not hit ʿAmr”. The hitting is denied, yet Zayd is the fāʿil: the verb is still predicated of him. Being the fāʿil is a matter of the sentence's form, not of what happened.

“Every verb must have a marfūʿ fāʿil”: an explicit noun, dhahaba Zaydun; a visible pronoun, ḍarabtu Zaydan, where the tāʾ is the fāʿil; or a hidden one, Zaydun dhahaba, where the fāʿil is a pronoun hidden in dhahaba. If the verb is transitive it also has a mafʿūl bihi: ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran.

With an explicit fāʿil “the verb is always singular”: ḍaraba Zaydun, ḍaraba al-Zaydāni, ḍaraba al-Zaydūna. With a pronoun the verb agrees: Zaydun ḍaraba, al-Zaydāni ḍarabā, al-Zaydūna ḍarabū. The alif of ḍarabā and the wāw of ḍarabū are not marks of number on the verb but the pronouns themselves, the fāʿil; a verb with an explicit fāʿil needs no second one.

terms.en: the eight marfūʿ nouns
the noun after a verb or adjective predicated of it, the act standing in it
the object of a verb whose doer is not named: the deputy
the transitive verb, which has a mafʿūl bihi too

examples.en: the fāʿil of an adjective: abūhu
a fāʿil of a denied act

tasks.prompt: Find the fāʿil and say what kind it is: dhahaba Zaydun; ḍarabtu Zaydan; Zaydun dhahaba; Zaydun ḍāribun abūhu ʿAmran.
tasks.arabic: ذَهَبَ زَيْدٌ — ضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا — زَيْدٌ ذَهَبَ — زَيْدٌ ضَارِبٌ أَبُوهُ عَمْرًا
tasks.answer: Zaydun: an explicit fāʿil. The tāʾ of ḍarabtu: a visible pronoun. In Zaydun dhahaba: a pronoun hidden in dhahaba. Abūhu: the explicit fāʿil of the adjective ḍāribun.

tasks.prompt: Why is Zaydun not the fāʿil in ḍuriba Zaydun, by the book's definition?
tasks.answer: The fāʿil is the one in whom the act stands, not on whom it falls. In ḍuriba Zaydun the hitting falls on Zayd; he is the object put in the place of the dropped fāʿil.

tasks.prompt: Correct the mistake: ḍarabā al-Zaydāni; al-Zaydūna ḍaraba.
tasks.answer: Ḍaraba al-Zaydāni: with an explicit fāʿil the verb is always singular. Al-Zaydūna ḍarabū: with a pronoun the verb agrees, and the wāw is the pronoun of the plural.

tasks.prompt: Name the eight marfūʿ of the book.
tasks.answer: The fāʿil; the object of a verb whose doer is not named; the mubtadaʾ; the khabar; the khabar of inna and its sisters; the ism of kāna and its sisters; the ism of mā and lā like laysa; the khabar of the lā that denies the kind.

quiz.prompt: How many marfūʿ nouns does the book count?
quiz.explanation: The muḍāriʿ is left to the part on the verb.

quiz.prompt: In the definition of the fāʿil, “stands in it, not falls upon it” leaves out…
options: the object whose fāʿil is not named
quiz.explanation: In ḍuriba Zaydun the act falls on Zayd.

quiz.prompt: In Zaydun ḍāribun abūhu ʿAmran, the fāʿil of ḍāribun is…
quiz.explanation: An adjective may have a fāʿil.

quiz.prompt: In mā ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran, Zaydun is…
quiz.explanation: The act is denied, but the verb is still predicated of him.

quiz.prompt: In Zaydun dhahaba, the fāʿil of dhahaba is…
quiz.explanation: Every verb must have a marfūʿ fāʿil.

In al-Zaydūna ḍarabū, the wāw is…

text.original: الْأَسْمَاءُ الْمَرْفُوعَةُ ثَمَانِيَةُ أَقْسَامٍ: الْفَاعِلُ، وَمَفْعُولُ مَا لَمْ يُسَمَّ فَاعِلُهُ، وَالْمُبْتَدَأُ، وَالْخَبَرُ، وَخَبَرُ إِنَّ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا، وَاسْمُ كَانَ وَأَخَوَاتِهَا، وَاسْمُ مَا وَلَا الْمُشَبَّهَتَيْنِ بِلَيْسَ، وَخَبَرُ لَا الَّتِي لِنَفْيِ الْجِنْسِ.
text.en: The marfūʿ nouns are of eight kinds: the fāʿil; the object of a verb whose doer is not named (mafʿūl mā lam yusamma fāʿiluhu); the mubtadaʾ; the khabar; the khabar of inna and its sisters; the ism of kāna and its sisters; the ism of mā and lā that resemble laysa; and the khabar of the lā that denies the whole kind.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الْفَاعِلُ كُلُّ اسْمٍ قَبْلَهُ فِعْلٌ أَوْ صِفَةٌ أُسْنِدَ إِلَيْهِ عَلَى مَعْنَى أَنَّهُ قَامَ بِهِ لَا وَقَعَ عَلَيْهِ، نَحْوُ: قَامَ زَيْدٌ، وَزَيْدٌ ضَارِبٌ أَبُوهُ عَمْرًا، وَمَا ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا. وَكُلُّ فِعْلٍ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ فَاعِلٍ مَرْفُوعٍ: مُظْهَرٍ، كَذَهَبَ زَيْدٌ، أَوْ مُضْمَرٍ بَارِزٍ، كَضَرَبْتُ زَيْدًا، أَوْ مُسْتَتِرٍ، كَزَيْدٌ ذَهَبَ. وَإِنْ كَانَ الْفِعْلُ مُتَعَدِّيًا كَانَ لَهُ مَفْعُولٌ بِهِ أَيْضًا، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ عَمْرًا.
text.en: Section. The fāʿil is every noun before which there is a verb or an adjective that is predicated of it, in the sense that [the act] stands in it, not that it falls upon it, as qāma Zaydun “Zayd stood”, Zaydun ḍāribun abūhu ʿAmran “Zayd, his father is hitting ʿAmr” and mā ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran “Zayd did not hit ʿAmr”. Every verb must have a marfūʿ fāʿil: explicit, as dhahaba Zaydun “Zayd went”; or a visible pronoun, as ḍarabtu Zaydan “I hit Zayd”; or a hidden one, as Zaydun dhahaba “Zayd, he went”. If the verb is transitive, it also has a mafʿūl bihi, as ḍaraba Zaydun ʿAmran “Zayd hit ʿAmr”.

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ الْفَاعِلُ مُظْهَرًا وُحِّدَ الْفِعْلُ أَبَدًا، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ، وَضَرَبَ الزَّيْدَانِ، وَضَرَبَ الزَّيْدُونَ، وَإِنْ كَانَ مُضْمَرًا وُحِّدَ لِلْوَاحِدِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ ضَرَبَ، وَثُنِّيَ لِلْمُثَنَّى، نَحْوُ: الزَّيْدَانِ ضَرَبَا، وَجُمِعَ لِلْجَمْعِ، نَحْوُ: الزَّيْدُونَ ضَرَبُوا.
text.en: If the fāʿil is explicit, the verb is always singular, as ḍaraba Zaydun “Zayd hit”, ḍaraba al-Zaydāni “the two Zayds hit” and ḍaraba al-Zaydūna “the Zayds hit”; if it is a pronoun, [the verb] is singular for the singular, as Zaydun ḍaraba “Zayd, he hit”, dual for the dual, as al-Zaydāni ḍarabā “the two Zayds, they hit”, and plural for the plural, as al-Zaydūna ḍarabū “the Zayds, they hit”.

lessons.title: The feminine verb; the order of fāʿil and object; dropping
body: A true feminine is “one over against which there is a male among living beings”. When the fāʿil is a true feminine the verb is “always feminine if you do not separate the verb and the fāʿil”: qāmat Hindun. If something comes between, you may choose: ḍaraba al-yawma Hindun, or ḍarabati al-yawma Hindun. With a feminine that is not true, as al-shams, you may choose even without a separation: ṭalaʿati al-shamsu, or ṭalaʿa al-shamsu.

All this is when the verb is predicated of an explicit noun. When it is predicated of a pronoun it is “always feminine”: al-shamsu ṭalaʿat. The broken plural is “like the feminine that is not true”: qāma al-rijālu, or qāmati al-rijālu; and with its pronoun, al-rijālu qāmat, or al-rijālu qāmū.

Order. The fāʿil normally comes before the object, and it must come first “when both are maqṣūr and you fear confusion”: in ḍaraba Mūsā ʿĪsā neither word shows its iʿrāb, so only the order says who hit whom. Where nothing is confused, the object may come first: akala al-kummathrā Yaḥyā, “Yaḥyā ate the pear”, where the meaning tells (a pear does not eat), and ḍaraba ʿAmran Zaydun, where the iʿrāb tells.

Dropping. The verb may be dropped when the context shows it: Zaydun, in answer to man ḍaraba, “who hit?”. The verb and the fāʿil may be dropped together: naʿam, “yes”, in answer to a-qāma Zaydun, stands for qāma Zaydun. And the fāʿil may be dropped and the object put in its place, when the verb is passive: ḍuriba Zaydun. That is the second of the marfūʿ (lesson 13).

terms.en: the true feminine: with a male facing it among living beings
the feminine that is not true, as al-shams
confusion: when the order alone shows the fāʿil
the passive verb, whose fāʿil is dropped

examples.en: a true feminine, joined to its verb: the feminine required
separated: the masculine allowed
a feminine pronoun: the feminine required
both maqṣūr: the fāʿil must come first
no confusion: the object may come first

tasks.prompt: Must the verb be feminine? qāma Hindun; ṭalaʿa al-shamsu; ḍaraba al-yawma Hindun; al-shamsu ṭalaʿa.
tasks.answer: Qāma Hindun: wrong; a true feminine joined to the verb needs qāmat. Ṭalaʿa al-shamsu: allowed; al-shams is not a true feminine. Ḍaraba al-yawma Hindun: allowed; the fāʿil is separated. Al-shamsu ṭalaʿa: wrong; with a feminine pronoun one must say ṭalaʿat.

tasks.prompt: Why must Mūsā come first in ḍaraba Mūsā ʿĪsā, while ʿAmran may come first in ḍaraba ʿAmran Zaydun?
tasks.arabic: ضَرَبَ مُوسَى عِيسَى — ضَرَبَ عَمْرًا زَيْدٌ
tasks.answer: Mūsā and ʿĪsā are both maqṣūr: their iʿrāb is implied, so only the order shows who is the fāʿil. In ḍaraba ʿAmran Zaydun the fatḥa and the ḍamma show it, so there is no confusion and the object may come first.

tasks.prompt: What is dropped in each answer: Zaydun, to man ḍaraba; naʿam, to a-qāma Zaydun?
tasks.answer: In Zaydun the verb is dropped: ḍaraba Zaydun. In naʿam the verb and its fāʿil are dropped together: naʿam, qāma Zaydun.

tasks.prompt: Give the four ways the book allows with al-rijāl.
tasks.answer: Qāma al-rijālu and qāmati al-rijālu (the verb before it, masculine or feminine); al-rijālu qāmat and al-rijālu qāmū (with its pronoun, feminine singular or masculine plural).

text.original: وَإِنْ كَانَ الْفَاعِلُ مُؤَنَّثًا حَقِيقِيًّا، وَهُوَ مَا بِإِزَائِهِ ذَكَرٌ مِنَ الْحَيَوَانِ، أُنِّثَ الْفِعْلُ أَبَدًا إِنْ لَمْ تَفْصِلْ بَيْنَ الْفِعْلِ وَالْفَاعِلِ، نَحْوُ: قَامَتْ هِنْدٌ، وَإِنْ فَصَلْتَ فَلَكَ الْخِيَارُ فِي التَّذْكِيرِ وَالتَّأْنِيثِ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ الْيَوْمَ هِنْدٌ، وَإِنْ شِئْتَ قُلْتَ: ضَرَبَتِ الْيَوْمَ هِنْدٌ. وَكَذَلِكَ فِي الْمُؤَنَّثِ الْغَيْرِ الْحَقِيقِيِّ، نَحْوُ: طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ، وَإِنْ شِئْتَ قُلْتَ: طَلَعَ الشَّمْسُ. هَذَا إِذَا كَانَ الْفِعْلُ مُسْنَدًا إِلَى الْمُظْهَرِ، وَإِنْ كَانَ مُسْنَدًا إِلَى الْمُضْمَرِ أُنِّثَ أَبَدًا، نَحْوُ: الشَّمْسُ طَلَعَتْ.
text.en: If the fāʿil is a true feminine — that is, one over against which there is a male among living beings — the verb is always feminine if you do not separate the verb and the fāʿil, as qāmat Hindun “Hind stood”; if you separate them, you may choose between the masculine and the feminine, as ḍaraba al-yawma Hindun “Hind hit today”, and if you wish you say ḍarabati al-yawma Hindun. Likewise with the feminine that is not true, as ṭalaʿati al-shamsu “the sun rose”, and if you wish you say ṭalaʿa al-shamsu. This is when the verb is predicated of an explicit noun; if it is predicated of a pronoun, it is always feminine, as al-shamsu ṭalaʿat “the sun, it rose”.

text.original: وَجَمْعُ التَّكْسِيرِ كَالْمُؤَنَّثِ الْغَيْرِ الْحَقِيقِيِّ، تَقُولُ: قَامَ الرِّجَالُ، وَإِنْ شِئْتَ قُلْتَ: قَامَتِ الرِّجَالُ، وَالرِّجَالُ قَامَتْ، وَيَجُوزُ فِيهِ: الرِّجَالُ قَامُوا. وَيَجِبُ تَقْدِيمُ الْفَاعِلِ عَلَى الْمَفْعُولِ إِذَا كَانَا مَقْصُورَيْنِ وَخِفْتَ اللَّبْسَ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَ مُوسَى عِيسَى، وَيَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُ الْمَفْعُولِ عَلَى الْفَاعِلِ إِنْ لَمْ تَخَفِ اللَّبْسَ، نَحْوُ: أَكَلَ الْكُمَّثْرَى يَحْيَى، وَضَرَبَ عَمْرًا زَيْدٌ.
text.en: The broken plural is like the feminine that is not true; you say qāma al-rijālu “the men stood”, and if you wish qāmati al-rijālu and al-rijālu qāmat; and al-rijālu qāmū is also allowed with it. The fāʿil must be put before the mafʿūl when both are maqṣūr and you fear confusion, as ḍaraba Mūsā ʿĪsā “Mūsā hit ʿĪsā”; the mafʿūl may be put before the fāʿil if you do not fear confusion, as akala al-kummathrā Yaḥyā “Yaḥyā ate the pear” and ḍaraba ʿAmran Zaydun “Zayd hit ʿAmr”.

text.original: وَيَجُوزُ حَذْفُ الْفِعْلِ حَيْثُ كَانَتْ قَرِينَةٌ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ، فِي جَوَابِ مَنْ قَالَ: مَنْ ضَرَبَ؟ وَكَذَا يَجُوزُ حَذْفُ الْفِعْلِ وَالْفَاعِلِ مَعًا، كَنَعَمْ، فِي جَوَابِ مَنْ قَالَ: أَقَامَ زَيْدٌ؟ وَقَدْ يُحْذَفُ الْفَاعِلُ وَيُقَامُ الْمَفْعُولُ مَقَامَهُ إِذَا كَانَ الْفِعْلُ مَجْهُولًا، نَحْوُ: ضُرِبَ زَيْدٌ، وَهُوَ الْقِسْمُ الثَّانِي مِنَ الْمَرْفُوعَاتِ.
text.en: The verb may be dropped where there is an indication, as Zaydun “Zayd” in answer to one who says man ḍaraba “who hit?”; likewise the verb and the fāʿil may be dropped together, as naʿam “yes” in answer to one who says a-qāma Zaydun “did Zayd stand?”. Sometimes the fāʿil is dropped and the mafʿūl is put in its place, when the verb is passive, as ḍuriba Zaydun “Zayd was hit”; this is the second kind of the marfūʿ nouns.

lessons.title: Two verbs contending for one noun: the Baṣran way
body: Contention (tanāzuʿ) is when two verbs stand before one explicit noun and “each of the two verbs wants to govern that noun”. There are four kinds. Both want it as fāʿil: ḍarabanī wa-akramanī Zaydun. Both want it as object: ḍarabtu wa-akramtu Zaydan. The first wants a fāʿil and the second an object: ḍarabanī wa-akramtu Zaydan. Or the reverse: ḍarabtu wa-akramanī Zaydun.

In all four, either verb may be the one that governs the noun. Al-Farrāʾ alone refuses to let the second govern in the first and third kinds, where the first verb wants a fāʿil: then the first verb would have to lose its fāʿil, or carry a pronoun of a noun not yet mentioned, “and both are to be avoided”. That is the question of what is allowed. As to what is preferred, the schools differ: the Baṣrans let the second govern, for its nearness to the noun; the Kūfans the first, because it comes first and has the right.

The Baṣran way: the second verb governs the noun. If the first verb wants a fāʿil, a pronoun is put in it: ḍarabanī wa-akramanī Zaydun; ḍarabānī wa-akramanī al-Zaydāni; ḍarabūnī wa-akramanī al-Zaydūna, and so with verbs that differ, ḍarabūnī wa-akramtu al-Zaydīna. The alif and wāw of ḍarabānī and ḍarabūnī are the fāʿil of the first verb. The Baṣrans accept here a pronoun before its noun, because a fāʿil can never be dropped.

If the first verb wants an object, and the two are not verbs of the heart, the object of the first is simply dropped: ḍarabtu wa-akramtu Zaydan, ḍarabtu wa-akramtu al-Zaydayni; and with verbs that differ, ḍarabtu wa-akramanī Zaydun. An object may be left out, so there is no need for a pronoun before its noun.

With verbs of the heart, which take two objects, “the mafʿūl of the first verb must be expressed”: ḥasibanī munṭaliqan wa-ḥasibtu Zaydan munṭaliqan. It cannot be dropped, since a verb of the heart may not lose its object, and it cannot be a pronoun before its noun. “This is the school of the Baṣrans.”

a pronoun before its noun is mentioned
two verbs that agree, or differ, in what they want
the verbs of the heart, with two objects that may not be dropped

tasks.prompt: Say which kind of contention each is: ḍarabanī wa-akramanī Zaydun; ḍarabtu wa-akramtu Zaydan; ḍarabanī wa-akramtu Zaydan; ḍarabtu wa-akramanī Zaydun.
tasks.answer: The first: both want a fāʿil. The second: both want an object. The third: the first wants a fāʿil, the second an object. The fourth: the first wants an object, the second a fāʿil.

tasks.prompt: In ḍarabānī wa-akramanī al-Zaydāni, which verb governs al-Zaydāni, and what is the fāʿil of ḍarabānī?
tasks.answer: The second, akramanī, governs al-Zaydāni as its fāʿil (the Baṣran way). The fāʿil of ḍarabānī is the alif, a dual pronoun standing for the two Zayds.

tasks.prompt: Why does the book drop the object of the first verb in ḍarabtu wa-akramanī Zaydun, but not its fāʿil in ḍarabanī wa-akramtu Zaydan?
tasks.answer: An object may be dropped, so the first verb's object is left out. A fāʿil may never be dropped, so when the first verb wants a fāʿil it is given a pronoun instead.

tasks.prompt: What did al-Farrāʾ refuse, and why?
tasks.answer: He refused to let the second verb govern when the first wants a fāʿil (the first and third kinds), because then the first verb would either lose its fāʿil or take a pronoun before its noun is mentioned, and both are to be avoided.
