text.original: فَصْلٌ: أَسْمَاءُ الْأَفْعَالِ، هُوَ كُلُّ اسْمٍ بِمَعْنَى الْأَمْرِ وَالْمَاضِي، نَحْوُ: رُوَيْدَ زَيْدًا، أَيْ أَمْهِلْهُ، وَهَيْهَاتَ زَيْدٌ، أَيْ بَعُدَ. وَمَا كَانَ عَلَى وَزْنِ فَعَالِ بِمَعْنَى الْأَمْرِ، وَهُوَ مِنَ الثُّلَاثِيِّ قِيَاسٌ، كَنَزَالِ بِمَعْنَى انْزِلْ، وَتَرَاكِ بِمَعْنَى اتْرُكْ.
text.en: Section. The nouns of verbs: it is every noun in the meaning of the imperative or of the past, as ruwayda Zaydan “give Zayd time”, that is, amhilhu “give him time”, and hayhāta Zaydun “far is Zayd!”, that is, baʿuda “he is far”. What is on the pattern faʿāli in the meaning of the imperative is by rule from the triliteral, as nazāli in the meaning of inzil “dismount!” and tarāki in the meaning of utruk “leave!”.

text.original: وَيَلْحَقُ بِهِ فَعَالِ مَصْدَرًا مَعْرِفَةً، كَفَجَارِ بِمَعْنَى الْفُجُورِ، أَوْ صِفَةً لِلْمُؤَنَّثِ، نَحْوُ: يَا فَسَاقِ بِمَعْنَى فَاسِقَةٍ، وَيَا لَكَاعِ بِمَعْنَى لَاكِعَةٍ، أَوْ عَلَمًا لِلْأَعْيَانِ الْمُؤَنَّثَةِ، كَقَطَامِ وَغَلَابِ وَحَضَارِ. وَهَذِهِ الثَّلَاثَةُ لَيْسَتْ مِنْ أَسْمَاءِ الْأَفْعَالِ، وَإِنَّمَا ذُكِرَتْ هَهُنَا لِلْمُنَاسَبَةِ.
text.en: Joined to it is faʿāli as a definite maṣdar, as fajāri in the meaning of al-fujūri “wickedness”; or as an adjective of the feminine, as yā fasāqi in the meaning of fāsiqatin “O wicked woman!” and yā lakāʿi in the meaning of lākiʿatin “O base woman!”; or as a proper name of feminine individuals, as Qaṭāmi, Ghalābi and Ḥaḍāri. These three are not among the nouns of verbs; they are only mentioned here because they fit.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الْأَصْوَاتُ كُلُّ لَفْظٍ حُكِيَ بِهِ صَوْتٌ، كَغَاقِ لِصَوْتِ الْغُرَابِ، أَوْ صُوِّتَ بِهِ لِلْبَهَائِمِ، كَنَخْ لِإِنَاخَةِ الْبَعِيرِ. فَصْلٌ: الْمُرَكَّبَاتُ كُلُّ اسْمٍ رُكِّبَ مِنْ كَلِمَتَيْنِ لَيْسَتْ بَيْنَهُمَا نِسْبَةٌ؛ فَإِنْ تَضَمَّنَ الثَّانِي حَرْفًا يَجِبُ بِنَاؤُهُمَا عَلَى الْفَتْحِ، كَأَحَدَ عَشَرَ إِلَى تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ، إِلَّا اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ؛ فَإِنَّهَا مُعْرَبَةٌ كَالْمُثَنَّى.
text.en: Section. The sounds (aṣwāt): every utterance by which a sound is imitated, as ghāqi for the sound of the crow, or by which beasts are called, as nakh for making the camel kneel. Section. The compounds: every noun compounded of two words between which there is no relation. If the second contains [the meaning of] a particle, both must be fixed on the fatḥa, as aḥada ʿashara “eleven” to tisʿata ʿashara “nineteen”, except ithnay ʿashara “twelve”, for it is inflected like the dual.

text.original: وَإِنْ لَمْ يَتَضَمَّنْ فَفِيهَا لُغَاتٌ، أَفْصَحُهَا بِنَاءُ الْأَوَّلِ عَلَى الْفَتْحِ وَإِعْرَابُ الثَّانِي إِعْرَابَ غَيْرِ الْمُنْصَرِفِ، كَبَعْلَبَكَّ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي بَعْلَبَكُّ، وَرَأَيْتُ بَعْلَبَكَّ، وَمَرَرْتُ بِبَعْلَبَكَّ.
text.en: If it does not contain [it], there are [several] dialects in it; the most correct is to fix the first on the fatḥa and to inflect the second with the iʿrāb of the diptote, as Baʿlabakka: jāʾanī Baʿlabakku “Baʿlabakk came to me”, raʾaytu Baʿlabakka “I saw Baʿlabakk” and marartu bi-Baʿlabakka “I passed by Baʿlabakk”.

lessons.title: The allusive nouns: kam, kadhā, kayta
body: The allusive nouns (kināyāt) stand for a vague number, kam and kadhā, or a vague report, kayta and dhayta, “such and such”. Kam is of two kinds. Interrogative kam asks, and the word after it is in naṣb and singular, as a tamyīz: kam rajulan ʿindaka, “how many men are with you?”. Declarative kam (khabariyya) tells of a great number, and the word after it is in jarr, singular or plural: kam mālin anfaqtuhu, “how much wealth I have spent!”; kam rijālin laqītuhum.
Min may come in both: kam min rajulin laqītahu. And the tamyīz may be dropped with a context: kam māluka, “that is, kam dīnāran māluka”; kam ḍarabta, “that is, kam ḍarbatan ḍarabta”.

Kam itself is built, so it has only a place in iʿrāb, and the book shows how to find it. It is in naṣb when a verb after it is not kept busy away from it by its pronoun: as an object, kam rajulan ḍarabta; as an absolute object, kam ḍarbatan ḍarabta; as a mafʿūl fīhi, kam yawman sirta; and the same with declarative kam: kam ghulāmin malakta, kam ḍarbatin ḍarabtu, kam yawmin ṣumtu.

It is in jarr when a particle of jarr or a muḍāf comes before it: bi-kam rajulan mararta, ʿalā kam rajulin ḥakamta, ghulāma kam rajulan ḍarabta, māla kam rajulin salabta. Otherwise it is in rafʿ: a mubtadaʾ if it is not an adverb, kam rajulan akhūka, and kam rajulin ḍarabtuhu, where the verb is busy with the hāʾ; a khabar if it is an adverb, kam yawman safaruka, kam shahrin ṣawmī.

So to parse kam a student looks first at what comes before it, then at the verb after it, and only then at the word that follows. This is the question the madrasa asks of every built word: not what its ending is, which never changes, but what place it fills.

tasks.prompt: Asking or telling? Parse the word after kam: kam rajulan ʿindaka; kam mālin anfaqtuhu.
tasks.arabic: كَمْ رَجُلًا عِنْدَكَ — كَمْ مَالٍ أَنْفَقْتُهُ
tasks.answer: Kam rajulan ʿindaka asks: rajulan is its tamyīz, in naṣb, singular. Kam mālin anfaqtuhu tells of much: mālin is in jarr, the muḍāf ilayhi of kam.

tasks.prompt: Give the place of kam in kam rajulan ḍarabta and in kam rajulin ḍarabtuhu.
tasks.arabic: كَمْ رَجُلًا ضَرَبْتَ — كَمْ رَجُلٍ ضَرَبْتُهُ
tasks.answer: In the first, ḍarabta is not busy with a pronoun, so kam is its object, in naṣb in its place. In the second, ḍarabtuhu is busy with the hāʾ, so kam is a mubtadaʾ, in rafʿ in its place, and the sentence after it is its khabar.

tasks.prompt: Supply the dropped tamyīz: kam māluka; kam ḍarabta.
tasks.answer: Kam dīnāran māluka, “how many dinars is your wealth?”; kam ḍarbatan ḍarabta, “how many blows did you strike?”.

tasks.prompt: Why is kam in jarr in ghulāma kam rajulan ḍarabta, and what is ghulāma?
tasks.answer: A muḍāf, ghulāma, comes before it, so kam is in jarr in its place as the muḍāf ilayhi. Ghulāma is the object of ḍarabta, put first, in naṣb.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الْكِنَايَاتُ هِيَ أَسْمَاءٌ تَدُلُّ عَلَى عَدَدٍ مُبْهَمٍ، وَهِيَ كَمْ وَكَذَا، أَوْ حَدِيثٍ مُبْهَمٍ، وَهُوَ كَيْتَ وَذَيْتَ. وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ كَمْ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: اسْتِفْهَامِيَّةٌ، وَمَا بَعْدَهَا مَنْصُوبٌ مُفْرَدٌ عَلَى التَّمْيِيزِ، نَحْوُ: كَمْ رَجُلًا عِنْدَكَ؟ وَخَبَرِيَّةٌ، وَمَا بَعْدَهَا مَجْرُورٌ مُفْرَدٌ، نَحْوُ: كَمْ مَالٍ أَنْفَقْتُهُ، أَوْ مَجْمُوعٌ، نَحْوُ: كَمْ رِجَالٍ لَقِيتُهُمْ، وَمَعْنَاهُ التَّكْثِيرُ.
text.en: Section. The allusive nouns (kināyāt) are nouns that indicate a vague number — they are kam and kadhā — or a vague report — that is, kayta and dhayta. Know that kam is of two kinds. Interrogative (istifhāmiyya): what comes after it is manṣūb and singular, as a tamyīz, as kam rajulan ʿindaka “how many men are with you?”. And declarative (khabariyya): what comes after it is majrūr, singular, as kam mālin anfaqtuhu “how much wealth I have spent!”, or plural, as kam rijālin laqītuhum “how many men I have met!”; and its meaning is a great number.

text.original: وَتَدْخُلُ مِنْ فِيهِمَا، تَقُولُ: كَمْ مِنْ رَجُلٍ لَقِيتَهُ، وَكَمْ مِنْ مَالٍ أَنْفَقْتَهُ. وَقَدْ يُحْذَفُ التَّمْيِيزُ لِقِيَامِ قَرِينَةٍ، نَحْوُ: كَمْ مَالُكَ؟ أَيْ كَمْ دِينَارًا مَالُكَ، وَكَمْ ضَرَبْتَ؟ أَيْ كَمْ ضَرْبَةً ضَرَبْتَ.
text.en: Min comes in both; you say kam min rajulin laqītahu “how many a man you met!” and kam min mālin anfaqtahu “how much wealth you spent!”. The tamyīz may be dropped because there is an indication, as kam māluka “how much is your wealth?”, that is, kam dīnāran māluka “how many dinars is your wealth?”, and kam ḍarabta “how many did you strike?”, that is, kam ḍarbatan ḍarabta “how many blows did you strike?”.

text.original: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ كَمْ فِي الْوَجْهَيْنِ يَقَعُ مَنْصُوبًا إِذَا كَانَ بَعْدَهُ فِعْلٌ غَيْرُ مُشْتَغِلٍ عَنْهُ بِضَمِيرِهِ، نَحْوُ: كَمْ رَجُلًا ضَرَبْتَ، وَكَمْ غُلَامٍ مَلَكْتَ، مَفْعُولًا بِهِ، وَنَحْوُ: كَمْ ضَرْبَةً ضَرَبْتَ، وَكَمْ ضَرْبَةٍ ضَرَبْتُ، مَصْدَرًا، وَكَمْ يَوْمًا سِرْتَ، وَكَمْ يَوْمٍ صُمْتُ، مَفْعُولًا فِيهِ.
text.en: Know that kam, in both ways, is manṣūb when after it there is a verb not kept busy away from it by its pronoun: as mafʿūl bihi, as kam rajulan ḍarabta “how many men did you hit?” and kam ghulāmin malakta “how many servants you have owned!”; as maṣdar, as kam ḍarbatan ḍarabta “how many blows did you strike?” and kam ḍarbatin ḍarabtu “how many blows I struck!”; and as mafʿūl fīhi, as kam yawman sirta “how many days did you travel?” and kam yawmin ṣumtu “how many days I fasted!”.

text.original: وَمَجْرُورًا إِذَا كَانَ قَبْلَهُ حَرْفُ جَرٍّ أَوْ مُضَافٌ، نَحْوُ: بِكَمْ رَجُلًا مَرَرْتَ، وَعَلَى كَمْ رَجُلٍ حَكَمْتَ، وَغُلَامَ كَمْ رَجُلًا ضَرَبْتَ، وَمَالَ كَمْ رَجُلٍ سَلَبْتَ. وَمَرْفُوعًا إِذَا لَمْ يَكُنْ شَيْئًا مِنَ الْأَمْرَيْنِ، مُبْتَدَأً إِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ ظَرْفًا، نَحْوُ: كَمْ رَجُلًا أَخُوكَ، وَكَمْ رَجُلٍ ضَرَبْتُهُ، وَخَبَرًا إِنْ كَانَ ظَرْفًا، نَحْوُ: كَمْ يَوْمًا سَفَرُكَ، وَكَمْ شَهْرٍ صَوْمِي.
text.en: It is majrūr when before it there is a particle of jarr or a muḍāf, as bi-kam rajulan mararta “by how many men did you pass?”, ʿalā kam rajulin ḥakamta “over how many men you have judged!”, ghulāma kam rajulan ḍarabta “the servant of how many men did you hit?” and māla kam rajulin salabta “the wealth of how many men you have taken!”. It is marfūʿ when it is neither of the two: a mubtadaʾ if it is not an adverb, as kam rajulan akhūka “how many men are your brothers?” and kam rajulin ḍarabtuhu “how many a man I have hit!”; and a khabar if it is an adverb, as kam yawman safaruka “how many days is your journey?” and kam shahrin ṣawmī “how many months my fast has been!”.

lessons.title: The built adverbs: qablu, ḥaythu, idhā, idh, ayna, annā
body: Some adverbs are built because they have been cut off from the iḍāfa: their muḍāf ilayhi is dropped but still intended. Qablu, baʿdu, fawqu, taḥtu: li-Allāhi al-amru min qablu wa-min baʿdu (Q 30:4), “that is, min qabli kulli shayʾin wa-min baʿdi kulli shayʾin”. If the dropped word is not intended, they are inflected, and so the verse has also been read min qablin wa-min baʿdin. They are called the ghāyāt, “end-words”: the commentators explain that, the muḍāf ilayhi gone, the adverb itself becomes the end of the phrase.

Ḥaythu is built because it resembles them: it is “mostly bound to iḍāfa to a sentence”, as sa-nastadrijuhum min ḥaythu lā yaʿlamūna, “We shall draw them on from where they do not know” (Q 7:182). In verse it is sometimes muḍāf to a single word, amā tarā ḥaythu Suhaylin ṭāliʿan, “do you not see where Suhayl is, rising?”, that is, makāna Suhaylin. But its condition is the sentence: ijlis ḥaythu jalasa Zaydun.

Idhā is for the future, and it turns a past verb after it into a future: idhā jāʾa naṣru Allāhi (Q 110:1), “when the help of God comes”. It has the meaning of a condition. A nominal sentence may follow it, ātīka idhā al-shamsu ṭāliʿatun, but a verbal one is preferred, idhā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu. It may also be for surprise, and then a mubtadaʾ is preferred after it: kharajtu fa-idhā al-sabuʿu wāqifun, “I went out, and there was the lion, standing”.

Idh is for the past, and both kinds of sentence follow it: jiʾtuka idh ṭalaʿati al-shamsu, and idhi al-shamsu ṭāliʿatun. Ayna and annā are for place: as questions, ayna tamshī, “where are you walking?”, annā taqʿudu; and as conditions, which put both verbs in jazm, ayna tajlis ajlis, “wherever you sit, I sit”, annā taqum aqum.

tasks.prompt: Explain the two readings min qablu wa-min baʿdu and min qablin wa-min baʿdin.
tasks.answer: In min qablu wa-min baʿdu the muḍāf ilayhi (kulli shayʾin) is dropped but intended, so the adverbs are built on ḍamma. In min qablin wa-min baʿdin it is not intended; the adverbs are inflected, in jarr after min, with tanwīn.

tasks.prompt: Why is ḥaythu built, and what is its condition?
tasks.answer: It is built by likeness to the ghāyāt, because it is mostly bound to iḍāfa to a sentence. Its condition is to be muḍāf to a sentence, as ijlis ḥaythu jalasa Zaydun; with a single word, as ḥaythu Suhaylin, it is found only in verse.

tasks.prompt: Which is preferred, and why: ātīka idhā al-shamsu ṭāliʿatun or ātīka idhā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu? And after the idhā of surprise?
tasks.answer: After idhā of time, which has the meaning of a condition, the verbal sentence is preferred: idhā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu. After the idhā of surprise a mubtadaʾ is preferred: fa-idhā al-sabuʿu wāqifun.

tasks.prompt: Give ayna as a question and as a condition, with the iʿrāb of the verbs.
tasks.answer: As a question: ayna tamshī, “where are you walking?”; the verb is in rafʿ. As a condition: ayna tajlis ajlis, “wherever you sit, I sit”; both verbs are in jazm, as condition and response.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الظُّرُوفُ الْمَبْنِيَّةُ عَلَى أَقْسَامٍ: مِنْهَا مَا قُطِعَ عَنِ الْإِضَافَةِ، بِأَنْ حُذِفَ الْمُضَافُ إِلَيْهِ، كَقَبْلُ وَبَعْدُ وَفَوْقُ وَتَحْتُ، قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى: لِلَّهِ الْأَمْرُ مِنْ قَبْلُ وَمِنْ بَعْدُ، أَيْ مِنْ قَبْلِ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ وَمِنْ بَعْدِ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ. هَذَا إِذَا كَانَ الْمَحْذُوفُ مَنْوِيًّا لِلْمُتَكَلِّمِ، وَإِلَّا كَانَتْ مُعْرَبَةً، وَعَلَى هَذَا قُرِئَ: لِلَّهِ الْأَمْرُ مِنْ قَبْلٍ وَمِنْ بَعْدٍ، وَتُسَمَّى الْغَايَاتِ.
text.en: Section. The fixed adverbs are of [several] kinds. Among them is what is cut off from iḍāfa, in that the muḍāf ilayhi is dropped, as qablu “before”, baʿdu “after”, fawqu “above” and taḥtu “below”; God Most High said: li-Allāhi al-amru min qablu wa-min baʿdu “to God belongs the command, before and after”, that is, min qabli kulli shayʾin wa-min baʿdi kulli shayʾin “before everything and after everything”. This is when what is dropped is intended by the speaker; otherwise they are inflected, and in this way it has been read li-Allāhi al-amru min qablin wa-min baʿdin. They are called the ghāyāt (end-words).

text.original: وَمِنْهَا حَيْثُ، بُنِيَتْ تَشْبِيهًا لَهَا بِالْغَايَاتِ؛ لِمُلَازَمَتِهَا الْإِضَافَةَ إِلَى الْجُمْلَةِ فِي الْأَكْثَرِ، قَالَ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى: سَنَسْتَدْرِجُهُمْ مِنْ حَيْثُ لَا يَعْلَمُونَ، وَقَدْ يُضَافُ إِلَى الْمُفْرَدِ، كَقَوْلِ الشَّاعِرِ: أَمَا تَرَى حَيْثُ سُهَيْلٍ طَالِعًا، أَيْ مَكَانَ سُهَيْلٍ؛ فَحَيْثُ هَهُنَا بِمَعْنَى مَكَانٍ، وَشَرْطُهَا أَنْ تُضَافَ إِلَى الْجُمْلَةِ، نَحْوُ: اجْلِسْ حَيْثُ جَلَسَ زَيْدٌ.
text.en: Among them is ḥaythu “where”: it is fixed by comparison with the ghāyāt, because it is mostly bound to iḍāfa to a sentence; God Most High said: sa-nastadrijuhum min ḥaythu lā yaʿlamūna “We shall draw them on by degrees from where they do not know”. It is sometimes made muḍāf to a single word, as in the poet's saying: amā tarā ḥaythu Suhaylin ṭāliʿan “do you not see where Suhayl (Canopus) is, rising?”, that is, makāna Suhaylin “the place of Suhayl”; so ḥaythu here is in the meaning of “place”. Its condition is that it is made muḍāf to a sentence, as ijlis ḥaythu jalasa Zaydun “sit where Zayd sat”.

text.original: وَمِنْهَا إِذَا، وَهِيَ لِلْمُسْتَقْبَلِ، وَإِذَا دَخَلَتْ عَلَى الْمَاضِي صَارَ مُسْتَقْبَلًا، نَحْوُ: إِذَا جَاءَ نَصْرُ اللَّهِ، وَفِيهَا مَعْنَى الشَّرْطِ. وَيَجُوزُ أَنْ تَقَعَ بَعْدَهَا الْجُمْلَةُ الِاسْمِيَّةُ، نَحْوُ: آتِيكَ إِذَا الشَّمْسُ طَالِعَةٌ، وَالْمُخْتَارُ الْفِعْلِيَّةُ، نَحْوُ: آتِيكَ إِذَا طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ. وَقَدْ تَكُونُ لِلْمُفَاجَأَةِ، فَيُخْتَارُ بَعْدَهَا الْمُبْتَدَأُ، نَحْوُ: خَرَجْتُ فَإِذَا السَّبُعُ وَاقِفٌ.
text.en: Among them is idhā “when”: it is for the future, and when it comes upon the past, [the past] becomes future, as idhā jāʾa naṣru Allāhi “when the help of God comes”; and there is a meaning of condition in it. A nominal sentence may stand after it, as ātīka idhā al-shamsu ṭāliʿatun “I will come to you when the sun is risen”, but the verbal one is preferred, as ātīka idhā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu “I will come to you when the sun rises”. It may be for surprise (mufājaʾa), and then a mubtadaʾ is preferred after it, as kharajtu fa-idhā al-sabuʿu wāqifun “I went out, and there was the beast of prey, standing”.

text.original: وَمِنْهَا إِذْ، وَهِيَ لِلْمَاضِي، وَتَقَعُ بَعْدَهَا الْجُمْلَتَانِ الِاسْمِيَّةُ وَالْفِعْلِيَّةُ، نَحْوُ: جِئْتُكَ إِذْ طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ، وَإِذِ الشَّمْسُ طَالِعَةٌ. وَمِنْهَا أَيْنَ وَأَنَّى لِلْمَكَانِ بِمَعْنَى الِاسْتِفْهَامِ، نَحْوُ: أَيْنَ تَمْشِي؟ وَأَنَّى تَقْعُدُ؟ وَبِمَعْنَى الشَّرْطِ، نَحْوُ: أَيْنَ تَجْلِسْ أَجْلِسْ، وَأَنَّى تَقُمْ أَقُمْ.
text.en: Among them is idh: it is for the past, and both sentences, the nominal and the verbal, stand after it, as jiʾtuka idh ṭalaʿati al-shamsu “I came to you when the sun rose” and wa-idhi al-shamsu ṭāliʿatun “and when the sun was risen”. Among them are ayna and annā, for place, in the meaning of question, as ayna tamshī “where are you walking?” and wa-annā taqʿudu “and where will you sit?”, and in the meaning of condition, as ayna tajlis ajlis “wherever you sit, I sit” and wa-annā taqum aqum “and wherever you stand, I stand”.

lessons.title: The built adverbs: matā, kayfa, mudh, ladā, qaṭṭu; adverbs before a sentence
body: Matā is for time, as condition and as question: matā taṣum aṣum, “whenever you fast, I fast”; matā tusāfiru, “when will you travel?”. Kayfa asks about the state: kayfa anta, “that is, fī ayyi ḥālin anta”, in what state are you? Ayyāna asks about time: ayyāna yawmu al-dīni, “when is the Day of Judgement?” (Q 51:12).

Mudh and mundhu mean “the beginning of the period” when they can answer “matā?”: mā raʾaytuhu mudh yawm al-jumuʿa, said to one who asks since when you have not seen Zayd; the first day of not seeing him was Friday. They mean “the whole period” when they can answer “kam?”: mā raʾaytuhu mudh yawmāni, said to one who asks for how long; the whole time is two days. The test of the two questions tells the student which meaning he has.

Ladā and ladun mean ʿinda, “with”: al-mālu ladayka. The difference: ʿinda does not need the thing to be present, ladā and ladun do; one may say that wealth is ʿindī while it is in another town. Ladun also has the forms ladnu, ladin, ladu and lad. Qaṭṭu is for the negated past, mā raʾaytuhu qaṭṭu, “I have never seen him”; ʿawḍu for the negated future, lā aḍribuhu ʿawḍu, “I will never hit him”. So for “never” in the future the book gives ʿawḍu, not qaṭṭu.

Last, an adverb made muḍāf to a sentence, or to idh, “may be built on the fatḥa”: hādhā yawma yanfaʿu al-ṣādiqīna ṣidquhum (Q 5:119), in the reading with yawma, where yawm stands as a khabar; and yawmaʾidhin, ḥīnaʾidhin. So too mithl and ghayr before mā, an and anna: ḍarabtuhu mithla mā ḍaraba Zaydun, wa-ghayra an ḍaraba Zaydun. And amsi, “yesterday”, is built on kasra among the people of the Ḥijāz.

tasks.prompt: Which meaning of mudh, and which question does each answer? mā raʾaytuhu mudh yawm al-jumuʿa; mā raʾaytuhu mudh yawmāni.
tasks.answer: The first gives the beginning of the period and answers matā, “since when?”: since Friday. The second gives the whole period and answers kam, “for how long?”: two days.

tasks.prompt: Say “I have never seen him” and “I will never hit him” as the book does, and explain the choice of word.
tasks.answer: Mā raʾaytuhu qaṭṭu, with qaṭṭu, which is for the negated past; lā aḍribuhu ʿawḍu, with ʿawḍu, which is for the negated future.

tasks.prompt: How does ladā differ from ʿinda?
tasks.answer: Both mean “with”. Ladā and ladun require the thing to be present with the person; ʿinda does not.

tasks.prompt: Why may yawma in hādhā yawma yanfaʿu be built on fatḥa, though it is the khabar of hādhā?
tasks.answer: It is an adverb made muḍāf to a sentence (yanfaʿu al-ṣādiqīna ṣidquhum), and such an adverb may be built on fatḥa. It is then in rafʿ only in its place.

text.original: وَمِنْهَا مَتَى لِلزَّمَانِ، شَرْطًا وَاسْتِفْهَامًا، نَحْوُ: مَتَى تَصُمْ أَصُمْ، وَمَتَى تُسَافِرُ؟ وَمِنْهَا كَيْفَ لِلِاسْتِفْهَامِ حَالًا، نَحْوُ: كَيْفَ أَنْتَ؟ أَيْ فِي أَيِّ حَالٍ أَنْتَ. وَمِنْهَا أَيَّانَ لِلزَّمَانِ اسْتِفْهَامًا، نَحْوُ: أَيَّانَ يَوْمُ الدِّينِ؟
text.en: Among them is matā “when”, for time, as condition and as question, as matā taṣum aṣum “whenever you fast, I fast” and wa-matā tusāfiru “and when will you travel?”. Among them is kayfa “how”, for the question about the state, as kayfa anta “how are you?”, that is, fī ayyi ḥālin anta “in what state are you?”. Among them is ayyāna “when”, for time, as a question, as ayyāna yawmu al-dīni “when is the Day of Judgement?”.

text.original: وَمِنْهَا مُذْ وَمُنْذُ بِمَعْنَى أَوَّلِ الْمُدَّةِ إِنْ صَلُحَ جَوَابًا لِمَتَى، نَحْوُ: مَا رَأَيْتُهُ مُذْ أَوْ مُنْذُ يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ، فِي جَوَابِ مَنْ قَالَ: مَتَى مَا رَأَيْتَ زَيْدًا؟ أَيْ أَوَّلُ مُدَّةِ انْقِطَاعِ رُؤْيَتِي إِيَّاهُ يَوْمُ الْجُمُعَةِ؛ وَبِمَعْنَى جَمِيعِ الْمُدَّةِ إِنْ صَلُحَ جَوَابًا لِكَمْ، نَحْوُ: مَا رَأَيْتُهُ مُذْ أَوْ مُنْذُ يَوْمَانِ، فِي جَوَابِ مَنْ قَالَ: كَمْ مُدَّةً مَا رَأَيْتَ زَيْدًا؟ أَيْ جَمِيعُ مُدَّةِ مَا رَأَيْتُهُ يَوْمَانِ.
text.en: Among them are mudh and mundhu “since”: in the meaning of the beginning of the period if it can be the answer to matā, as mā raʾaytuhu mudh aw mundhu yawmi al-jumuʿati “I have not seen him since Friday”, in answer to one who says matā mā raʾayta Zaydan “since when have you not seen Zayd?”, that is, the beginning of the period in which my seeing him has been cut off is Friday; and in the meaning of the whole period if it can be the answer to kam, as mā raʾaytuhu mudh aw mundhu yawmāni “I have not seen him for two days”, in answer to one who says kam muddatan mā raʾayta Zaydan “for how long have you not seen Zayd?”, that is, the whole period in which I have not seen him is two days.

text.original: وَمِنْهَا لَدَى وَلَدُنْ بِمَعْنَى عِنْدَ، نَحْوُ: الْمَالُ لَدَيْكَ، وَالْفَرْقُ بَيْنَهُمَا أَنَّ عِنْدَ لَا يُشْتَرَطُ فِيهِ الْحُضُورُ، وَيُشْتَرَطُ ذَلِكَ فِي لَدَى وَلَدُنْ، وَجَاءَ فِيهِ لُغَاتٌ أُخَرُ: لَدْنُ، وَلَدِنْ، وَلَدُ، وَلَدْ. وَمِنْهَا قَطُّ لِلْمَاضِي الْمَنْفِيِّ، نَحْوُ: مَا رَأَيْتُهُ قَطُّ. وَمِنْهَا عَوْضُ لِلْمُسْتَقْبَلِ الْمَنْفِيِّ، نَحْوُ: لَا أَضْرِبُهُ عَوْضُ.
text.en: Among them are ladā and ladun in the meaning of ʿinda “with”, as al-mālu ladayka “the wealth is with you”. The difference between them is that presence is not a condition in ʿinda, while it is a condition in ladā and ladun. Other dialect forms of it have come: ladnu, ladin, ladu and lad. Among them is qaṭṭu “ever”, for the negated past, as mā raʾaytuhu qaṭṭu “I have never seen him”. Among them is ʿawḍu “ever”, for the negated future, as lā aḍribuhu ʿawḍu “I will never hit him”.

text.original: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ إِذَا أُضِيفَ الظَّرْفُ إِلَى الْجُمْلَةِ وَإِلَى إِذْ جَازَ بِنَاؤُهَا عَلَى الْفَتْحِ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: هَذَا يَوْمَ يَنْفَعُ الصَّادِقِينَ صِدْقُهُمْ، وَكَيَوْمَئِذٍ وَحِينَئِذٍ. وَكَذَلِكَ مِثْلُ وَغَيْرُ مَعَ مَا وَأَنْ وَأَنَّ، تَقُولُ: ضَرَبْتُهُ مِثْلَ مَا ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ، وَغَيْرَ أَنْ ضَرَبَ زَيْدٌ. وَمِنْهَا أَمْسِ بِالْكَسْرِ عِنْدَ أَهْلِ الْحِجَازِ.
text.en: Know that when an adverb is made muḍāf to a sentence or to idh, it may be fixed on the fatḥa, as in His saying, exalted is He: hādhā yawma yanfaʿu al-ṣādiqīna ṣidquhum “this is the day when their truthfulness will profit the truthful”, and as yawmaʾidhin “on that day” and ḥīnaʾidhin “at that time”. Likewise mithl and ghayr with mā, an and anna; you say ḍarabtuhu mithla mā ḍaraba Zaydun “I hit him as Zayd hit” and wa-ghayra an ḍaraba Zaydun “and other than that Zayd hit”. Among them is amsi “yesterday”, with the kasra, among the people of the Ḥijāz.

parts.title: The other rules of the noun

lessons.title: The definite and the indefinite; the number words
body: The conclusion of the part on the noun gathers “the remaining rules of the noun, other than iʿrāb and binā”. First, the noun is definite or indefinite. The definite is “a noun laid down for a specific thing”, and it is of six kinds: the pronouns; the proper names; the vague nouns (mubhamāt), that is, the demonstratives and the relatives; the noun with the lām; the noun muḍāf to one of these by an iḍāfa of meaning (lesson 24); and the noun made definite by being called (lesson 18).

The proper name is “laid down for a specific thing and does not, by one laying down, include anything else”. Many men are called Zayd, but each was named by a laying down of his own; the name was not made once for them all, as rajul was.

The definites have ranks. “The most definite of them is the pronoun of the speaker”, anā, naḥnu, then of the one addressed, anta, then of the absent, huwa; then the proper name; then the vague nouns; then the noun with the lām; then the noun made definite by calling. A muḍāf “has the strength of its muḍāf ilayhi”: ghulāmu Zaydin ranks with Zayd. The order makes sense: nothing is clearer to a speaker than himself, and a word that needs pointing or a ṣila is less clear than a name.
The indefinite is “laid down for a thing that is not specific”: rajul, faras, any man, any horse.

The number nouns tell “the quantity of the units of things”. Their roots are twelve words: one to ten, a hundred and a thousand; every other number is made from them. One and two “follow the rule”: the masculine without the tāʾ, the feminine with it: wāḥidun, ithnāni for men; wāḥidatun, ithnatāni or thintāni for women. The next lesson shows why the book calls this “the rule”.

the proper name: for one thing, by one laying down
the vague nouns: the demonstratives and the relatives
the twelve root words of number

examples.en: the most definite: the pronoun of the speaker
indefinites: laid down for no specific thing

tasks.prompt: Name the kind of definite: anta; ʿAmrun; hādhā; al-rajulu; ghulāmu Zaydin; yā rajulu.
tasks.answer: Anta: a pronoun. ʿAmrun: a proper name. Hādhā: a vague noun (a demonstrative). Al-rajulu: defined by the lām. Ghulāmu Zaydin: muḍāf to a definite by an iḍāfa of meaning. Yā rajulu: made definite by being called.

tasks.prompt: Put in order, most definite first: al-rajulu; huwa; Zaydun; anā; hādhā.
tasks.answer: Anā (the speaker), huwa (the absent pronoun), Zaydun (the proper name), hādhā (a vague noun), al-rajulu (the noun with the lām).

tasks.prompt: Many men are called Zayd. Why is Zayd still a proper name?
tasks.answer: The proper name is laid down for a specific thing and does not include anything else by one laying down. Each Zayd was named by a laying down of his own; rajul, by contrast, was laid down once for every man.

tasks.prompt: What are the twelve root words of number?
tasks.answer: The numbers one to ten, a hundred and a thousand. All other numbers are made from these.

quiz.prompt: The definite is a noun laid down for…
quiz.explanation: The indefinite for a thing not specific.

quiz.prompt: How many kinds of definite does the book count?
quiz.explanation: Pronoun, name, vague, lām, iḍāfa, calling.

quiz.prompt: The vague nouns are…
The most definite of all is…
A muḍāf ranks…
quiz.explanation: It has the strength of its muḍāf ilayhi.

quiz.prompt: How many root words of number are there?
quiz.explanation: One to ten, a hundred, a thousand.

quiz.prompt: “Two”, for women, is…
quiz.explanation: One and two take the tāʾ for the feminine.

text.original: وَالْخَاتِمَةُ فِي سَائِرِ أَحْكَامِ الِاسْمِ وَلَوَاحِقِهِ غَيْرِ الْإِعْرَابِ وَالْبِنَاءِ، وَفِيهَا فُصُولٌ. فَصْلٌ: اعْلَمْ أَنَّ الِاسْمَ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: مَعْرِفَةٌ وَنَكِرَةٌ. الْمَعْرِفَةُ اسْمٌ وُضِعَ لِشَيْءٍ مُعَيَّنٍ، وَهِيَ سِتَّةُ أَقْسَامٍ: الْمُضْمَرَاتُ، وَالْأَعْلَامُ، وَالْمُبْهَمَاتُ، أَعْنِي أَسْمَاءَ الْإِشَارَاتِ وَالْمَوْصُولَاتِ، وَالْمُعَرَّفُ بِاللَّامِ، وَالْمُضَافُ إِلَى أَحَدِهَا إِضَافَةً مَعْنَوِيَّةً، وَالْمُعَرَّفُ بِالنِّدَاءِ.
text.en: The conclusion, on the remaining rules of the noun and what is joined to it, other than iʿrāb and bināʾ; it has [several] sections. Section. Know that the noun is of two kinds: definite (maʿrifa) and indefinite (nakira). The definite is a noun laid down for a specific thing. It is of six kinds: the pronouns; the proper names; the vague nouns (mubhamāt), I mean the demonstratives and the relatives; the noun defined by the lām; the noun muḍāf to one of these by iḍāfa by meaning; and the noun defined by the vocative.

text.original: وَالْعَلَمُ مَا وُضِعَ لِشَيْءٍ مُعَيَّنٍ لَا يَتَنَاوَلُ غَيْرَهُ بِوَضْعٍ وَاحِدٍ. وَأَعْرَفُ الْمَعَارِفِ الْمُضْمَرُ الْمُتَكَلِّمُ، نَحْوُ: أَنَا وَنَحْنُ، ثُمَّ الْمُخَاطَبُ، نَحْوُ: أَنْتَ، ثُمَّ الْغَائِبُ، نَحْوُ: هُوَ، ثُمَّ الْعَلَمُ، ثُمَّ الْمُبْهَمَاتُ، ثُمَّ الْمُعَرَّفُ بِاللَّامِ، ثُمَّ الْمُعَرَّفُ بِالنِّدَاءِ، وَالْمُضَافُ فِي قُوَّةِ الْمُضَافِ إِلَيْهِ. وَالنَّكِرَةُ مَا وُضِعَ لِشَيْءٍ غَيْرِ مُعَيَّنٍ، كَرَجُلٍ وَفَرَسٍ.
text.en: The proper name is what is laid down for a specific thing and does not, by one laying down, include anything else. The most definite of the definite nouns is the pronoun of the speaker, as anā “I” and naḥnu “we”; then the one addressed, as anta “you”; then the absent, as huwa “he”; then the proper name; then the vague nouns; then the noun defined by the lām; then the noun defined by the vocative; and the muḍāf has the strength of its muḍāf ilayhi. The indefinite is what is laid down for a thing that is not specific, as rajulin “a man” and farasin “a horse”.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: أَسْمَاءُ الْعَدَدِ مَا وُضِعَ لِيَدُلَّ عَلَى كَمِّيَّةِ آحَادِ الْأَشْيَاءِ، وَأُصُولُ الْعَدَدِ اثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ كَلِمَةً: وَاحِدٌ إِلَى عَشَرَةٍ، وَمِائَةٌ، وَأَلْفٌ. وَاسْتِعْمَالُهُ مِنْ وَاحِدٍ إِلَى اثْنَيْنِ عَلَى الْقِيَاسِ، أَعْنِي لِلْمُذَكَّرِ بِدُونِ التَّاءِ، وَلِلْمُؤَنَّثِ بِالتَّاءِ، تَقُولُ فِي رَجُلٍ: وَاحِدٌ، وَفِي رَجُلَيْنِ: اثْنَانِ، وَفِي امْرَأَةٍ: وَاحِدَةٌ، وَفِي امْرَأَتَيْنِ: اثْنَتَانِ وَثِنْتَانِ.
text.en: Section. The number nouns are what is laid down to indicate the quantity of the units of things. The roots of number are twelve words: one to ten, a hundred and a thousand. Their use from one to two follows the rule, I mean without the tāʾ for the masculine and with the tāʾ for the feminine: you say for a man wāḥidun “one”, for two men ithnāni “two”, for a woman wāḥidatun “one” and for two women ithnatāni and thintāni “two”.

lessons.title: Counting from three to the thousands
body: From three to ten the numbers go “against the rule”: the tāʾ is on the number for men and off it for women: thalāthatu rijālin … ʿasharatu rijālin; thalāthu niswatin … ʿashru niswatin. A student who has learned that the tāʾ marks the feminine must unlearn it here.

After ten: aḥada ʿashara rajulan, ithnā ʿashara rajulan, thalāthata ʿashara rajulan … tisʿata ʿashara rajulan; and for women iḥdā ʿashrata imraʾatan, ithnatā ʿashrata imraʾatan, thalātha ʿashrata imraʾatan … tisʿa ʿashrata imraʾatan. The unit keeps the rule of its own number, against the rule from three; the ten, ʿashara or ʿashrata, takes the gender of the counted, and in the feminine its shīn is quiet.

The tens, ʿishrūna to tisʿūna, are the same for men and women: ʿishrūna rajulan, ʿishrūna imraʾatan. With a unit before them, the unit keeps its own rule: aḥadun wa-ʿishrūna rajulan, iḥdā wa-ʿishrūna imraʾatan, ithnāni or ithnatāni wa-ʿishrūna, thalāthatun or thalāthun wa-ʿishrūna, up to tisʿatun or tisʿun wa-tisʿūna. A hundred and a thousand, and their duals, are again the same for both: miʾatu rajulin, miʾatu imraʾatin, alfu rajulin, miʾatā rajulin, alfā imraʾatin.

Beyond a hundred and a thousand, one builds “by the analogy of what you have learned”, in a fixed order: the thousand before the hundred, the hundred before the units, and the units before the tens. ʿIndī alfun wa-miʾatun wa-aḥadun wa-ʿishrūna rajulan, “one thousand one hundred and twenty-one men”; arbaʿatu ālāfin wa-tisʿumiʾatin wa-khamsun wa-arbaʿūna imraʾatan, “four thousand nine hundred and forty-five women”. “And keep to the analogy.”

terms.en: against the rule: the tāʾ with men from three to ten
the compound numbers, eleven to nineteen
the tens, twenty to ninety, alike for both genders
a unit joined to a ten: one and twenty

examples.en: three to ten: the tāʾ with men

examples.arabic: إِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً، وَاثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً
examples.en: eleven and twelve, feminine

examples.arabic: وَأَحَدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا، وَإِحْدَى وَعِشْرُونَ امْرَأَةً
examples.en: a unit joined to a ten

examples.arabic: عِنْدِي أَلْفٌ وَمِائَةٌ وَأَحَدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا
examples.en: thousand, hundred, units, tens

tasks.prompt: Give the book's forms for “three men”, “three women”, “thirteen men” and “thirteen women”.
tasks.arabic: ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ — ثَلَاثُ نِسْوَةٍ — ثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا — ثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً
tasks.answer: Thalāthatu rijālin and thalāthu niswatin (from three to ten the tāʾ goes with men); thalāthata ʿashara rajulan and thalātha ʿashrata imraʾatan (the unit keeps its rule, the ten takes the gender of the counted).

tasks.prompt: Which numbers are the same for men and women?
tasks.answer: The tens from twenty to ninety (ʿishrūna rajulan, ʿishrūna imraʾatan), and a hundred and a thousand with their duals (miʾatu rajulin, miʾatu imraʾatin, alfā rajulin, alfā imraʾatin).

tasks.prompt: Say “twenty-two men” and “twenty-two women”.
tasks.answer: Ithnāni wa-ʿishrūna rajulan; ithnatāni wa-ʿishrūna imraʾatan. The unit keeps its own rule; the ten does not change.

tasks.prompt: In what order are the parts of a large number said? Give the book's example with women.
tasks.answer: The thousand before the hundred, the hundred before the units, the units before the tens: arbaʿatu ālāfin wa-tisʿumiʾatin wa-khamsun wa-arbaʿūna imraʾatan, “four thousand nine hundred and forty-five women”.

quiz.prompt: From three to ten the masculine is counted…
“Ten women” is…
“Eleven women” is…
The tens from twenty to ninety…
options: are the same for both genders

quiz.prompt: “Twenty-one women” is…
quiz.explanation: The unit before the ten, with its own gender.

quiz.prompt: A hundred and a thousand are…
options: the same for men and women

quiz.prompt: In a large number, which comes first?

text.original: وَمِنْ ثَلَاثَةٍ إِلَى عَشَرَةٍ عَلَى خِلَافِ الْقِيَاسِ، أَعْنِي لِلْمُذَكَّرِ بِالتَّاءِ، تَقُولُ: ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ إِلَى عَشَرَةِ رِجَالٍ، وَلِلْمُؤَنَّثِ بِدُونِهَا، تَقُولُ: ثَلَاثُ نِسْوَةٍ إِلَى عَشْرِ نِسْوَةٍ. وَبَعْدَ الْعَشَرَةِ تَقُولُ: أَحَدَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا، وَاثْنَا عَشَرَ رَجُلًا، وَثَلَاثَةَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا إِلَى تِسْعَةَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا، وَإِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً، وَاثْنَتَا عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً، وَثَلَاثَ عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً إِلَى تِسْعَ عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً.
text.en: From three to ten it goes against the rule, I mean with the tāʾ for the masculine — you say thalāthatu rijālin “three men” to ʿasharati rijālin “ten men” — and without it for the feminine — you say thalāthu niswatin “three women” to ʿashri niswatin “ten women”. After ten you say aḥada ʿashara rajulan “eleven men”, wa-ithnā ʿashara rajulan “and twelve men” and wa-thalāthata ʿashara rajulan “and thirteen men” to tisʿata ʿashara rajulan “nineteen men”; and wa-iḥdā ʿashrata imraʾatan “and eleven women”, wa-ithnatā ʿashrata imraʾatan “and twelve women” and wa-thalātha ʿashrata imraʾatan “and thirteen women” to tisʿa ʿashrata imraʾatan “nineteen women”.

text.original: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ تَقُولُ: عِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا، وَعِشْرُونَ امْرَأَةً، بِلَا فَرْقٍ بَيْنَ الْمُذَكَّرِ وَالْمُؤَنَّثِ إِلَى التِّسْعِينَ، وَأَحَدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا، وَإِحْدَى وَعِشْرُونَ امْرَأَةً، وَاثْنَانِ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا، وَاثْنَتَانِ وَعِشْرُونَ امْرَأَةً، وَثَلَاثَةٌ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا، وَثَلَاثٌ وَعِشْرُونَ امْرَأَةً، إِلَى تِسْعَةٍ وَتِسْعِينَ رَجُلًا، وَتِسْعٍ وَتِسْعِينَ امْرَأَةً. ثُمَّ تَقُولُ: مِائَةُ رَجُلٍ، وَمِائَةُ امْرَأَةٍ، وَأَلْفُ رَجُلٍ، وَأَلْفُ امْرَأَةٍ، وَمِائَتَا رَجُلٍ، وَمِائَتَا امْرَأَةٍ، وَأَلْفَا رَجُلٍ، وَأَلْفَا امْرَأَةٍ، بِلَا فَرْقٍ بَيْنَ الْمُذَكَّرِ وَالْمُؤَنَّثِ.
text.en: After that you say ʿishrūna rajulan “twenty men” and wa-ʿishrūna imraʾatan “and twenty women”, without difference between the masculine and the feminine, up to ninety; and wa-aḥadun wa-ʿishrūna rajulan “and twenty-one men”, wa-iḥdā wa-ʿishrūna imraʾatan “and twenty-one women”, wa-ithnāni wa-ʿishrūna rajulan “and twenty-two men”, wa-ithnatāni wa-ʿishrūna imraʾatan “and twenty-two women”, wa-thalāthatun wa-ʿishrūna rajulan “and twenty-three men” and wa-thalāthun wa-ʿishrūna imraʾatan “and twenty-three women”, up to tisʿatin wa-tisʿīna rajulan “ninety-nine men” and wa-tisʿin wa-tisʿīna imraʾatan “and ninety-nine women”. Then you say miʾatu rajulin “a hundred men”, wa-miʾatu imraʾatin “and a hundred women”, wa-alfu rajulin “and a thousand men”, wa-alfu imraʾatin “and a thousand women”, wa-miʾatā rajulin “and two hundred men”, wa-miʾatā imraʾatin “and two hundred women”, wa-alfā rajulin “and two thousand men” and wa-alfā imraʾatin “and two thousand women”, without difference between the masculine and the feminine.

text.original: فَإِذَا زَادَ عَلَى الْمِائَةِ وَالْأَلْفِ يُسْتَعْمَلُ عَلَى قِيَاسِ مَا عَرَفْتَ، وَيُقَدَّمُ الْأَلْفُ عَلَى الْمِائَةِ، وَالْمِائَةُ عَلَى الْآحَادِ، وَالْآحَادُ عَلَى الْعَشَرَاتِ، تَقُولُ: عِنْدِي أَلْفٌ وَمِائَةٌ وَأَحَدٌ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا، وَأَلْفَانِ وَمِائَتَانِ وَاثْنَانِ وَعِشْرُونَ رَجُلًا، وَأَرْبَعَةُ آلَافٍ وَتِسْعُمِائَةٍ وَخَمْسٌ وَأَرْبَعُونَ امْرَأَةً، وَعَلَيْكَ بِالْقِيَاسِ.
text.en: When it goes beyond the hundred and the thousand, it is used by the analogy of what you have learned; the thousand is put before the hundred, the hundred before the units and the units before the tens; you say ʿindī alfun wa-miʾatun wa-aḥadun wa-ʿishrūna rajulan “I have one thousand one hundred and twenty-one men”, wa-alfāni wa-miʾatāni wa-ithnāni wa-ʿishrūna rajulan “and two thousand two hundred and twenty-two men” and wa-arbaʿatu ālāfin wa-tisʿumiʾatin wa-khamsun wa-arbaʿūna imraʾatan “and four thousand nine hundred and forty-five women”; and keep to the analogy.

lessons.title: The specifier of the numbers; masculine and feminine
body: One and two have no specifier (mumayyiz), “because the word of the specified thing makes the mention of the number needless”: ʿindī rajulun wa-rajulāni. Rajulun already says one, and rajulāni two. Every other number needs its specifier, and each range takes it in its own way.

The specifier of three to ten is in khafḍ and plural: thalāthatu rijālin, thalāthu niswatin; except when it is the word miʾa, which stays singular: thalāthumiʾatin … tisʿumiʾatin, “while the analogy would be thalāthu miʾātin or miʾīna”. The specifier of eleven to ninety-nine is in naṣb and singular, a tamyīz: aḥada ʿashara rajulan, tisʿatun wa-tisʿūna imraʾatan. The specifier of a hundred, a thousand, their duals, and the plural of thousand is in khafḍ and singular: miʾatu rajulin, alfā imraʾatin, thalāthatu ālāfi rajulin.

A noun is masculine or feminine. The feminine has a sign of the feminine, “in the wording or implied”. The signs are three: the tāʾ, as Ṭalḥa; the short alif, as ḥublā; the long alif, as ḥamrāʾ. Only the tāʾ can be implied, as in arḍ, “earth”, and dār, “house”, “as is shown by urayḍa and duwayra”: the diminutive brings back the tāʾ the word was hiding.

The feminine is true (ḥaqīqī) when a male faces it among living beings, imraʾa, nāqa; otherwise it is verbal (lafẓī), ẓulma, “darkness”, ʿayn, “eye”. How the verb agrees with each was taught in lesson 10, “so we do not repeat it”.

terms.en: the specifier of a number: what is counted
the sign of the feminine: the tāʾ, the short alif, the long alif
the implied tāʾ, shown by the diminutive
the true and the verbal feminine

examples.en: one and two need no specifier
miʾa as specifier of three to nine: singular
eleven to ninety-nine: naṣb, singular
the diminutives that show the implied tāʾ of arḍ and dār

tasks.prompt: Give the state and number of the specifier: thalāthatu rijālin; aḥada ʿashara rajulan; miʾatu rajulin.
tasks.arabic: ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ — أَحَدَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا — مِائَةُ رَجُلٍ
tasks.answer: Rijālin: khafḍ and plural (three to ten). Rajulan: naṣb and singular (eleven to ninety-nine). Rajulin: khafḍ and singular (a hundred).

tasks.prompt: Why does one not say wāḥidu rajulin or ithnā rajulayni?
tasks.answer: One and two have no specifier: the counted noun itself, rajulun or rajulāni, already tells the number, so the number word is not needed.

tasks.prompt: What would the analogy give for “three hundred”, and what is actually said?
tasks.answer: The analogy of three to ten (a plural specifier) would give thalāthu miʾātin or miʾīna; but the Arabs say thalāthumiʾatin, with the singular miʾa.

tasks.prompt: How does the book prove that arḍ and dār are feminine?
tasks.answer: Their diminutives are urayḍa and duwayra, with a tāʾ; the diminutive brings back the implied tāʾ, so the words are feminine though no sign is written.

quiz.prompt: Which numbers have no specifier?
The specifier of three to ten is…
The specifier of twenty is…
Thalāthumiʾatin keeps miʾa…
quiz.explanation: The analogy would be miʾātin or miʾīna.

quiz.prompt: The specifier of a thousand is…
Which sign of the feminine can be implied?
ʿAyn, “eye”, is…
quiz.explanation: No male faces it among living beings.

text.original: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ الْوَاحِدَ وَالِاثْنَيْنِ لَا مُمَيِّزَ لَهُمَا؛ لِأَنَّ لَفْظَ الْمُمَيَّزِ يُغْنِي عَنْ ذِكْرِ الْعَدَدِ فِيهِمَا، تَقُولُ: عِنْدِي رَجُلٌ وَرَجُلَانِ. وَأَمَّا سَائِرُ الْأَعْدَادِ فَلَا بُدَّ لَهَا مِنْ مُمَيِّزٍ؛ فَمُمَيِّزُ الثَّلَاثَةِ إِلَى الْعَشَرَةِ مَخْفُوضٌ مَجْمُوعٌ، تَقُولُ: ثَلَاثَةُ رِجَالٍ، وَثَلَاثُ نِسْوَةٍ، إِلَّا إِذَا كَانَ الْمُمَيِّزُ لَفْظَ الْمِائَةِ، فَحِينَئِذٍ يَكُونُ مَخْفُوضًا مُفْرَدًا، تَقُولُ: ثَلَاثُمِائَةٍ إِلَى تِسْعِمِائَةٍ، وَالْقِيَاسُ: ثَلَاثُ مِئَاتٍ أَوْ مِئِينَ.
text.en: Know that one and two have no specifier (mumayyiz), because the word of the specified [thing] makes the mention of the number needless in them; you say ʿindī rajulun wa-rajulāni “I have a man and two men”. All the other numbers must have a specifier. The specifier of three to ten is in khafḍ and plural; you say thalāthatu rijālin “three men” and wa-thalāthu niswatin “and three women”; except when the specifier is the word miʾa (hundred), for then it is in khafḍ and singular; you say thalāthumiʾatin “three hundred” to tisʿimiʾatin “nine hundred”, while the analogy would be thalāthu miʾātin or miʾīna.

text.original: وَمُمَيِّزُ أَحَدَ عَشَرَ إِلَى تِسْعَةٍ وَتِسْعِينَ مَنْصُوبٌ مُفْرَدٌ، تَقُولُ: أَحَدَ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا، وَإِحْدَى عَشْرَةَ امْرَأَةً، وَتِسْعَةٌ وَتِسْعُونَ رَجُلًا، وَتِسْعٌ وَتِسْعُونَ امْرَأَةً. وَمُمَيِّزُ مِائَةٍ وَأَلْفٍ وَتَثْنِيَتِهِمَا وَجَمْعِهِ مَخْفُوضٌ مُفْرَدٌ، تَقُولُ: مِائَةُ رَجُلٍ، وَمِائَةُ امْرَأَةٍ، وَأَلْفُ رَجُلٍ، وَأَلْفُ امْرَأَةٍ، وَمِائَتَا رَجُلٍ، وَمِائَتَا امْرَأَةٍ، وَأَلْفَا رَجُلٍ، وَأَلْفَا امْرَأَةٍ، وَثَلَاثَةُ آلَافِ رَجُلٍ، وَثَلَاثَةُ آلَافِ امْرَأَةٍ، وَقِسْ عَلَى هَذَا.
text.en: The specifier of eleven to ninety-nine is in naṣb and singular; you say aḥada ʿashara rajulan “eleven men”, wa-iḥdā ʿashrata imraʾatan “and eleven women”, wa-tisʿatun wa-tisʿūna rajulan “and ninety-nine men” and wa-tisʿun wa-tisʿūna imraʾatan “and ninety-nine women”. The specifier of a hundred and a thousand, of their duals and of its plural, is in khafḍ and singular; you say miʾatu rajulin, wa-miʾatu imraʾatin, wa-alfu rajulin, wa-alfu imraʾatin, wa-miʾatā rajulin, wa-miʾatā imraʾatin, wa-alfā rajulin, wa-alfā imraʾatin, wa-thalāthatu ālāfi rajulin “and three thousand men” and wa-thalāthatu ālāfi imraʾatin “and three thousand women”; and measure [the rest] by this.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الِاسْمُ إِمَّا مُذَكَّرٌ وَإِمَّا مُؤَنَّثٌ؛ فَالْمُؤَنَّثُ مَا فِيهِ عَلَامَةُ التَّأْنِيثِ لَفْظًا أَوْ تَقْدِيرًا، وَالْمُذَكَّرُ بِخِلَافِهِ. وَعَلَامَةُ التَّأْنِيثِ ثَلَاثَةٌ: التَّاءُ، كَطَلْحَةَ، وَالْأَلِفُ الْمَقْصُورَةُ، كَحُبْلَى، وَالْأَلِفُ الْمَمْدُودَةُ، كَحَمْرَاءَ. وَالْمُقَدَّرَةُ إِنَّمَا هُوَ التَّاءُ فَقَطْ، كَأَرْضٍ وَدَارٍ، بِدَلِيلِ أُرَيْضَةٍ وَدُوَيْرَةٍ.
text.en: Section. The noun is either masculine or feminine. The feminine is one in which there is a sign of the feminine, in the wording or implied; the masculine is the opposite. The signs of the feminine are three: the tāʾ, as Ṭalḥata; the short alif, as ḥublā “pregnant”; and the long alif, as ḥamrāʾa “red (f.)”. The implied one is the tāʾ only, as arḍin “earth” and dārin “house”, as is shown by urayḍatin and duwayratin [their diminutives].

text.original: ثُمَّ الْمُؤَنَّثُ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: حَقِيقِيٌّ، وَهُوَ مَا بِإِزَائِهِ ذَكَرٌ مِنَ الْحَيَوَانِ، كَامْرَأَةٍ وَنَاقَةٍ، وَلَفْظِيٌّ، وَهُوَ مَا بِخِلَافِهِ، كَظُلْمَةٍ وَعَيْنٍ. وَقَدْ عَرَفْتَ أَحْكَامَ الْفِعْلِ إِذَا أُسْنِدَ إِلَى الْمُؤَنَّثِ، فَلَا نُعِيدُهَا.
text.en: Then the feminine is of two kinds: true (ḥaqīqī), which is one over against which there is a male among living beings, as imraʾatin “a woman” and nāqatin “a she-camel”; and verbal (lafẓī), which is the opposite, as ẓulmatin “darkness” and ʿaynin “an eye”. You have learned the rules of the verb when it is predicated of a feminine, so we do not repeat them.

lessons.title: The dual
body: The dual is a noun with an alif, or a yāʾ with a fatḥa before it, and a nūn with a kasra joined to its end, “to indicate that there is with it another like it of its kind”: rajulāni, rajulayni. That is all for a sound noun. The maqṣūr and the mamdūd need care, because their last letter must first be put right.

In the maqṣūr, if the alif comes from a wāw and the word has three letters, the wāw returns: ʿaṣan, ʿaṣawāni. If the alif comes from a yāʾ, or from a wāw in a word of more than three letters, or from nothing, it becomes a yāʾ: raḥan, raḥayāni; malhan, malhayāni; ḥubārā, “bustard”, ḥubārayāni; ḥublā, ḥublayāni. A student who knows the root (ʿ-ṣ-w, r-ḥ-y) knows the dual.

In the mamdūd, an original hamza stays: qurrāʾun, “a devout reader”, qurrāʾāni. A hamza of the feminine becomes a wāw: ḥamrāʾu, ḥamrāwāni. A hamza that replaced an original wāw or yāʾ allows both: kisāʾāni or kisāwāni, “two garments”.

The nūn of the dual drops in iḍāfa: ghulāmā Zaydin, muslimā Miṣra. And the tāʾ of the feminine drops in the dual of two words only, khuṣya and alya: khuṣyāni, alyāni, “because they belong together, so it is as if they were one thing”.

When a dual is muḍāf to a dual, the first is said in the plural: fa-qad ṣaghat qulūbukumā (Q 66:4), “your [two] hearts have inclined”; fa-iqṭaʿū aydiyahumā (Q 5:38), “cut off their [two] hands”. Two duals together in words so closely joined are disliked, and since each of the two has one heart, or one hand cut, the plural makes no confusion.

terms.en: the dual: alif or yāʾ, with a nūn that has kasra
a noun ending in a short alif: its dual depends on the alif's origin
a noun ending in a long alif with hamza
an alif turned from a wāw or a yāʾ

examples.en: an alif from wāw, three letters: the wāw returns
an alif from yāʾ: a yāʾ
a hamza of the feminine: a wāw
the tāʾ dropped in the dual
a dual muḍāf to a dual, said as a plural (Q 66:4)

tasks.prompt: Give the dual of ʿaṣan, raḥan and ḥublā, with the reason.
tasks.answer: ʿAṣawāni: the alif comes from a wāw in a three-letter word, so the wāw returns. Raḥayāni: the alif comes from a yāʾ, so it becomes a yāʾ. Ḥublayāni: the alif comes from nothing (it is the alif of the feminine), so it becomes a yāʾ.

tasks.prompt: Give the dual of qurrāʾ, ḥamrāʾ and kisāʾ, with the reason.
tasks.answer: Qurrāʾāni: the hamza is original and stays. Ḥamrāwāni: the hamza is for the feminine and becomes a wāw. Kisāʾāni or kisāwāni: the hamza replaced an original letter, so both are allowed.

tasks.prompt: Why is the first word plural in fa-iqṭaʿū aydiyahumā?
tasks.answer: A dual made muḍāf to a dual is said in the plural, because two duals together in words so closely joined are disliked. Each of the two has one hand cut, so aydiyahumā is clear.

tasks.prompt: Put the dual into iḍāfa: ghulāmāni li-Zaydin; muslimāni min Miṣra.
tasks.answer: Ghulāmā Zaydin and muslimā Miṣra: the nūn of the dual is dropped in iḍāfa.

quiz.prompt: The dual shows that there is with the noun…
options: another like it of its kind

quiz.prompt: The dual of ʿaṣan is…
quiz.explanation: The alif from a wāw returns in a three-letter word.

quiz.prompt: The dual of malhan is malhayāni because its alif…
options: is from a wāw in a word of more than three letters

quiz.prompt: The dual of ḥamrāʾ is…
quiz.explanation: The hamza of the feminine becomes a wāw.

quiz.prompt: Kisāʾ in the dual may be…
quiz.explanation: Its hamza replaced an original letter.

quiz.prompt: The tāʾ drops in the dual of…
quiz.explanation: They belong together, as one thing.

quiz.prompt: Qulūbukumā in Q 66:4 is plural because…
quiz.explanation: A dual muḍāf to a dual is said in the plural.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الْمُثَنَّى اسْمٌ أُلْحِقَ بِآخِرِهِ أَلِفٌ أَوْ يَاءٌ مَفْتُوحٌ مَا قَبْلَهَا وَنُونٌ مَكْسُورَةٌ؛ لِيَدُلَّ عَلَى أَنَّ مَعَهُ مِثْلَهُ مِنْ جِنْسِهِ، نَحْوُ: رَجُلَانِ وَرَجُلَيْنِ. هَذَا فِي الصَّحِيحِ، أَمَّا الْمَقْصُورُ فَإِنْ كَانَتْ أَلِفُهُ مُنْقَلِبَةً عَنْ وَاوٍ وَكَانَ ثُلَاثِيًّا رُدَّتْ إِلَى الْأَصْلِ، كَعَصَوَانِ فِي عَصًا، وَإِنْ كَانَتْ عَنْ يَاءٍ، أَوْ عَنْ وَاوٍ وَهُوَ أَكْثَرُ مِنَ الثُّلَاثِيِّ، أَوْ لَيْسَتْ مُنْقَلِبَةً عَنْ شَيْءٍ، تُقْلَبُ يَاءً، كَرَحَيَانِ فِي رَحًى، وَمَلْهَيَانِ فِي مَلْهًى، وَحُبَارَيَانِ فِي حُبَارَى، وَحُبْلَيَانِ فِي حُبْلَى.
text.en: Section. The dual (muthannā) is a noun to whose end are joined an alif, or a yāʾ with a fatḥa before it, and a nūn with a kasra, to indicate that there is with it another like it of its kind, as rajulāni and rajulayni “two men”. This is in the sound [noun]. As for the maqṣūr: if its alif is turned from a wāw and it is triliteral, [the alif] is brought back to the original, as ʿaṣawāni for ʿaṣan “stick”; if it is from a yāʾ, or from a wāw and it is more than triliteral, or is not turned from anything, it is turned into a yāʾ, as raḥayāni for raḥan “mill”, malhayāni for malhan “place of amusement”, ḥubārayāni for ḥubārā “bustard” and ḥublayāni for ḥublā “pregnant”.

text.original: وَأَمَّا الْمَمْدُودُ فَإِنْ كَانَتْ هَمْزَتُهُ أَصْلِيَّةً تَثْبُتُ، كَقُرَّاءَانِ فِي قُرَّاءٍ، وَإِنْ كَانَتْ لِلتَّأْنِيثِ تُقْلَبُ وَاوًا، كَحَمْرَاوَانِ فِي حَمْرَاءَ، وَإِنْ كَانَتْ بَدَلًا مِنْ أَصْلٍ، وَاوٍ أَوْ يَاءٍ، جَازَ فِيهِ الْوَجْهَانِ، كَكِسَاءَانِ وَكِسَاوَانِ.
text.en: As for the mamdūd: if its hamza is original, it stays, as qurrāʾāni for qurrāʾin “devout reader”; if it is for the feminine, it is turned into a wāw, as ḥamrāwāni for ḥamrāʾa “red (f.)”; and if it is a replacement of an original wāw or yāʾ, both ways are allowed in it, as kisāʾāni and kisāwāni “two garments”.

text.original: وَيَجِبُ حَذْفُ نُونِهِ عِنْدَ الْإِضَافَةِ، تَقُولُ: جَاءَنِي غُلَامَا زَيْدٍ، وَمُسْلِمَا مِصْرَ. وَكَذَلِكَ تُحْذَفُ تَاءُ التَّأْنِيثِ فِي تَثْنِيَةِ الْخُصْيَةِ وَالْأَلْيَةِ خَاصَّةً، تَقُولُ: خُصْيَانِ وَأَلْيَانِ؛ لِأَنَّهُمَا مُتَلَازِمَانِ، فَكَأَنَّهُمَا شَيْءٌ وَاحِدٌ.
text.en: Its nūn must be dropped in iḍāfa; you say jāʾanī ghulāmā Zaydin “Zayd's two servants came to me” and wa-muslimā Miṣra “and the two Muslims of Egypt”. Likewise the tāʾ of the feminine is dropped in the dual of khuṣya (testicle) and alya (buttock) only; you say khuṣyāni and wa-alyāni, because they belong together, so it is as if they were one thing.

text.original: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ إِذَا أُرِيدَ إِضَافَةُ مُثَنًّى إِلَى الْمُثَنَّى يُعَبَّرُ عَنِ الْأَوَّلِ بِلَفْظِ الْجَمْعِ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: فَقَدْ صَغَتْ قُلُوبُكُمَا، وَفَاقْطَعُوا أَيْدِيَهُمَا؛ وَذَلِكَ لِكَرَاهَةِ اجْتِمَاعِ تَثْنِيَتَيْنِ فِيمَا تَأَكَّدَ الِاتِّصَالُ بَيْنَهُمَا لَفْظًا وَمَعْنًى.
text.en: Know that when a dual is to be made muḍāf to a dual, the first is expressed by the word of the plural, as in His saying, exalted is He: fa-qad ṣaghat qulūbukumā “for your hearts have inclined” and fa-iqṭaʿū aydiyahumā “so cut off their hands”; this is because of the dislike of two duals coming together in what is closely joined in wording and meaning.

lessons.title: The plural; the sound masculine plural
body: The plural is “a noun that indicates intended units, by the letters of its singular with some change”. The change may be in the wording, rijāl from rajul, or only implied: fulk, “ships”, is the same in the singular and the plural, but as a plural it is on the pattern of usd, “lions”, and as a singular on the pattern of qufl, “lock”. So qawm, “people”, and rahṭ, “band”, are not plurals, though they mean many: they have no singular from their own letters.

The plural is sound (muṣaḥḥaḥ), when the singular's form is kept, or broken (mukassar), when it is changed. The sound masculine plural joins to the singular a wāw with a ḍamma before it and a nūn with a fatḥa, muslimūna, or a yāʾ with a kasra before it and a nūn the same, muslimīna, “to indicate that there is with it more than it”.

In the manqūṣ the yāʾ is dropped: qāḍūna, dāʿūna. In the maqṣūr the alif is dropped and the fatḥa before it stays “to indicate a dropped alif”: muṣṭafawna. This plural “belongs to those endowed with reason”; the Arabs' sinūna, “years”, araḍūna, “lands”, thubūna and qulūna are irregular.

An adjective may not take it if it is an afʿal whose feminine is faʿlāʾ, as aḥmar, ḥamrāʾ; a faʿlān whose feminine is faʿlā, as sakrān, sakrā; a faʿīl meaning mafʿūl, as jarīḥ, “wounded”; or a faʿūl meaning fāʿil, as ṣabūr, “patient”. And its nūn is dropped in iḍāfa: muslimū Miṣra.

terms.en: the plural: the singular's letters with some change
the sound plural and the broken plural
those endowed with reason, to whom the masculine sound plural belongs
a word meaning many with no singular of its own, as qawm

examples.en: a plural whose change is only implied
the sound masculine plural
the manqūṣ: its yāʾ dropped
the maqṣūr: its alif dropped, the fatḥa kept
irregular plurals of things without reason

tasks.prompt: Why is fulk a plural, though it is the same as its singular?
tasks.answer: The change from singular to plural is implied: as a singular fulk is on the pattern of qufl, as a plural on the pattern of usd. The letters are the same, the pattern supposed is different.

tasks.prompt: Why are qawm and rahṭ not plurals?
tasks.answer: A plural is made from the letters of its singular. Qawm and rahṭ mean many, but they have no singular from their own letters, so they are not plurals.

tasks.prompt: Make the sound masculine plural of qāḍin and of muṣṭafan, and explain.
tasks.answer: Qāḍūna: the yāʾ of the manqūṣ is dropped. Muṣṭafawna: the alif of the maqṣūr is dropped and the fatḥa before it is kept, to show that an alif was there.

tasks.prompt: Why does one not say aḥmarūna or jarīḥūna?
tasks.answer: The sound masculine plural is not made from an afʿal whose feminine is faʿlāʾ (aḥmar, ḥamrāʾ), nor from a faʿīl in the sense of mafʿūl (jarīḥ, “wounded”). The book lists these among the patterns that do not take it.

quiz.prompt: A plural is made…
options: from the letters of its singular, with a change
quiz.explanation: So qawm is not a plural.

quiz.prompt: In the broken plural the singular's form is…
The nūn of the sound masculine plural has…
quiz.explanation: The dual's nūn has a kasra.

quiz.prompt: The sound masculine plural of qāḍin is…
quiz.explanation: The yāʾ of the manqūṣ is dropped.

quiz.prompt: In muṣṭafawna the fatḥa before the wāw shows…
Sinūna, “years”, is called irregular because…
quiz.explanation: This plural belongs to those endowed with reason.

quiz.prompt: Which may NOT take the sound masculine plural?
quiz.explanation: A faʿūl in the sense of fāʿil.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الْمَجْمُوعُ اسْمٌ دَلَّ عَلَى آحَادٍ مَقْصُودَةٍ بِحُرُوفٍ مُفْرَدِهِ بِتَغْيِيرٍ مَا، لَفْظِيٍّ، كَرِجَالٍ فِي رَجُلٍ، أَوْ تَقْدِيرِيٍّ، كَفُلْكٍ عَلَى وَزْنِ أُسْدٍ؛ فَإِنَّ مُفْرَدَهُ أَيْضًا فُلْكٌ، لَكِنَّهُ عَلَى وَزْنِ قُفْلٍ. فَقَوْمٌ وَرَهْطٌ وَنَحْوُهُمَا وَإِنْ دَلَّ عَلَى آحَادٍ لَكِنَّهُ لَيْسَ بِجَمْعٍ؛ إِذْ لَا مُفْرَدَ لَهُ.
text.en: Section. The plural (majmūʿ) is a noun that indicates intended units, by the letters of its singular with some change, in the wording, as rijālin for rajulin, or implied, as fulkin “ships”, on the pattern of usdin “lions”; for its singular is also fulkun, but on the pattern of quflin “lock”. So qawmun “people”, rahṭun “band” and the like, although they indicate units, are not plurals, since they have no singular.

text.original: ثُمَّ الْجَمْعُ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: مُصَحَّحٌ، وَهُوَ مَا لَمْ يَتَغَيَّرْ بِنَاءُ وَاحِدِهِ، وَمُكَسَّرٌ، وَهُوَ مَا يَتَغَيَّرُ فِيهِ بِنَاءُ وَاحِدِهِ. وَالْمُصَحَّحُ عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: مُذَكَّرٌ، وَهُوَ مَا أُلْحِقَ بِآخِرِهِ وَاوٌ مَضْمُومٌ مَا قَبْلَهَا وَنُونٌ مَفْتُوحَةٌ، كَمُسْلِمُونَ، أَوْ يَاءٌ مَكْسُورٌ مَا قَبْلَهَا وَنُونٌ كَذَلِكَ؛ لِيَدُلَّ عَلَى أَنَّ مَعَهُ أَكْثَرَ مِنْهُ، نَحْوُ: مُسْلِمِينَ.
text.en: Then the plural is of two kinds: sound (muṣaḥḥaḥ), in which the form of its singular is not changed, and broken (mukassar), in which the form of its singular is changed. The sound is of two kinds. Masculine, which is one to whose end are joined a wāw with a ḍamma before it and a nūn with a fatḥa, as muslimūna, or a yāʾ with a kasra before it and a nūn likewise, to indicate that there is with it more than it, as muslimīna “Muslims”.

text.original: وَهَذَا فِي الصَّحِيحِ، أَمَّا الْمَنْقُوصُ فَتُحْذَفُ يَاؤُهُ، مِثْلُ: قَاضُونَ وَدَاعُونَ، وَالْمَقْصُورُ تُحْذَفُ أَلِفُهُ وَيَبْقَى مَا قَبْلَهَا مَفْتُوحًا لِيَدُلَّ عَلَى أَلِفٍ مَحْذُوفَةٍ، مِثْلُ: مُصْطَفَوْنَ. وَيَخْتَصُّ بِأُولِي الْعِلْمِ، وَأَمَّا قَوْلُهُمْ: سِنُونَ، وَأَرَضُونَ، وَثُبُونَ، وَقُلُونَ، فَشَاذٌّ.
text.en: This is in the sound [noun]. As for the manqūṣ, its yāʾ is dropped, as qāḍūna “judges” and dāʿūna “callers”; and the maqṣūr, its alif is dropped and the letter before it stays with a fatḥa, to indicate a dropped alif, as muṣṭafawna “chosen ones”. It belongs to those endowed with reason; as for their saying sinūna “years”, araḍūna “lands”, thubūna “groups” and qulūna “sticks”, it is irregular.

text.original: وَيَجِبُ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ أَفْعَلَ مُؤَنَّثُهُ فَعْلَاءُ، كَأَحْمَرَ وَحَمْرَاءَ، وَلَا فَعْلَانَ مُؤَنَّثُهُ فَعْلَى، كَسَكْرَانَ وَسَكْرَى، وَلَا فَعِيلًا بِمَعْنَى مَفْعُولٍ، كَجَرِيحٍ بِمَعْنَى مَجْرُوحٍ، وَلَا فَعُولًا بِمَعْنَى فَاعِلٍ، كَصَبُورٍ بِمَعْنَى صَابِرٍ. وَيَجِبُ حَذْفُ نُونِهِ بِالْإِضَافَةِ، نَحْوُ: مُسْلِمُو مِصْرَ.
text.en: It must not be an afʿal whose feminine is faʿlāʾ, as aḥmara and ḥamrāʾa “red”, nor a faʿlān whose feminine is faʿlā, as sakrāna and sakrā “drunk”, nor a faʿīl in the meaning of mafʿūl, as jarīḥin “wounded” in the meaning of majrūḥin, nor a faʿūl in the meaning of fāʿil, as ṣabūrin “patient” in the meaning of ṣābirin. Its nūn must be dropped in iḍāfa, as muslimū Miṣra “the Muslims of Egypt”.

lessons.title: The sound feminine plural; the broken plural; paucity and multitude
body: The sound feminine plural joins an alif and a tāʾ to the singular: muslimāt. If the word is an adjective that has a masculine, its masculine must have taken the plural with wāw and nūn: muslima has muslimāt because muslim has muslimūna. It follows that ḥamrāʾ does not take it, since aḥmar does not take aḥmarūna (last lesson). If the adjective has no masculine, it must not be a feminine without the tāʾ, as al-ḥāʾiḍ and al-ḥāmil. If the word is a noun, not an adjective, it takes the plural with alif and tāʾ “without condition”: Hindāt.

The broken plural has many forms in the triliteral, “known by hearing”: rijāl, afrās, fulūs; a student learns each word's plural with the word. In words of more than three letters it is by rule, on faʿālil and faʿālīl, “as you have learned in taṣrīf”. The book here sends the student back to his ṣarf books, read before it.

Plurals are also of two sizes. The plural of paucity (jamʿ qilla) is used for ten and fewer, and its forms are afʿul, afʿāl, afʿila and fiʿla, with the two sound plurals “without the lām”: Zaydūna, muslimāt. The plural of multitude (jamʿ kathra) is used for more than ten, in every other form. The words “without the lām” matter: al-muslimūna, with the lām, may take in all the Muslims there are.

terms.en: the sound feminine plural, with alif and tāʾ
the broken plural: by hearing in the triliteral, by rule beyond it
the plural of paucity: ten and fewer
the plural of multitude: more than ten

examples.en: an adjective whose masculine takes wāw and nūn
a noun, not an adjective: no condition
broken plurals of the triliteral, known by hearing
sound plurals without the lām: plurals of paucity

tasks.prompt: Why may one say muslimāt and Hindāt, and why does the book's rule shut out al-ḥāʾiḍāt?
tasks.answer: Muslima is an adjective whose masculine, muslim, takes the plural with wāw and nūn, so it takes the plural with alif and tāʾ. Hind is a noun, not an adjective, so it takes it without condition. Ḥāʾiḍ is an adjective with no masculine and without the tāʾ, so it does not take it.

tasks.prompt: How does a student know the broken plural of a three-letter word, and of a longer one?
tasks.answer: For a three-letter word the plural is known by hearing: rajul, rijāl; faras, afrās; fals, fulūs. For a longer word it is by rule, on the patterns faʿālil and faʿālīl, as taught in the books of taṣrīf.

tasks.prompt: Is muslimūna a plural of paucity or of multitude? And al-muslimūna?
tasks.answer: Muslimūna, a sound plural without the lām, is counted a plural of paucity, used for ten and fewer. With the lām, al-muslimūna is not bound to that and may take in all.

tasks.prompt: Name the four broken patterns of paucity.
tasks.answer: Afʿul, afʿāl, afʿila and fiʿla.

quiz.prompt: The sound feminine plural joins to the singular…

options: its masculine takes wāw and nūn

quiz.prompt: A noun that is not an adjective takes it…
The broken plurals of the triliteral are known…

Which is a pattern of multitude?
quiz.explanation: Every pattern outside the four of paucity.

text.original: وَمُؤَنَّثٌ، وَهُوَ مَا أُلْحِقَ بِآخِرِهِ أَلِفٌ وَتَاءٌ، نَحْوُ: مُسْلِمَاتٌ. وَشَرْطُهُ إِنْ كَانَ صِفَةً وَلَهُ مُذَكَّرٌ أَنْ يَكُونَ مُذَكَّرُهُ قَدْ جُمِعَ بِالْوَاوِ وَالنُّونِ، نَحْوُ: مُسْلِمَاتٌ، وَإِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ لَهُ مُذَكَّرٌ فَشَرْطُهُ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ مُؤَنَّثًا مُجَرَّدًا عَنِ التَّاءِ، كَالْحَائِضِ وَالْحَامِلِ. وَإِنْ كَانَ اسْمًا غَيْرَ صِفَةٍ جُمِعَ بِالْأَلِفِ وَالتَّاءِ بِلَا شَرْطٍ، كَهِنْدَاتٍ.
text.en: And feminine, which is one to whose end an alif and a tāʾ are joined, as muslimātun “Muslim women”. Its condition, if it is an adjective that has a masculine, is that its masculine has been made plural with the wāw and the nūn, as muslimātun; and if it has no masculine, its condition is that it is not a feminine free of the tāʾ, as al-ḥāʾiḍi “the menstruating woman” and al-ḥāmili “the pregnant woman”. If it is a noun that is not an adjective, it is made plural with the alif and the tāʾ without condition, as Hindātin “Hinds”.

text.original: وَالْمُكَسَّرُ صِيغَتُهُ فِي الثُّلَاثِيِّ كَثِيرَةٌ تُعْرَفُ بِالسَّمَاعِ، كَرِجَالٍ وَأَفْرَاسٍ وَفُلُوسٍ، وَفِي غَيْرِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ عَلَى وَزْنِ فَعَالِلَ وَفَعَالِيلَ قِيَاسًا، كَمَا عَرَفْتَ فِي التَّصْرِيفِ.
text.en: The forms of the broken plural in the triliteral are many and are known by hearing, as rijālin “men”, afrāsin “horses” and fulūsin “coins”; and in what is not triliteral they are on the patterns faʿālila and faʿālīla, by rule, as you have learned in taṣrīf.

text.original: ثُمَّ الْجَمْعُ أَيْضًا عَلَى قِسْمَيْنِ: جَمْعُ قِلَّةٍ، وَهُوَ مَا يُطْلَقُ عَلَى الْعَشَرَةِ فَمَا دُونَهَا، وَأَبْنِيَتُهُ: أَفْعُلٌ، وَأَفْعَالٌ، وَأَفْعِلَةٌ، وَفِعْلَةٌ، وَجَمْعَا الصَّحِيحِ بِدُونِ اللَّامِ، كَزَيْدُونَ وَمُسْلِمَاتٌ؛ وَجَمْعُ كَثْرَةٍ، وَهُوَ مَا يُطْلَقُ عَلَى مَا فَوْقَ الْعَشَرَةِ، وَأَبْنِيَتُهُ مَا عَدَا هَذِهِ الْأَبْنِيَةَ.
text.en: Then the plural is also of two kinds. The plural of paucity (jamʿ qilla), which is applied to ten and below; its forms are afʿulun, afʿālun, afʿilatun and fiʿlatun, and the two sound plurals without the lām, as Zaydūna and muslimātun. And the plural of multitude (jamʿ kathra), which is applied to what is above ten; its forms are those other than these forms.

lessons.title: The maṣdar and its governing
body: The maṣdar is “a noun that indicates the event only, and from which the verbs are derived”: al-ḍarb, al-naṣr. “The event only”: it has no time, unlike the verb, and no doer, unlike the participle. And the verbs come from it, as the book said when it named the verb after its origin (lesson 2). Its forms from the bare triliteral “are not fixed and are known by hearing”; from the other verbs they are by rule: ifʿāl, infiʿāl, istifʿāl, faʿlala, tafaʿʿul, and the rest the ṣarf books list.

A maṣdar that is not an absolute object “governs as its verb governs”: it raises a fāʿil if the verb is intransitive, aʿjabanī qiyāmu Zaydin, “Zayd's standing pleased me”, and puts an object in naṣb as well if it is transitive, aʿjabanī ḍarbu Zaydin ʿAmran. What it governs may not come before it: one does not say aʿjabanī Zaydun ḍarbu ʿAmrin, nor ʿAmran ḍarbu Zaydin.

It may be muḍāf to its fāʿil, karihtu ḍarba Zaydin ʿAmran, “I disliked Zayd's hitting ʿAmr”, or to its object, karihtu ḍarba ʿAmrin Zaydun, “I disliked the hitting of ʿAmr by Zayd”. In the first, Zayd is in jarr in its wording but the fāʿil in meaning; in the second the fāʿil comes after, in rafʿ.
But when the maṣdar is an absolute object, “the governing belongs to the verb before it”: in ḍarabtu ḍarban Zaydan, Zaydan is in naṣb by ḍarabtu, and ḍarban only strengthens the verb (lesson 16).

terms.en: the noun of the event only, the origin of the verbs
the event: the act without its time or doer
the maṣdar made muḍāf to its fāʿil
the patterns of the maṣdar by rule, beyond the bare triliteral

examples.en: the maṣdar of an intransitive verb, with its fāʿil
the maṣdar of a transitive verb, with fāʿil and object
muḍāf to the object, the fāʿil after it
an absolute object: the verb governs

head: Case
The book's example
What governs

tasks.prompt: Parse aʿjabanī ḍarbu Zaydin ʿAmran.
tasks.answer: Aʿjaba: a past verb; the yāʾ its object. Ḍarbu: the fāʿil of aʿjaba, a maṣdar made muḍāf to its own fāʿil. Zaydin: in jarr as muḍāf ilayhi, the fāʿil of the maṣdar in meaning. ʿAmran: the object of the maṣdar, in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Why is aʿjabanī Zaydun ḍarbu ʿAmrin not said?
tasks.answer: Zaydun would be governed by the maṣdar ḍarbu as its fāʿil, and what the maṣdar governs may not come before it.

tasks.prompt: In ḍarabtu ḍarban Zaydan, what governs Zaydan, and why not the maṣdar?
tasks.answer: Ḍarabtu governs it. Ḍarban is an absolute object here, and a maṣdar that is an absolute object leaves the governing to the verb before it.

tasks.prompt: Which maṣdar patterns are by hearing, and which by rule?
tasks.answer: The maṣdars of the bare triliteral are by hearing: they have no fixed pattern (ḍarb, naṣr, qiyām). Those of the other verbs are by rule: ifʿāl, infiʿāl, istifʿāl, faʿlala, tafaʿʿul and the rest.

quiz.prompt: The maṣdar indicates…
According to the book, the verbs are derived from…

options: the fāʿil of the maṣdar in meaning

quiz.prompt: May what the maṣdar governs come before it?
In karihtu ḍarba ʿAmrin Zaydun, Zaydun is…
quiz.explanation: The maṣdar is muḍāf to its object.

quiz.prompt: When the maṣdar is an absolute object, its object is governed by…

text.original: فَصْلٌ: الْمَصْدَرُ اسْمٌ يَدُلُّ عَلَى الْحَدَثِ فَقَطْ، وَيُشْتَقُّ مِنْهُ الْأَفْعَالُ، كَالضَّرْبِ وَالنَّصْرِ مَثَلًا. وَأَبْنِيَتُهُ مِنَ الثُّلَاثِيِّ الْمُجَرَّدِ غَيْرُ مَضْبُوطَةٍ تُعْرَفُ بِالسَّمَاعِ، وَمِنْ غَيْرِهِ قِيَاسِيَّةٌ، كَالْإِفْعَالِ وَالِانْفِعَالِ وَالِاسْتِفْعَالِ وَالْفَعْلَلَةِ وَالتَّفَعُّلِ، مَثَلًا.
text.en: Section. The maṣdar is a noun that indicates the event only, and from which the verbs are derived, as al-ḍarbi “hitting” and al-naṣri “helping”, for example. Its forms from the bare triliteral are not fixed and are known by hearing; from the others they are by rule, as al-ifʿāli, al-infiʿāli, al-istifʿāli, al-faʿlalati and al-tafaʿʿuli, for example.

text.original: وَالْمَصْدَرُ إِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ مَفْعُولًا مُطْلَقًا يَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ، أَعْنِي يَرْفَعُ الْفَاعِلَ إِنْ كَانَ لَازِمًا، نَحْوُ: أَعْجَبَنِي قِيَامُ زَيْدٍ، وَيَنْصِبُ مَفْعُولًا أَيْضًا إِنْ كَانَ مُتَعَدِّيًا، نَحْوُ: أَعْجَبَنِي ضَرْبُ زَيْدٍ عَمْرًا. وَلَا يَجُوزُ تَقْدِيمُ مَعْمُولِ الْمَصْدَرِ عَلَيْهِ، فَلَا يُقَالُ: أَعْجَبَنِي زَيْدٌ ضَرْبُ عَمْرٍو، وَلَا عَمْرًا ضَرْبُ زَيْدٍ.
text.en: The maṣdar, if it is not an absolute object, governs as its verb governs; I mean it puts the fāʿil in rafʿ if [the verb] is intransitive, as aʿjabanī qiyāmu Zaydin “Zayd's standing pleased me”, and puts a mafʿūl in naṣb as well if it is transitive, as aʿjabanī ḍarbu Zaydin ʿAmran “Zayd's hitting ʿAmr pleased me”. A word governed by the maṣdar may not be put before it; so one does not say aʿjabanī Zaydun ḍarbu ʿAmrin, nor ʿAmran ḍarbu Zaydin.

text.original: وَيَجُوزُ إِضَافَتُهُ إِلَى الْفَاعِلِ، نَحْوُ: كَرِهْتُ ضَرْبَ زَيْدٍ عَمْرًا، وَإِلَى الْمَفْعُولِ، نَحْوُ: كَرِهْتُ ضَرْبَ عَمْرٍو زَيْدٌ. وَأَمَّا إِنْ كَانَ مَفْعُولًا مُطْلَقًا فَالْعَمَلُ لِلْفِعْلِ الَّذِي قَبْلَهُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبْتُ ضَرْبًا زَيْدًا، فَزَيْدًا مَنْصُوبٌ بِضَرَبْتُ.
text.en: It may be made muḍāf to the fāʿil, as karihtu ḍarba Zaydin ʿAmran “I disliked Zayd's hitting ʿAmr”, and to the mafʿūl, as karihtu ḍarba ʿAmrin Zaydun “I disliked the hitting of ʿAmr by Zayd”. But if it is an absolute object, the governing belongs to the verb before it, as ḍarabtu ḍarban Zaydan “I hit Zayd a hitting”: Zaydan is in naṣb by ḍarabtu.

lessons.title: The active participle and the passive participle
body: The active participle is “derived from a verb to indicate the one in whom the act stands, in the sense of happening (ḥudūth)”: something done at a time, not a lasting quality. From the bare triliteral it is on fāʿil: ḍārib, nāṣir. From the other verbs it is the muḍāriʿ with a mīm with ḍamma in place of the prefix and a kasra before the last letter: yudkhilu, mudkhil; yastakhriju, mustakhrij.

It governs as its active verb governs on two conditions. It must have the meaning of the present or the future, and it must lean on something. The book names six: a mubtadaʾ, Zaydun qāʾimun abūhu; the owner of a ḥāl, jāʾanī Zaydun ḍāriban abūhu ʿAmran; a relative, marartu bi-l-ḍāribi abūhu ʿAmran; a described noun, ʿindī rajulun ḍāribun abūhu ʿAmran; the hamza of question, a-qāʾimun Zaydun; and a particle of negation, mā qāʾimun Zaydun.

With a past meaning, “iḍāfa in meaning is necessary”: Zaydun ḍāribu ʿAmrin amsi, “Zayd is the one who hit ʿAmr yesterday”; ḍārib does not put ʿAmr in naṣb. All this is for the participle without the lām. With the lām “all times are equal”: Zaydun al-ḍāribu abūhu ʿAmran al-āna, or ghadan, or amsi. The reason was taught in lesson 32: the lām there is the relative alladhī, and al-ḍārib is “the one who hit”, a verb in all but form.

The passive participle is derived from a transitive verb and “indicates the one on whom the act falls”. From the bare triliteral it is on mafʿūl, in the wording, maḍrūb, or by implication, maqūl and marmiyy, where the weak letters have changed the pattern's look. From the other verbs it is like the active participle with a fatḥa before the last letter: mudkhal, mustakhraj. It governs as its passive verb governs, on the same conditions: Zaydun maḍrūbun ghulāmuhu al-āna, “Zayd, his servant is being hit now”.

terms.en: the active participle: the one in whom the act happens
the passive participle: the one on whom the act falls
happening: an act at a time, the sense of the participle
leaning: on a mubtadaʾ, a ḥāl's owner, a relative, a described noun, a question or a negation

examples.en: active participles beyond the bare triliteral
leaning on the owner of a ḥāl
leaning on a described noun
a past meaning: iḍāfa necessary
passive participles on mafʿūl by implication

grid.caption: The participle governs when it leans on… (p. 62)
head: It leans on
The book's example

tasks.prompt: Give the participle of the bare triliteral and of a longer verb as the book forms them.
tasks.answer: From the bare triliteral on the pattern fāʿil: ḍārib, nāṣir. From a longer verb, the muḍāriʿ with a mīm with ḍamma for the prefix and a kasra before the last letter: mudkhil from yudkhilu, mustakhrij from yastakhriju. The passive takes a fatḥa there instead: mudkhal, mustakhraj.

tasks.prompt: Does the participle govern? Zaydun ḍāribun abūhu ʿAmran al-āna; Zaydun ḍāribu ʿAmrin amsi.
tasks.answer: In the first, yes: it has a present meaning and leans on the mubtadaʾ Zaydun; abūhu is its fāʿil and ʿAmran its object. In the second, no: it has a past meaning, so it is made muḍāf to ʿAmrin and does not put it in naṣb.

tasks.prompt: Why does al-ḍārib govern even with amsi?
tasks.answer: With the lām all times are equal: the lām is the relative alladhī and al-ḍārib means “the one who hit”, standing for a verb, so it governs in any time.

tasks.prompt: On what does the participle lean in mā qāʾimun Zaydun and a-qāʾimun Zaydun?
tasks.answer: In the first on a particle of negation, in the second on the hamza of question; in both it governs Zaydun as its fāʿil.

quiz.prompt: The active participle has the sense of…
quiz.explanation: Ḥudūth; the resembling adjective has thubūt.

quiz.prompt: From the bare triliteral the active participle is on…
Mustakhrij is formed from the muḍāriʿ by…
options: a mīm with ḍamma for the prefix, a kasra before the last

quiz.prompt: Which is NOT one of the six things the participle leans on?
quiz.explanation: Mubtadaʾ, ḥāl's owner, relative, described noun, question, negation.

quiz.prompt: With a past meaning, the participle without the lām…
options: is made muḍāf, governing in meaning only

quiz.prompt: With the lām, the participle governs…
quiz.explanation: The lām is the relative alladhī.

quiz.prompt: Marmiyy is on the pattern mafʿūl…
quiz.explanation: Its weak letters change the look of the pattern.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: اسْمُ الْفَاعِلِ اسْمٌ مُشْتَقٌّ مِنْ فِعْلٍ لِيَدُلَّ عَلَى مَنْ قَامَ بِهِ الْفِعْلُ بِمَعْنَى الْحُدُوثِ، وَصِيغَتُهُ مِنَ الثُّلَاثِيِّ الْمُجَرَّدِ عَلَى وَزْنِ فَاعِلٍ، كَضَارِبٍ وَنَاصِرٍ، وَمِنْ غَيْرِهِ عَلَى صِيغَةِ الْمُضَارِعِ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْفِعْلِ، بِمِيمٍ مَضْمُومَةٍ مَكَانَ حَرْفِ الْمُضَارَعَةِ وَكَسْرِ مَا قَبْلَ الْآخِرِ، كَمُدْخِلٍ وَمُسْتَخْرِجٍ.
text.en: Section. The active participle (ism al-fāʿil) is a noun derived from a verb to indicate the one in whom the act stands, in the sense of happening (ḥudūth). Its form from the bare triliteral is on the pattern fāʿilin, as ḍāribin “hitter” and nāṣirin “helper”; and from the others it is on the form of the muḍāriʿ of that verb, with a mīm with ḍamma in the place of the prefix of the muḍāriʿ and a kasra on the letter before the last, as mudkhilin “one who brings in” and mustakhrijin “one who brings out”.

text.original: وَهُوَ يَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ الْمَعْرُوفِ إِنْ كَانَ بِمَعْنَى الْحَالِ أَوِ الِاسْتِقْبَالِ، وَمُعْتَمِدًا عَلَى الْمُبْتَدَإِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ أَبُوهُ، أَوْ ذِي الْحَالِ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ ضَارِبًا أَبُوهُ عَمْرًا، أَوِ الْمَوْصُولِ، نَحْوُ: مَرَرْتُ بِالضَّارِبِ أَبُوهُ عَمْرًا، أَوِ الْمَوْصُوفِ، نَحْوُ: عِنْدِي رَجُلٌ ضَارِبٌ أَبُوهُ عَمْرًا، أَوْ هَمْزَةِ الِاسْتِفْهَامِ، نَحْوُ: أَقَائِمٌ زَيْدٌ، أَوْ حَرْفِ النَّفْيِ، نَحْوُ: مَا قَائِمٌ زَيْدٌ.
text.en: It governs as its active verb governs if it is in the meaning of the present or the future, and leans on a mubtadaʾ, as Zaydun qāʾimun abūhu “Zayd, his father is standing”; or on the dhū al-ḥāl, as jāʾanī Zaydun ḍāriban abūhu ʿAmran “Zayd came to me, his father hitting ʿAmr”; or on the relative, as marartu bi-al-ḍāribi abūhu ʿAmran “I passed by the one whose father is hitting ʿAmr”; or on the described noun, as ʿindī rajulun ḍāribun abūhu ʿAmran “I have with me a man whose father is hitting ʿAmr”; or on the hamza of question, as a-qāʾimun Zaydun “is Zayd standing?”; or on a particle of negation, as mā qāʾimun Zaydun “Zayd is not standing”.

text.original: فَإِنْ كَانَ بِمَعْنَى الْمَاضِي وَجَبَتِ الْإِضَافَةُ مَعْنًى، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ ضَارِبُ عَمْرٍو أَمْسِ. هَذَا إِذَا كَانَ مُنَكَّرًا، أَمَّا إِذَا كَانَ مُعَرَّفًا بِاللَّامِ يَسْتَوِي فِيهِ جَمِيعُ الْأَزْمِنَةِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ الضَّارِبُ أَبُوهُ عَمْرًا الْآنَ، أَوْ غَدًا، أَوْ أَمْسِ.
text.en: If it is in the meaning of the past, iḍāfa in meaning is necessary, as Zaydun ḍāribu ʿAmrin amsi “Zayd is the hitter of ʿAmr yesterday”. This is when it is indefinite; when it is defined by the lām, all times are equal in it, as Zaydun al-ḍāribu abūhu ʿAmran al-āna “Zayd is the one whose father is hitting ʿAmr now”, or ghadan “tomorrow”, or amsi “yesterday”.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: اسْمُ الْمَفْعُولِ اسْمٌ مُشْتَقٌّ مِنْ فِعْلٍ مُتَعَدٍّ يَدُلُّ عَلَى مَنْ وَقَعَ عَلَيْهِ الْفِعْلُ، وَصِيغَتُهُ مِنْ مُجَرَّدِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ عَلَى وَزْنِ مَفْعُولٍ لَفْظًا، كَمَضْرُوبٍ، أَوْ تَقْدِيرًا، كَمَقُولٍ وَمَرْمِيٍّ، وَمِنْ غَيْرِهِ كَاسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ بِفَتْحِ مَا قَبْلَ الْآخِرِ، كَمُدْخَلٍ وَمُسْتَخْرَجٍ. وَيَعْمَلُ عَمَلَ فِعْلِهِ الْمَجْهُولِ بِالشَّرَائِطِ الْمَذْكُورَةِ فِي اسْمِ الْفَاعِلِ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ مَضْرُوبٌ غُلَامُهُ الْآنَ، أَوْ غَدًا، أَوْ أَمْسِ.
text.en: Section. The passive participle (ism al-mafʿūl) is a noun derived from a transitive verb that indicates the one on whom the act falls. Its form from the bare triliteral is on the pattern mafʿūlin, in the wording, as maḍrūbin “hit”, or by implication, as maqūlin “said” and marmiyyin “thrown”; and from the others it is like the active participle, with a fatḥa on the letter before the last, as mudkhalin “brought in” and mustakhrajin “brought out”. It governs as its passive verb governs, under the conditions mentioned for the active participle, as Zaydun maḍrūbun ghulāmuhu al-āna “Zayd, his servant is being hit now”, or ghadan “tomorrow”, or amsi “yesterday”.

lessons.title: The resembling adjective and its eighteen questions
body: The resembling adjective (al-ṣifa al-mushabbaha) is derived from an intransitive verb “to indicate the one in whom the act stands, in the sense of lasting (thubūt)”: a quality that stays, not an act that happens. Its forms differ from the participles' and are “known only by hearing”: ḥasan, ṣaʿb, ẓarīf. It governs as its verb governs “in every case”, with no condition of time, which would mean nothing for a lasting quality, but on the condition of leaning given in the last lesson.

Its “questions are eighteen”. The adjective has the lām or not (two); the word it governs is muḍāf to a pronoun, has the lām, or has neither (three: six so far); and that word is in rafʿ, naṣb or jarr (three: eighteen). So al-ḥasanu wajhuhu, wajhahu, wajhihi; al-ḥasanu al-wajhu, al-wajha, al-wajhi; al-ḥasanu wajhun, wajhan, wajhin; and the same nine with ḥasanun.

They fall into five judgements. Two are impossible: al-ḥasanu wajhihi and al-ḥasanu wajhin, an adjective with the lām made muḍāf to a word without it. One is disputed: ḥasanu wajhihi. The rest are judged by their pronouns: “best” with one pronoun, “good” with two, “ugly” with none.

How are the pronouns counted? “Whenever you put its governed word in rafʿ by it, there is no pronoun in the adjective”, since the governed word is its fāʿil; “whenever you put it in naṣb or jarr, there is in it the pronoun of the described noun”. Add the hāʾ if the governed word has one. So ḥasanun wajhuhu has one, the hāʾ: best. Ḥasanun wajhahu, the book's example, has two, the hidden one and the hāʾ: good. Ḥasanun al-wajhu has none: ugly. The table gives the nine without the lām.
