tasks.prompt: Name the additional particle and what it is added with: (a) mā in Zaydun qāʾimun; (b) fa-lammā an jāʾa al-bashīru; (c) idhā mā ṣumta ṣumtu; (d) mā manaʿaka an lā tasjuda.
tasks.answer: (a) In, added with the negating mā. (b) An, added with lammā. (c) Mā, added with the conditional idhā. (d) Lā, added after the an of the maṣdar.

tasks.prompt: Does lā uqsimu bi-hādhā al-baladi deny an oath? Explain.
tasks.answer: No. Lā is added before the oath, and the meaning is uqsimu, “I swear by this land”.

tasks.prompt: Why is an a particle of explanation in wa-nādaynāhu an yā Ibrāhīmu, but not in qultu lahu ani uktub?
tasks.answer: An explains only a verb in the meaning of saying. Nādaynā, “We called”, has the meaning of saying without its word, so an explains it. In qultu the word of saying itself is mentioned, so an has no place there.

tasks.prompt: Turn each into its maṣdar, as the book does: bi-mā raḥubat; illā an qālū; ʿalimtu annaka qāʾimun.
tasks.answer: Bi-mā raḥubat: bi-ruḥbihā. Illā an qālū: illā qawluhum. ʿAlimtu annaka qāʾimun: ʿalimtu qiyāmaka. Mā and an are for the verbal sentence, anna for the nominal.

quiz.prompt: How many additional particles does the book count?
quiz.explanation: In, an, mā, lā, min, the bāʾ and the lām.

quiz.prompt: In mā in Zaydun qāʾimun, in is…
quiz.explanation: In is added with the negating mā.

quiz.prompt: An is added between law and…
In fa-bi-mā raḥmatin mina Allāhi, mā is…
options: additional after a particle of jarr
quiz.explanation: Q 3:159; raḥmatin stays in jarr after the bāʾ.

quiz.prompt: Lā uqsimu bi-hādhā al-baladi means…
options: I do not swear by this land
do not swear by this land
quiz.explanation: The book: in the meaning of uqsimu.

quiz.prompt: The explaining an explains only…
options: a verb in the meaning of saying
quiz.explanation: Wa-nādaynāhu an yā Ibrāhīmu; not qultu lahu ani uktub.

quiz.prompt: As a particle of the maṣdar, anna goes with…
quiz.explanation: ʿAlimtu annaka qāʾimun, that is, qiyāmaka.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: حُرُوفُ الزِّيَادَةِ سَبْعَةٌ: إِنْ، وَأَنْ، وَمَا، وَلَا، وَمِنْ، وَالْبَاءُ، وَاللَّامُ. فَإِنْ تُزَادُ مَعَ مَا النَّافِيَةِ، نَحْوُ: مَا إِنْ زَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، وَمَعَ مَا الْمَصْدَرِيَّةِ، نَحْوُ: انْتَظِرْ مَا إِنْ يَجْلِسُ الْأَمِيرُ، وَمَعَ لَمَّا، نَحْوُ: لَمَّا إِنْ جَلَسْتَ جَلَسْتُ. وَأَنْ تُزَادُ مَعَ لَمَّا، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: فَلَمَّا أَنْ جَاءَ الْبَشِيرُ، وَبَيْنَ لَوْ وَالْقَسَمِ الْمُتَقَدِّمِ عَلَيْهَا، نَحْوُ: وَاللَّهِ أَنْ لَوْ قُمْتَ قُمْتُ.
text.en: Section. The additional particles are seven: in, an, mā, lā, min, the bāʾ and the lām. In is added with the negating mā, as mā in Zaydun qāʾimun “Zayd is not standing”; with the mā of the maṣdar, as intaẓir mā in yajlisu al-amīru “wait as long as the prince sits”; and with lammā, as lammā in jalasta jalastu “when you sat, I sat”. An is added with lammā, as in His saying, exalted is He: fa-lammā an jāʾa al-bashīru “then when the bearer of good news came”, and between law and an oath put before it, as wa-Allāhi an law qumta qumtu “by God, if you had stood, I would have stood”.

text.original: وَمَا تُزَادُ مَعَ إِذَا، وَمَتَى، وَأَيٍّ، وَأَنَّى، وَأَيْنَ، وَإِنْ شَرْطِيَّاتٍ، كَمَا تَقُولُ: إِذَا مَا صُمْتَ صُمْتُ، وَكَذَا الْبَوَاقِي، وَبَعْدَ بَعْضِ حُرُوفِ الْجَرِّ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: فَبِمَا رَحْمَةٍ مِنَ اللَّهِ، وَعَمَّا قَلِيلٍ لَيُصْبِحُنَّ نَادِمِينَ، وَمِمَّا خَطِيئَاتِهِمْ أُغْرِقُوا، وَزَيْدٌ صَدِيقِي كَمَا أَنَّ عَمْرًا أَخِي.
text.en: Mā is added with the conditional idhā, matā, ayy, annā, ayna and in, as you say idhā mā ṣumta ṣumtu “when you fast, I fast”, and likewise the rest; and after some particles of jarr, as His saying, exalted is He: fa-bi-mā raḥmatin mina Allāhi “it is by a mercy from God”, ʿammā qalīlin la-yuṣbiḥunna nādimīna “in a little while they will surely become regretful” and mimmā khaṭīʾātihim ughriqū “because of their sins they were drowned”; and Zaydun ṣadīqī ka-mā anna ʿAmran akhī “Zayd is my friend, just as ʿAmr is my brother”.

text.original: وَلَا تُزَادُ مَعَ الْوَاوِ بَعْدَ النَّفْيِ، نَحْوُ: مَا جَاءَنِي زَيْدٌ وَلَا عَمْرٌو، وَبَعْدَ أَنِ الْمَصْدَرِيَّةِ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: مَا مَنَعَكَ أَنْ لَا تَسْجُدَ، وَقَبْلَ الْقَسَمِ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: لَا أُقْسِمُ بِهَذَا الْبَلَدِ، بِمَعْنَى أُقْسِمُ. وَأَمَّا مِنْ وَالْبَاءُ وَاللَّامُ فَقَدْ مَرَّ ذِكْرُهَا فِي حُرُوفِ الْجَرِّ، فَلَا نُعِيدُهَا.
text.en: Lā is added with the wāw after a negation, as mā jāʾanī Zaydun wa-lā ʿAmrun “neither Zayd nor ʿAmr came to me”; after the an of the maṣdar, as in His saying, exalted is He: mā manaʿaka an lā tasjuda “what prevented you from prostrating?”; and before the oath, as in His saying, exalted is He: lā uqsimu bi-hādhā al-baladi “I swear by this land”, in the meaning of uqsimu “I swear”. As for min, the bāʾ and the lām, they have been mentioned among the particles of jarr, so we do not repeat them.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: حَرْفَا التَّفْسِيرِ: أَيْ وَأَنْ؛ فَأَيْ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَاسْأَلِ الْقَرْيَةَ، أَيْ أَهْلَ الْقَرْيَةِ، كَأَنَّكَ تُفَسِّرُهُ بِأَهْلِ الْقَرْيَةِ. وَأَنْ إِنَّمَا يُفَسَّرُ بِهَا فِعْلٌ بِمَعْنَى الْقَوْلِ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَنَادَيْنَاهُ أَنْ يَا إِبْرَاهِيمُ، فَلَا يُقَالُ: قُلْتُ لَهُ أَنِ اكْتُبْ؛ ذُكِرَ لَفْظُ الْقَوْلِ لَا مَعْنَاهُ.
text.en: Section. The two particles of explanation: ay and an. Ay, as in His saying, exalted is He: wa-isʾali al-qaryata “and ask the town”, that is, ahla al-qaryati “the people of the town”, as if you explained it by “the people of the town”. With an only a verb in the meaning of saying is explained, as in His saying, exalted is He: wa-nādaynāhu an yā Ibrāhīmu “and We called to him: O Ibrāhīm”; so one does not say qultu lahu ani uktub, [where] the word of saying is mentioned, not its meaning.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: حُرُوفُ الْمَصْدَرِ ثَلَاثَةٌ: مَا، وَأَنْ، وَأَنَّ؛ فَالْأُولَيَانِ لِلْجُمْلَةِ الْفِعْلِيَّةِ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَضَاقَتْ عَلَيْهِمُ الْأَرْضُ بِمَا رَحُبَتْ، أَيْ بِرُحْبِهَا، وَقَوْلِ الشَّاعِرِ، شِعْرٌ: يَسُرُّ الْمَرْءَ مَا ذَهَبَ اللَّيَالِي * وَكَانَ ذَهَابُهُنَّ لَهُ ذَهَابَا، وَأَنْ، نَحْوُ قَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: فَمَا كَانَ جَوَابَ قَوْمِهِ إِلَّا أَنْ قَالُوا، أَيْ قَوْلُهُمْ. وَأَنَّ لِلْجُمْلَةِ الِاسْمِيَّةِ، نَحْوُ: عَلِمْتُ أَنَّكَ قَائِمٌ، أَيْ قِيَامَكَ.
text.en: Section. The particles of the maṣdar are three: mā, an and anna. The first two are for the verbal sentence: [mā], as in His saying, exalted is He: wa-ḍāqat ʿalayhimu al-arḍu bi-mā raḥubat “and the earth, for all its breadth, became narrow for them”, that is, bi-ruḥbihā “for its breadth”, and in the poet's saying, verse: yasurru al-marʾa mā dhahaba al-layālī / wa-kāna dhahābuhunna lahu dhahābā “It pleases a man that the nights go by, / yet their going is his own going”; and an, as in His saying, exalted is He: fa-mā kāna jawāba qawmihi illā an qālū “and the answer of his people was only that they said”, that is, qawluhum “their saying”. Anna is for the nominal sentence, as ʿalimtu annaka qāʾimun “I knew that you are standing”, that is, qiyāmaka “your standing”.

lessons.title: Urging: hallā and its sisters; qad
body: The particles of urging (taḥḍīḍ) are four: hallā, allā, lawlā and lawmā. They claim the head of speech. Upon the muḍāriʿ they urge to the act: hallā taʾkulu, “why do you not eat?”. Upon the past they blame: hallā ḍarabta Zaydan, “why did you not hit Zayd?”, and then they urge only in regard to what has been missed.

They come only upon the verb. If a noun follows them, it is by a concealed verb: to one who has hit some people you say hallā Zaydan, that is, hallā ḍarabta Zaydan. All four are compounds: the second part is a particle of negation, and the first a particle of condition, of question or of the maṣdar; so, by this account, law with lā and with mā, hal with lā, an with lā.

Lawlā has another meaning: the second sentence is ruled out because the first exists. Lawlā ʿAliyyun la-halaka ʿUmaru, “were it not for ʿAlī, ʿUmar would have perished”. Then it needs two sentences, and the first is always nominal.

The particle of expectation (tawaqquʿ) is qad. With the past it brings the past near to the present: qad rakiba al-amīru, “the prince has ridden”, a little before now. For this it is also called the particle of nearing (taqrīb), and for this it is bound to a past verb that is to stand as a ḥāl (lesson 20). With the past it may also be for emphasis, answering one who asks hal qāma Zaydun?: qad qāma Zaydun.

With the muḍāriʿ qad is for fewness: inna al-kadhūba qad yaṣduqu, “the liar sometimes tells the truth”; inna al-jawāda qad yabkhalu, “the generous man is sometimes stingy”. It may be for making certain: qad yaʿlamu Allāhu al-muʿawwiqīna (Q 33:18). An oath may come between qad and its verb, qad wa-Allāhi aḥsanta; and the verb after qad may be dropped when something shows it, as at the end of the verse azifa al-taraḥḥulu…: wa-kaʾan qadi, that is, wa-kaʾan qad zālat, “and as if they had moved off”.

terms.en: the four particles of urging: hallā, allā, lawlā, lawmā
blame: the meaning of urging upon the past
the particle of expectation: qad
the particle of nearing: qad with the past
fewness: qad with the muḍāriʿ

examples.en: urging, upon the muḍāriʿ
blame, upon the past
lawlā: the second ruled out by the first
qad bringing the past near
qad for fewness

tasks.prompt: Urging or blame? (a) hallā taʾkulu; (b) hallā ḍarabta Zaydan.
tasks.answer: (a) Urging to the act: hallā has come upon the muḍāriʿ. (b) Blame: it has come upon the past, and urges only in regard to what has been missed.

tasks.prompt: What governs Zaydan in hallā Zaydan, said to one who has hit some people?
tasks.answer: A concealed verb: hallā ḍarabta Zaydan. The particles of urging come only upon the verb, so a noun after them is by a concealed verb.

tasks.prompt: By the book's rule, of what two parts is each of hallā, allā, lawlā and lawmā made?
tasks.answer: Hallā: hal, a particle of question, with lā. Allā: an, a particle of the maṣdar, with lā. Lawlā: law, a particle of condition, with lā. Lawmā: law with mā. In each the second part is a particle of negation.

tasks.prompt: What does qad do in qad rakiba al-amīru, and in inna al-kadhūba qad yaṣduqu?
tasks.answer: In qad rakiba al-amīru it brings the past near to the present: the prince rode a little before now. In inna al-kadhūba qad yaṣduqu, with the muḍāriʿ, it is for fewness: the liar sometimes tells the truth.

tasks.prompt: In the verse ending wa-kaʾan qadi, what is dropped, and what shows it?
tasks.answer: The verb after qad: wa-kaʾan qad zālat, “as if they had moved off”. The words before it, lammā tazul bi-riḥālinā, “they have not yet moved off with our saddles”, show which verb it is.

quiz.prompt: How many particles of urging does the book count?
Upon the past, hallā is for…
quiz.explanation: Hallā ḍarabta Zaydan: blame for what was missed.

quiz.prompt: In hallā Zaydan, Zaydan is in naṣb by…
In lawlā ʿAliyyun la-halaka ʿUmaru, the second sentence is…
options: ruled out because the first does not exist
ruled out because the first exists
quiz.explanation: This is the second meaning of lawlā; its first sentence is always nominal.

quiz.prompt: With the past, qad…
options: brings the past near to the present
quiz.explanation: Qad rakiba al-amīru: a little before now.

quiz.prompt: In inna al-kadhūba qad yaṣduqu, qad is for…
quiz.explanation: With the muḍāriʿ qad is for fewness: the liar sometimes tells the truth.

quiz.prompt: Qad wa-Allāhi aḥsanta shows that…
options: qad may come upon a noun
the verb after qad must be a muḍāriʿ
an oath may come between qad and its verb
quiz.explanation: The book allows the oath between them.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: حُرُوفُ التَّحْضِيضِ أَرْبَعَةٌ: هَلَّا، وَأَلَّا، وَلَوْلَا، وَلَوْمَا، وَلَهَا صَدْرُ الْكَلَامِ، وَمَعْنَاهَا الْحَضُّ عَلَى الْفِعْلِ إِنْ دَخَلَتْ عَلَى الْمُضَارِعِ، نَحْوُ: هَلَّا تَأْكُلُ، وَاللَّوْمُ إِنْ دَخَلَتْ عَلَى الْمَاضِي، نَحْوُ: هَلَّا ضَرَبْتَ زَيْدًا، وَحِينَئِذٍ لَا تَكُونُ تَحْضِيضًا إِلَّا بِاعْتِبَارِ مَا فَاتَ.
text.en: Section. The particles of urging (taḥḍīḍ) are four: hallā, allā, lawlā and lawmā. They have the head of speech; their meaning is urging to the act if they come upon the muḍāriʿ, as hallā taʾkulu “why do you not eat?”, and blame if they come upon the past, as hallā ḍarabta Zaydan “why did you not hit Zayd?”; and then they are urging only in regard to what has been missed.

text.original: وَلَا تَدْخُلُ إِلَّا عَلَى الْفِعْلِ، كَمَا مَرَّ، وَإِنْ وَقَعَ بَعْدَهَا اسْمٌ فَبِإِضْمَارِ فِعْلٍ، كَمَا تَقُولُ لِمَنْ ضَرَبَ قَوْمًا: هَلَّا زَيْدًا، أَيْ هَلَّا ضَرَبْتَ زَيْدًا. وَجَمِيعُهَا مُرَكَّبَةٌ، جُزْؤُهَا الثَّانِي حَرْفُ النَّفْيِ، وَالْأَوَّلُ حَرْفُ الشَّرْطِ أَوِ الِاسْتِفْهَامِ أَوْ حَرْفُ الْمَصْدَرِ. وَلِلَوْلَا مَعْنًى آخَرُ، وَهُوَ امْتِنَاعُ الْجُمْلَةِ الثَّانِيَةِ لِوُجُودِ الْجُمْلَةِ الْأُولَى، نَحْوُ: لَوْلَا عَلِيٌّ لَهَلَكَ عُمَرُ، وَحِينَئِذٍ تَحْتَاجُ إِلَى جُمْلَتَيْنِ، أُولَاهُمَا اسْمِيَّةٌ أَبَدًا.
text.en: They come only upon the verb, as has passed; and if a noun stands after them, it is by a concealed verb, as you say to one who has hit some people hallā Zaydan “why not Zayd?”, that is, hallā ḍarabta Zaydan. All of them are compounds: their second part is a particle of negation, and the first a particle of condition, or of question, or a particle of the maṣdar. Lawlā has another meaning: that the second sentence is ruled out because of the existence of the first, as lawlā ʿAliyyun la-halaka ʿUmaru “were it not for ʿAlī, ʿUmar would have perished”; then it needs two sentences, the first of which is always nominal.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: حَرْفُ التَّوَقُّعِ قَدْ، وَهِيَ فِي الْمَاضِي لِتَقْرِيبِ الْمَاضِي إِلَى الْحَالِ، نَحْوُ: قَدْ رَكِبَ الْأَمِيرُ، أَيْ قُبَيْلَ هَذَا، وَلِأَجْلِ ذَلِكَ سُمِّيَتْ حَرْفَ التَّقْرِيبِ أَيْضًا، وَلِهَذَا تَلْزَمُ الْمَاضِيَ لِيَصْلُحَ أَنْ يَقَعَ حَالًا. وَقَدْ تَجِيءُ لِلتَّأْكِيدِ إِذَا كَانَ جَوَابًا لِمَنْ يَسْأَلُ: هَلْ قَامَ زَيْدٌ؟ تَقُولُ: قَدْ قَامَ زَيْدٌ.
text.en: Section. The particle of expectation is qad. In the past it is for bringing the past near to the present, as qad rakiba al-amīru “the prince has ridden”, that is, a little before this; for that reason it is also called the particle of nearing (taqrīb), and for this it is bound to the past so that it may be fit to stand as a ḥāl. It may come for emphasis when it is an answer to one who asks hal qāma Zaydun “did Zayd stand?”: you say qad qāma Zaydun “Zayd has indeed stood”.

text.original: وَفِي الْمُضَارِعِ لِلتَّقْلِيلِ، نَحْوُ: إِنَّ الْكَذُوبَ قَدْ يَصْدُقُ، وَإِنَّ الْجَوَادَ قَدْ يَبْخَلُ، وَقَدْ تَجِيءُ لِلتَّحْقِيقِ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: قَدْ يَعْلَمُ اللَّهُ الْمُعَوِّقِينَ. وَيَجُوزُ الْفَصْلُ بَيْنَهَا وَبَيْنَ الْفِعْلِ بِالْقَسَمِ، نَحْوُ: قَدْ وَاللَّهِ أَحْسَنْتَ، وَقَدْ يُحْذَفُ الْفِعْلُ بَعْدَ قَدْ عِنْدَ الْقَرِينَةِ، كَقَوْلِ الشَّاعِرِ، شِعْرٌ: أَزِفَ التَّرَحُّلُ غَيْرَ أَنَّ رِكَابَنَا * لَمَّا تَزُلْ بِرِحَالِنَا وَكَأَنْ قَدِ، أَيْ وَكَأَنْ قَدْ زَالَتْ.
text.en: In the muḍāriʿ it is for fewness, as inna al-kadhūba qad yaṣduqu “the liar sometimes tells the truth” and wa-inna al-jawāda qad yabkhalu “and the generous man is sometimes stingy”; and it may come for making certain, as in His saying, exalted is He: qad yaʿlamu Allāhu al-muʿawwiqīna “God knows the hinderers”. It may be separated from the verb by an oath, as qad wa-Allāhi aḥsanta “you have, by God, done well”; and the verb after qad is sometimes dropped when there is an indication, as in the poet's saying, verse: azifa al-taraḥḥulu ghayra anna rikābanā / lammā tazul bi-riḥālinā wa-kaʾan qadi “The departure has drawn near, except that our mounts / have not yet moved off with our saddles, though it is as if they had”, that is, wa-kaʾan qad zālat “and as if they had moved off”.

lessons.title: The question: the hamza and hal; the condition: in and law
body: The two particles of question are the hamza and hal. They claim the head of speech and come upon the sentence, nominal, a-Zaydun qāʾimun, “is Zayd standing?”, or verbal, hal qāma Zaydun, “did Zayd stand?”. They come more often upon the verbal sentence, since asking with the verb is more fitting.

The hamza comes in places where hal may not: a-Zaydan ḍarabta, with the object put first; a-taḍribu Zaydan wa-huwa akhūka, “do you hit Zayd when he is your brother?”, a question the commentators call one of disapproval; a-Zaydun ʿindaka am ʿAmrun, with the connected am (lesson 65); and before the wāw, the fāʾ and thumma: a-wa-man kāna, a-fa-man kāna, a-thumma idhā mā waqaʿa. The book adds: “and here there is a matter for discussion”.

The particles of condition are in, law and ammā. They claim the head of speech, and each comes upon two sentences, both nominal, both verbal, or one of each. In is for the future even when it comes upon the past: in zurtanī akramtuka, “if you visit me, I will honour you”. Law is for the past even when it comes upon the muḍāriʿ: law tazūrunī akramtuka, “had you visited me, I would have honoured you”. A verb is bound to both, in the wording, or implied: in anta zāʾirī fa-anā ukrimuka.

In is used only in doubtful matters: one does not say in ṭalaʿati al-shamsu ātīka, but idhā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu, for the rising of the sun is not in doubt. Law shows that the second sentence is negated because the first is negated: law kāna fīhimā ālihatun illā Allāhu la-fasadatā (Q 21:22): the ruin is negated, because gods other than God are negated.

When an oath opens the speech and comes before the condition, the verb after the particle of condition must be past, in the wording, wa-Allāhi in ataytanī la-ukrimannaka, or in meaning, wa-Allāhi in lam taʾtinī la-ahjurannaka. The second sentence is then, in its wording, the answer of the oath, not the requital of the condition; so it takes what the answer of an oath takes, the lām and the like (lesson 60).

If the oath stands in the middle of the speech, it may be counted, with the answer belonging to it, in taʾtinī wa-Allāhi la-ātiyannaka; or it may be cancelled, in taʾtinī wa-Allāhi ātika, where ātika is the requital of the condition, in jazm.

terms.en: the two particles of question: the hamza and hal
the head of speech, which these particles claim
the particles of condition: in, law and ammā
doubtful matters: the only use of in
the answer of the oath, which wins over the requital when the oath comes first

examples.en: the hamza where hal may not come
in for the future, upon the past

the oath first: the answer is the oath's

tasks.prompt: Name two places where the hamza of question may come and hal may not.
tasks.answer: Any two of those the book gives: a-Zaydan ḍarabta, with the object put first; a-taḍribu Zaydan wa-huwa akhūka; a-Zaydun ʿindaka am ʿAmrun, with the connected am; and before the wāw, the fāʾ and thumma: a-wa-man kāna, a-fa-man kāna, a-thumma idhā mā waqaʿa.

tasks.prompt: Why is in ṭalaʿati al-shamsu ātīka wrong, and how is it mended?
tasks.answer: In is used only in doubtful matters, and the rising of the sun is not in doubt. One says idhā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu ātīka.

tasks.prompt: What does law show in law kāna fīhimā ālihatun illā Allāhu la-fasadatā?
tasks.arabic: لَوْ كَانَ فِيهِمَا آلِهَةٌ إِلَّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتَا
tasks.answer: That the second sentence is negated because the first is negated: the heavens and the earth are not ruined, because there are no gods in them other than God.

tasks.prompt: In wa-Allāhi in ataytanī la-ukrimannaka, is la-ukrimannaka the requital of the condition or the answer of the oath? How does it show this?
tasks.answer: The answer of the oath, since the oath opens the speech before the condition. It shows this by taking what an oath's answer takes, the lām (with the nūn of emphasis); and the verb after in, ataytanī, is past, as the book requires.

tasks.prompt: Compare in taʾtinī wa-Allāhi la-ātiyannaka with in taʾtinī wa-Allāhi ātika.
tasks.answer: In both the oath stands in the middle. In the first it is counted: the answer belongs to the oath and takes the lām and the nūn. In the second it is cancelled: ātika is the requital of the condition, in jazm.

quiz.prompt: The two particles of question are…
quiz.explanation: Both claim the head of speech.

quiz.prompt: The hamza and hal come more often upon…
quiz.explanation: Asking with the verb is more fitting.

quiz.prompt: In which may hal not take the place of the hamza?
quiz.explanation: The book lists a-Zaydan ḍarabta among the places of the hamza alone.

quiz.prompt: In is for the future…
options: even when it comes upon the past

quiz.prompt: In is used only in…
quiz.explanation: So not in ṭalaʿati al-shamsu, but idhā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu.

quiz.prompt: When the oath comes first, before the condition, the verb after in must be…
quiz.explanation: Wa-Allāhi in ataytanī; wa-Allāhi in lam taʾtinī.

quiz.prompt: In in taʾtinī wa-Allāhi ātika, the oath is…
quiz.explanation: Ātika is the requital of the condition, in jazm.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: حَرْفَا الِاسْتِفْهَامِ: الْهَمْزَةُ وَهَلْ، لَهُمَا صَدْرُ الْكَلَامِ، وَتَدْخُلَانِ عَلَى الْجُمْلَةِ، اسْمِيَّةً كَانَتْ، نَحْوُ: أَزَيْدٌ قَائِمٌ، أَوْ فِعْلِيَّةً، نَحْوُ: هَلْ قَامَ زَيْدٌ، وَدُخُولُهُمَا عَلَى الْفِعْلِيَّةِ أَكْثَرُ؛ إِذِ الِاسْتِفْهَامُ بِالْفِعْلِ أَوْلَى. وَقَدْ تَدْخُلُ الْهَمْزَةُ فِي مَوَاضِعَ لَا يَجُوزُ دُخُولُ هَلْ فِيهَا، نَحْوُ: أَزَيْدًا ضَرَبْتَ، وَأَتَضْرِبُ زَيْدًا وَهُوَ أَخُوكَ، وَأَزَيْدٌ عِنْدَكَ أَمْ عَمْرٌو، وَأَوَمَنْ كَانَ، وَأَفَمَنْ كَانَ، وَأَثُمَّ إِذَا مَا وَقَعَ، وَلَا تُسْتَعْمَلُ هَلْ فِي هَذِهِ الْمَوَاضِعِ، وَهَهُنَا بَحْثٌ.
text.en: Section. The two particles of question: the hamza and hal. They have the head of speech and come upon the sentence, whether nominal, as a-Zaydun qāʾimun “is Zayd standing?”, or verbal, as hal qāma Zaydun “did Zayd stand?”; their coming upon the verbal is more frequent, since asking with the verb is more fitting. The hamza may come in places where hal may not come in, as a-Zaydan ḍarabta “is it Zayd you hit?”, a-taḍribu Zaydan wa-huwa akhūka “do you hit Zayd when he is your brother?”, a-Zaydun ʿindaka am ʿAmrun “is Zayd with you, or ʿAmr?”, a-wa-man kāna “and is he who was …?”, a-fa-man kāna “is he then who was …?” and a-thumma idhā mā waqaʿa “is it then, when it has happened …?”; hal is not used in these places; and here there is [a matter for] discussion.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: حُرُوفُ الشَّرْطِ: إِنْ، وَلَوْ، وَأَمَّا، لَهَا صَدْرُ الْكَلَامِ، وَيَدْخُلُ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنْهَا عَلَى الْجُمْلَتَيْنِ، اسْمِيَّتَيْنِ كَانَتَا، أَوْ فِعْلِيَّتَيْنِ، أَوْ مُخْتَلِفَتَيْنِ. فَإِنْ لِلِاسْتِقْبَالِ وَإِنْ دَخَلَتْ عَلَى الْمَاضِي، نَحْوُ: إِنْ زُرْتَنِي أَكْرَمْتُكَ، وَلَوْ لِلْمَاضِي وَإِنْ دَخَلَتْ عَلَى الْمُضَارِعِ، نَحْوُ: لَوْ تَزُورُنِي أَكْرَمْتُكَ، وَيَلْزَمُهُمَا الْفِعْلُ لَفْظًا، كَمَا مَرَّ، أَوْ تَقْدِيرًا، نَحْوُ: إِنْ أَنْتَ زَائِرِي فَأَنَا أُكْرِمُكَ.
text.en: Section. The particles of condition: in, law and ammā. They have the head of speech, and each of them comes upon two sentences, whether both nominal, both verbal or differing. In is for the future, even if it comes upon the past, as in: in zurtanī akramtuka “if you visit me, I will honour you”; and law is for the past, even if it comes upon the muḍāriʿ, as law tazūrunī akramtuka “if you had visited me, I would have honoured you”. The verb is bound to both, in the wording, as has passed, or implied, as in: in anta zāʾirī fa-anā ukrimuka “if you are visiting me, I honour you”.

text.original: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ إِنْ لَا تُسْتَعْمَلُ إِلَّا فِي الْأُمُورِ الْمَشْكُوكَةِ، فَلَا يُقَالُ: إِنْ طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ آتِيكَ، بَلْ: إِذَا طَلَعَتِ الشَّمْسُ. وَلَوْ تَدُلُّ عَلَى نَفْيِ الْجُمْلَةِ الثَّانِيَةِ بِسَبَبِ نَفْيِ الْجُمْلَةِ الْأُولَى، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: لَوْ كَانَ فِيهِمَا آلِهَةٌ إِلَّا اللَّهُ لَفَسَدَتَا.
text.en: Know that in is used only in doubtful matters; so one does not say in ṭalaʿati al-shamsu ātīka “if the sun rises, I will come to you”, but idhā ṭalaʿati al-shamsu “when the sun rises”. Law indicates the negation of the second sentence because of the negation of the first, as in His saying, exalted is He: law kāna fīhimā ālihatun illā Allāhu la-fasadatā “if there were in them gods other than God, they would both have been ruined”.

text.original: وَإِذَا وَقَعَ الْقَسَمُ فِي أَوَّلِ الْكَلَامِ وَتَقَدَّمَ عَلَى الشَّرْطِ يَجِبُ أَنْ يَكُونَ الْفِعْلُ الَّذِي تَدْخُلُ عَلَيْهِ حَرْفُ الشَّرْطِ مَاضِيًا، لَفْظًا، نَحْوُ: وَاللَّهِ إِنْ أَتَيْتَنِي لَأُكْرِمَنَّكَ، أَوْ مَعْنًى، نَحْوُ: وَاللَّهِ إِنْ لَمْ تَأْتِنِي لَأَهْجُرَنَّكَ، فَحِينَئِذٍ تَكُونُ الْجُمْلَةُ الثَّانِيَةُ فِي اللَّفْظِ جَوَابًا لِلْقَسَمِ، لَا جَزَاءً لِلشَّرْطِ؛ فَلِذَلِكَ وَجَبَ فِيهَا مَا وَجَبَ فِي جَوَابِ الْقَسَمِ مِنَ اللَّامِ وَنَحْوِهَا، كَمَا رَأَيْتَ فِي الْمِثَالَيْنِ.
text.en: When an oath stands at the beginning of speech and before the condition, the verb that the particle of condition comes upon must be past, in the wording, as wa-Allāhi in ataytanī la-ukrimannaka “by God, if you come to me, I shall surely honour you”, or in meaning, as wa-Allāhi in lam taʾtinī la-ahjurannaka “by God, if you do not come to me, I shall surely shun you”. Then the second sentence is in the wording the answer to the oath, not the requital of the condition; therefore there is necessary in it what is necessary in the answer to the oath, the lām and the like, as you have seen in the two examples.

text.original: أَمَّا إِنْ وَقَعَ الْقَسَمُ فِي وَسَطِ الْكَلَامِ جَازَ أَنْ يُعْتَبَرَ الْقَسَمُ، بِأَنْ يَكُونَ الْجَوَابُ لَهُ، نَحْوُ: إِنْ تَأْتِنِي وَاللَّهِ لَآتِيَنَّكَ، وَجَازَ أَنْ يُلْغَى، نَحْوُ: إِنْ تَأْتِنِي وَاللَّهِ آتِكَ.
text.en: But if the oath stands in the middle of speech, the oath may be taken into account, in that the answer belongs to it, as in: in taʾtinī wa-Allāhi la-ātiyannaka “if you come to me, by God, I shall surely come to you”, and it may be cancelled, as in: in taʾtinī wa-Allāhi ātika “if you come to me, by God, I will come to you”.

lessons.title: Ammā, for setting out in detail; kallā
body: Ammā, the third particle of condition, is for setting out in detail what has been mentioned in summary: al-nāsu saʿīdun wa-shaqiyyun, “people are happy and wretched”; ammā alladhīna suʿidū fa-fī al-jannati, wa-ammā alladhīna shaqū fa-fī al-nāri.

Three things are necessary with it: the fāʾ in its answer; that the first part be a cause of the second; and that its verb be dropped, though a condition must have a verb. The verb is dropped to call attention that what is intended is the rule of the noun that comes after ammā: ammā Zaydun fa-munṭaliqun, “as for Zayd, he is departing”.

Its underlying form is mahmā yakun min shayʾin fa-Zaydun munṭaliqun, “whatever be the case, Zayd is departing”. The verb and the jārr and majrūr were dropped and ammā was put in their place, leaving ammā fa-Zaydun munṭaliqun. Since it was not fitting that a particle of condition come right upon the fāʾ of the requital, the fāʾ was moved to the second part, and the first part was put between ammā and the fāʾ, in exchange for the dropped verb.

That first part, if it is fit to be a mubtadaʾ, is a mubtadaʾ, as Zaydun above; otherwise its governor is what comes after the fāʾ: ammā yawma al-jumuʿati fa-Zaydun munṭaliqun, “as for Friday, Zayd is departing”, where munṭaliqun governs yawma al-jumuʿati as an adverb.

The particle of rebuke (radʿ) is kallā. It is laid down to restrain the speaker and rebuke him for what he has said: … fa-yaqūlu rabbī ahānani kallā (Q 89:16–17), that is, do not say this, for it is not so. That is after a report; it may also come after a command: to iḍrib Zaydan you say kallā, that is, lā afʿalu hādhā qaṭṭu, “I will never do this”.

Kallā may come in the meaning of ḥaqqan, “truly”: kallā sawfa taʿlamūna (Q 102:3). Then it is a built noun, because it resembles kallā the particle. It is also said to be a particle here, in the meaning of inna, making the sentence certain: kallā inna al-insāna la-yaṭghā (Q 96:6).

terms.en: setting out in detail what was said in summary: the meaning of ammā
the fāʾ of the requital, necessary in the answer of ammā
“whatever be the case”: the underlying form behind ammā
the particle of rebuke: kallā
kallā meaning “truly”: a built noun, or, it is said, a particle

tasks.prompt: Parse the first part in ammā Zaydun fa-munṭaliqun, and in ammā yawma al-jumuʿati fa-Zaydun munṭaliqun.
tasks.answer: Zaydun is fit to be a mubtadaʾ, so it is the mubtadaʾ and munṭaliqun its khabar. Yawma al-jumuʿati is not fit to be a mubtadaʾ, so it is an adverb in naṣb, governed by munṭaliqun, which comes after the fāʾ.

text.original: وَأَمَّا لِلتَّفْصِيلِ مَا ذُكِرَ مُجْمَلًا، نَحْوُ: النَّاسُ سَعِيدٌ وَشَقِيٌّ، أَمَّا الَّذِينَ سُعِدُوا فَفِي الْجَنَّةِ، وَأَمَّا الَّذِينَ شَقُوا فَفِي النَّارِ. وَيَجِبُ فِي جَوَابِهَا الْفَاءُ، وَأَنْ يَكُونَ الْأَوَّلُ سَبَبًا لِلثَّانِي، وَأَنْ يُحْذَفَ فِعْلُهَا، مَعَ أَنَّ الشَّرْطَ لَا بُدَّ لَهُ مِنْ فِعْلٍ؛ وَذَلِكَ لِيَكُونَ تَنْبِيهًا عَلَى أَنَّ الْمَقْصُودَ بِهَا حُكْمُ الِاسْمِ الْوَاقِعِ بَعْدَهَا، نَحْوُ: أَمَّا زَيْدٌ فَمُنْطَلِقٌ.
text.en: Ammā is for setting out in detail what has been mentioned in summary, as al-nāsu saʿīdun wa-shaqiyyun “people are happy and wretched”: ammā alladhīna suʿidū fa-fī al-jannati “as for those who are made happy, they are in Paradise”, wa-ammā alladhīna shaqū fa-fī al-nāri “and as for those who are wretched, they are in the Fire”. In its answer the fāʾ is necessary; the first must be a cause of the second; and its verb must be dropped, although the condition must have a verb; this is to call attention to the fact that what is intended by it is the rule of the noun that comes after it, as ammā Zaydun fa-munṭaliqun “as for Zayd, he is departing”.

text.original: تَقْدِيرُهُ: مَهْمَا يَكُنْ مِنْ شَيْءٍ فَزَيْدٌ مُنْطَلِقٌ، فَحُذِفَ الْفِعْلُ وَالْجَارُّ وَالْمَجْرُورُ، وَأُقِيمَ أَمَّا مَقَامَهُمَا، حَتَّى بَقِيَ: أَمَّا فَزَيْدٌ مُنْطَلِقٌ، وَلَمَّا لَمْ يُنَاسِبْ دُخُولُ حَرْفِ الشَّرْطِ عَلَى فَاءِ الْجَزَاءِ نُقِلَتِ الْفَاءُ إِلَى الْجُزْءِ الثَّانِي، وَوُضِعَ الْجُزْءُ الْأَوَّلُ بَيْنَ أَمَّا وَالْفَاءِ عِوَضًا عَنِ الْفِعْلِ الْمَحْذُوفِ.
text.en: Its underlying form is mahmā yakun min shayʾin fa-Zaydun munṭaliqun “whatever be the case, Zayd is departing”: the verb and the jārr and majrūr were dropped and ammā was put in their place, until there remained ammā fa-Zaydun munṭaliqun; and since it was not fitting that the particle of condition come upon the fāʾ of the requital, the fāʾ was moved to the second part, and the first part was put between ammā and the fāʾ, as a substitute for the dropped verb.

text.original: ثُمَّ ذَلِكَ الْجُزْءُ الْأَوَّلُ إِنْ كَانَ صَالِحًا لِلِابْتِدَاءِ فَهُوَ مُبْتَدَأٌ، كَمَا مَرَّ، وَإِلَّا فَعَامِلُهُ مَا يَكُونُ بَعْدَ الْفَاءِ، كَأَمَّا يَوْمَ الْجُمُعَةِ فَزَيْدٌ مُنْطَلِقٌ؛ فَمُنْطَلِقٌ عَامِلٌ فِي يَوْمِ الْجُمُعَةِ عَلَى الظَّرْفِيَّةِ.
text.en: Then that first part, if it is fit for being a mubtadaʾ, is a mubtadaʾ, as has passed; otherwise its governor is what comes after the fāʾ, as ammā yawma al-jumuʿati fa-Zaydun munṭaliqun “as for Friday, Zayd is departing”: munṭaliqun governs yawmi al-jumuʿati as an adverb.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: حَرْفُ الرَّدْعِ كَلَّا، وُضِعَتْ لِزَجْرِ الْمُتَكَلِّمِ وَرَدْعِهِ عَمَّا تَكَلَّمَ بِهِ، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: وَأَمَّا إِذَا مَا ابْتَلَاهُ فَقَدَرَ عَلَيْهِ رِزْقَهُ فَيَقُولُ رَبِّي أَهَانَنِ كَلَّا، أَيْ لَا تَتَكَلَّمْ بِهَذَا؛ فَإِنَّهُ لَيْسَ كَذَلِكَ. هَذَا بَعْدَ الْخَبَرِ، وَقَدْ تَجِيءُ بَعْدَ الْأَمْرِ أَيْضًا، كَمَا إِذَا قِيلَ لَكَ: اضْرِبْ زَيْدًا، فَقُلْتَ: كَلَّا، أَيْ لَا أَفْعَلُ هَذَا قَطُّ.
text.en: Section. The particle of rebuke (radʿ) is kallā; it is laid down to restrain the speaker and rebuke him for what he has said, as in His saying, exalted is He: wa-ammā idhā mā ibtalāhu fa-qadara ʿalayhi rizqahu fa-yaqūlu rabbī ahānani kallā “but when He tries him and straitens his provision for him, he says: my Lord has humiliated me. No indeed!”, that is, do not speak so, for it is not so. This is after a report; it may also come after a command, as when it is said to you iḍrib Zaydan “hit Zayd!”, and you say kallā, that is, lā afʿalu hādhā qaṭṭu “I will never do this”.

text.original: وَقَدْ تَجِيءُ بِمَعْنَى حَقًّا، كَقَوْلِهِ تَعَالَى: كَلَّا سَوْفَ تَعْلَمُونَ، وَحِينَئِذٍ تَكُونُ اسْمًا مَبْنِيًّا لِكَوْنِهِ مُشَابِهًا لِكَلَّا حَرْفًا، وَقِيلَ: تَكُونُ حَرْفًا أَيْضًا بِمَعْنَى إِنَّ لِتَحْقِيقِ الْجُمْلَةِ، نَحْوُ: كَلَّا إِنَّ الْإِنْسَانَ لَيَطْغَى.
text.en: It may come in the meaning of ḥaqqan “truly”, as in His saying, exalted is He: kallā sawfa taʿlamūna “truly, you will come to know”; then it is a mabnī noun, because it resembles kallā the particle; and it is said that it is a particle in this case too, in the meaning of inna, for making the sentence certain, as kallā inna al-insāna la-yaṭghā “truly, man does transgress”.

lessons.title: The tāʾ of the feminine; the signs of number; tanwīn
body: The quiescent tāʾ of the feminine is joined to the past to show that what the verb is predicated of is feminine: ḍarabat Hindun, “Hind hit”. Where it must be joined was learned before (lesson 10). When an unvowelled letter meets it, it must take a vowel, the kasra, for an unvowelled letter that is given a vowel is given the kasra: qad qāmati al-ṣalātu, “the prayer has begun”.

Its vowel does not bring back what was dropped because of its sukūn: one does not say ramāti al-marʾatu, bringing back the alif of ramā, for the kasra is accidental, there only to remove the meeting of two unvowelled letters. What some say, al-marʾatāni ramātā, is weak.

Joining the sign of the dual, of the masculine plural or of the feminine plural to the verb is weak: one does not say qāmā al-Zaydāni, qāmū al-Zaydūna, qumna al-nisāʾu. Where they are joined, they are not taken as pronouns, for a pronoun would then come before what it refers to is mentioned; they are signs that show the states of the fāʿil, like the tāʾ of the feminine.

Tanwīn is an unvowelled nūn that follows the vowel of the end of a word, not for emphasising the verb (that is the nūn of emphasis, lesson 72). It is of five kinds. The first is of being established (tamakkun): it shows that the noun is firmly a noun, that is, munṣarif: Zaydun, rajulun. The second is of indefiniteness (tankīr): ṣahin, “be silent, with some silence, at some time”; ṣah without it means “be silent with the silence, now”.

The third is of compensation (ʿiwaḍ), in exchange for the muḍāf ilayhi: ḥīnaʾidhin, sāʿataʾidhin, yawmaʾidhin, that is, ḥīna idh kāna kadhā, “at the time when such-and-such was”. The fourth is of correspondence (muqābala): the tanwīn of the sound feminine plural, muslimātin; the commentators say it answers the nūn of the masculine plural. These four belong to the noun.

The fifth is of singing (tarannum), joined to the ends of verses and half-verses: aqillī al-lawma ʿādhila wa-al-ʿitāban, wa-qūlī in aṣabtu la-qad aṣāban; and yā abatā ʿallaka aw ʿasākan. It is not limited to the noun: aṣāban is a verb. Last, the tanwīn may be dropped from a proper name described by ibn or ibna that is muḍāf to another proper name: jāʾanī Zaydu bnu ʿAmrin, wa-Hindu ibnatu Bakrin.

terms.en: the quiescent tāʾ of the feminine, joined to the past
the tanwīn of being established: the sign of the munṣarif noun
the tanwīn of indefiniteness: ṣahin
the tanwīn of compensation, for a muḍāf ilayhi: yawmaʾidhin
the tanwīn of correspondence, in the sound feminine plural
the tanwīn of singing, at the ends of verses

examples.en: the tāʾ given a kasra before an unvowelled letter
the tanwīn of indefiniteness
the tanwīn of compensation
the tanwīn dropped before ibn

tasks.prompt: Why does the tāʾ take a kasra in qad qāmati al-ṣalātu?
tasks.answer: The quiescent tāʾ meets an unvowelled letter, the first letter of al-ṣalātu after its hamza of joining falls away. To remove the meeting of two unvowelled letters the tāʾ is given a vowel, and an unvowelled letter that is given a vowel takes the kasra.

tasks.prompt: Why is ramāti al-marʾatu wrong?
tasks.answer: The alif of ramā was dropped because the tāʾ after it is unvowelled. The kasra the tāʾ takes before al-marʾatu is accidental, there only to remove the meeting of two unvowelled letters, so it does not bring the alif back.

tasks.prompt: Name the kind of tanwīn: (a) rajulun; (b) ṣahin; (c) yawmaʾidhin; (d) muslimātin; (e) aṣāban at the end of a verse.
tasks.answer: (a) Being established (tamakkun). (b) Indefiniteness (tankīr). (c) Compensation (ʿiwaḍ), for the muḍāf ilayhi: yawma idh kāna kadhā. (d) Correspondence (muqābala). (e) Singing (tarannum).

tasks.prompt: What is the difference between ṣahin and ṣah?
tasks.answer: Ṣahin, with the tanwīn of indefiniteness, means “be silent, with some silence, at some time”. Ṣah, with sukūn, means “be silent with the silence, now”: without the tanwīn the silence asked for is a known one.

tasks.prompt: Why has Zaydu no tanwīn in jāʾanī Zaydu bnu ʿAmrin?
tasks.answer: Zaydu is a proper name described by ibn, and ibn is muḍāf to another proper name, ʿAmrin; in that case the tanwīn may be dropped from the first name.

quiz.prompt: The quiescent tāʾ of the feminine is joined to…
When an unvowelled letter meets it, the tāʾ takes…
Qāmū al-Zaydūna, with the sign of the plural on the verb, is…
quiz.explanation: The book: joining the signs of the dual and the plurals is weak.

quiz.prompt: The tanwīn of Zaydun and rajulun is the tanwīn of…
quiz.explanation: It shows that the noun is munṣarif.

quiz.prompt: The tanwīn of yawmaʾidhin is in exchange for…
The tanwīn of muslimātin is the tanwīn of…
quiz.explanation: It is the tanwīn of the sound feminine plural.

quiz.prompt: Which tanwīn does not belong to the noun alone?
quiz.explanation: The book says the other four belong to the noun; aṣāban is a verb.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: تَاءُ التَّأْنِيثِ السَّاكِنَةُ تَلْحَقُ الْمَاضِيَ لِتَدُلَّ عَلَى تَأْنِيثِ مَا أُسْنِدَ إِلَيْهِ الْفِعْلُ، نَحْوُ: ضَرَبَتْ هِنْدٌ، وَقَدْ عَرَفْتَ مَوَاضِعَ وُجُوبِ إِلْحَاقِهَا. وَإِذَا لَقِيَهَا سَاكِنٌ بَعْدَهَا وَجَبَ تَحْرِيكُهَا بِالْكَسْرِ؛ لِأَنَّ السَّاكِنَ إِذَا حُرِّكَ حُرِّكَ بِالْكَسْرِ، نَحْوُ: قَدْ قَامَتِ الصَّلَاةُ. وَحَرَكَتُهَا لَا تُوجِبُ رَدَّ مَا حُذِفَ لِأَجْلِ سُكُونِهَا، فَلَا يُقَالُ: رَمَاتِ الْمَرْأَةُ؛ لِأَنَّ حَرَكَتَهَا عَارِضِيَّةٌ وَاقِعَةٌ لِرَفْعِ الْتِقَاءِ السَّاكِنَيْنِ، وَقَوْلُهُمُ: الْمَرْأَتَانِ رَمَاتَا، ضَعِيفٌ.
text.en: Section. The quiescent tāʾ of the feminine is joined to the past to indicate that what the verb is predicated of is feminine, as ḍarabat Hindun “Hind hit”; and you have learned the places where joining it is necessary. When an unvowelled letter meets it after it, it must be given a vowel, the kasra; for when an unvowelled letter is given a vowel, it is given the kasra, as qad qāmati al-ṣalātu “the prayer has begun”. Its vowel does not require bringing back what was dropped because of its sukūn; so one does not say ramāti al-marʾatu, because its vowel is accidental, coming in to remove the meeting of two unvowelled letters; and their saying al-marʾatāni ramātā “the two women threw” is weak.

text.original: وَأَمَّا إِلْحَاقُ عَلَامَةِ التَّثْنِيَةِ وَجَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ وَجَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ فَضَعِيفٌ، فَلَا يُقَالُ: قَامَا الزَّيْدَانِ، وَقَامُوا الزَّيْدُونَ، وَقُمْنَ النِّسَاءُ، وَيُنْتَقَدُ الْإِلْحَاقُ لِكَوْنِ الضَّمَائِرِ لِئَلَّا يَلْزَمَ الْإِضْمَارُ قَبْلَ الذِّكْرِ، بَلْ عَلَامَاتٌ دَالَّةٌ عَلَى أَحْوَالِ الْفَاعِلِ، كَتَاءِ التَّأْنِيثِ.
text.en: As for joining the sign of the dual, of the masculine plural and of the feminine plural [to the verb], it is weak; so one does not say qāmā al-Zaydāni, wa-qāmū al-Zaydūna and wa-qumna al-nisāʾu; and the joining is criticised as [taking them as] pronouns — [they are not pronouns,] lest a pronoun come before [its noun is] mentioned —; rather they are signs that indicate the states of the fāʿil, like the tāʾ of the feminine.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: التَّنْوِينُ نُونٌ سَاكِنَةٌ تَتْبَعُ حَرَكَةَ آخِرِ الْكَلِمَةِ، لَا لِتَأْكِيدِ الْفِعْلِ، وَهِيَ خَمْسَةُ أَقْسَامٍ: الْأَوَّلُ لِلتَّمَكُّنِ، وَهُوَ مَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ الِاسْمَ مُتَمَكِّنٌ فِي مُقْتَضَى الِاسْمِيَّةِ، أَيْ أَنَّهُ مُنْصَرِفٌ، نَحْوُ: زَيْدٌ وَرَجُلٌ. وَالثَّانِي لِلتَّنْكِيرِ، وَهُوَ مَا يَدُلُّ عَلَى أَنَّ الِاسْمَ نَكِرَةٌ، نَحْوُ: صَهٍ، أَيِ اسْكُتْ سُكُوتًا مَا فِي وَقْتٍ مَا، وَأَمَّا صَهْ بِالسُّكُونِ فَمَعْنَاهُ: اسْكُتِ السُّكُوتَ الْآنَ.
text.en: Section. Tanwīn is an unvowelled nūn that follows the vowel of the end of the word, not for emphasising the verb. It is of five kinds. The first is for being established (tamakkun): it indicates that the noun is firmly established in what being a noun requires, that is, that it is munṣarif, as Zaydun and rajulun. The second is for indefiniteness (tankīr): it indicates that the noun is indefinite, as ṣahin, that is, uskut sukūtan mā fī waqtin mā “be silent with some silence at some time”; as for ṣah with the sukūn, its meaning is uskuti al-sukūta al-āna “be silent with [all] silence now”.

text.original: وَالثَّالِثُ لِلْعِوَضِ، وَهُوَ مَا يَكُونُ عِوَضًا عَنِ الْمُضَافِ إِلَيْهِ، نَحْوُ: حِينَئِذٍ وَسَاعَتَئِذٍ وَيَوْمَئِذٍ، أَيْ حِينَ إِذْ كَانَ كَذَا. وَالرَّابِعُ لِلْمُقَابَلَةِ، وَهُوَ التَّنْوِينُ الَّذِي فِي جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ السَّالِمِ، نَحْوُ: مُسْلِمَاتٍ. وَهَذِهِ الْأَرْبَعَةُ تَخْتَصُّ بِالِاسْمِ.
text.en: The third is for compensation (ʿiwaḍ): it is one that is in exchange for the muḍāf ilayhi, as ḥīnaʾidhin, sāʿataʾidhin and yawmaʾidhin, that is, ḥīna idh kāna kadhā “at the time when such-and-such was”. The fourth is for correspondence (muqābala): it is the tanwīn that is in the sound feminine plural, as muslimātin. These four belong to the noun.

text.original: وَالْخَامِسُ لِلتَّرَنُّمِ، وَهُوَ الَّذِي يَلْحَقُ آخِرَ الْأَبْيَاتِ وَالْمَصَارِيعِ، كَقَوْلِ الشَّاعِرِ، شِعْرٌ: أَقِلِّي اللَّوْمَ عَاذِلَ وَالْعِتَابَنْ * وَقُولِي إِنْ أَصَبْتُ لَقَدْ أَصَابَنْ. وَكَقَوْلِهِ: يَا أَبَتَا عَلَّكَ أَوْ عَسَاكَنْ. وَقَدْ يُحْذَفُ التَّنْوِينُ مِنَ الْعَلَمِ إِذَا كَانَ مَوْصُوفًا بِابْنٍ أَوِ ابْنَةٍ مُضَافًا إِلَى عَلَمٍ آخَرَ، نَحْوُ: جَاءَنِي زَيْدُ بْنُ عَمْرٍو، وَهِنْدُ ابْنَةُ بَكْرٍ.
text.en: The fifth is for singing (tarannum): it is what is joined to the end of verses and hemistichs, as in the poet's saying, verse: aqillī al-lawma ʿādhila wa-al-ʿitāban / wa-qūlī in aṣabtu la-qad aṣāban “Lessen the blame, O you who blame me, and the reproach; / and say, if I have hit the mark: he has hit it”; and as in his saying: yā abatā ʿallaka aw ʿasākan “O my father, perhaps you, or it may be you”. The tanwīn may be dropped from a proper name when it is qualified by ibn or ibna made muḍāf to another proper name, as jāʾanī Zaydu bnu ʿAmrin “Zayd son of ʿAmr came to me” and wa-Hindu ibnatu Bakrin “and Hind daughter of Bakr”.

lessons.title: The nūn of emphasis
body: The nūn of emphasis is laid down to emphasise the imperative, and the muḍāriʿ when there is a request in it, over against qad, which emphasises the past (lesson 68). It is of two kinds: light (khafīfa), always unvowelled, iḍriban; and heavy (thaqīla), doubled, always with a fatḥa if there is no alif before it, iḍribanna, and with a kasra if there is, iḍribānni, iḍribnānni.

It comes by choice in the imperative, the prohibition, the question, the wish and the offer, because in each of them there is a request: iḍribanna, lā taḍribanna, hal taḍribanna, laytaka taḍribanna, alā tanzilanna bi-nā fa-tuṣība khayran. It comes in the oath necessarily: an oath mostly falls on what the speaker wants, so he wanted its end not to be empty of emphasis, as its beginning is not: wa-Allāhi la-afʿalanna kadhā (lesson 60).

The letter before it takes a ḍamma in the masculine plural, iḍribunna, to show the dropped wāw; a kasra in the feminine addressed, iḍribinna, to show the dropped yāʾ; and a fatḥa in the rest. In the singular, a ḍamma would confuse it with the masculine plural and a kasra with the feminine addressed; in the dual and the feminine plural the letter before the nūn is an alif: iḍribānni, iḍribnānni.
The alif was added before the nūn in the feminine plural for dislike of three nūns together: the nūn of the pronoun and the nūn of emphasis, which, being doubled, is two.

The light nūn never comes in the dual, nor in the feminine plural, for it would follow an alif. If it were given a vowel it would no longer be light, as it is by origin; if it were left unvowelled, two unvowelled letters would meet out of their proper bounds, which is not allowed. The commentators give the proper bounds as a long letter followed by a doubled one, as in iḍribānni.
This is the last section of the book: with the nūn of emphasis, the third part, the particle, comes to its end.

terms.en: the nūn of emphasis, for the imperative and the muḍāriʿ with a request
the light nūn: always unvowelled
the heavy nūn: doubled, with fatḥa, or kasra after an alif
request: what the imperative, prohibition, question, wish and offer share
the meeting of two unvowelled letters

tasks.prompt: Light or heavy, and why that vowel on the nūn? iḍriban; iḍribanna; iḍribānni.
tasks.answer: Iḍriban: light, always unvowelled. Iḍribanna: heavy, with a fatḥa, since there is no alif before it. Iḍribānni: heavy, with a kasra, since an alif comes before it.

tasks.prompt: Why does the letter before the nūn take a ḍamma in iḍribunna and a kasra in iḍribinna?
tasks.answer: The ḍamma shows the wāw of the masculine plural, dropped before the nūn; the kasra shows the yāʾ of the feminine addressed, dropped in the same way.

tasks.prompt: Why is the alif added in iḍribnānni?
tasks.answer: Without it three nūns would come together: the nūn of the feminine pronoun and the heavy nūn of emphasis, which is doubled and so two. The alif keeps them apart.

tasks.prompt: Why can the light nūn not be joined to the dual?
tasks.answer: It would follow the alif of the dual. Given a vowel, it would no longer be light; left unvowelled, two unvowelled letters would meet out of their proper bounds, which is not allowed.

tasks.prompt: In which is the nūn of emphasis necessary, and in which by choice: wa-Allāhi la-afʿalanna kadhā; hal taḍribanna?
tasks.answer: Wa-Allāhi la-afʿalanna kadhā: necessary, in the answer of the oath. Hal taḍribanna: by choice, in the question, which has a request in it.

quiz.prompt: The nūn of emphasis emphasises…
options: the imperative, and the muḍāriʿ with a request
quiz.explanation: Qad is the one that emphasises the past.

quiz.prompt: The light nūn is…
quiz.explanation: Iḍriban: the light nūn has no vowel of its own.

quiz.prompt: After an alif the heavy nūn takes…
In iḍribunna the ḍamma shows…
In the answer of an oath the nūn of emphasis is…
The alif in iḍribnānni was added because…
quiz.explanation: The nūn of the pronoun and the doubled nūn of emphasis.

quiz.prompt: The light nūn does not come in…
options: the dual and the feminine plural
quiz.explanation: After their alif, two unvowelled letters would meet out of their bounds.

text.original: فَصْلٌ: نُونُ التَّأْكِيدِ، وُضِعَتْ لِتَأْكِيدِ الْأَمْرِ وَالْمُضَارِعِ إِذَا كَانَ فِيهِ طَلَبٌ، بِإِزَاءِ قَدْ لِتَأْكِيدِ الْمَاضِي، وَهِيَ عَلَى ضَرْبَيْنِ: خَفِيفَةٌ، أَيْ سَاكِنَةٌ أَبَدًا، نَحْوُ: اضْرِبَنْ، وَثَقِيلَةٌ، أَيْ مُشَدَّدَةٌ، مَفْتُوحَةٌ أَبَدًا إِنْ لَمْ يَكُنْ قَبْلَهَا أَلِفٌ، نَحْوُ: اضْرِبَنَّ، وَمَكْسُورَةٌ إِنْ كَانَ قَبْلَهَا أَلِفٌ، نَحْوُ: اضْرِبَانِّ، وَاضْرِبْنَانِّ.
text.en: Section. The nūn of emphasis is laid down to emphasise the imperative and the muḍāriʿ when there is a request in it, over against qad for emphasising the past. It is of two kinds: light (khafīfa), that is, always unvowelled, as iḍriban; and heavy (thaqīla), that is, doubled, always with a fatḥa if there is no alif before it, as iḍribanna “do hit!”, and with a kasra if there is an alif before it, as iḍribānni and iḍribnānni.

text.original: وَتَدْخُلُ فِي الْأَمْرِ وَالنَّهْيِ وَالِاسْتِفْهَامِ وَالتَّمَنِّي وَالْعَرْضِ جَوَازًا؛ لِأَنَّ فِي كُلٍّ مِنْهَا طَلَبًا، نَحْوُ: اضْرِبَنَّ، وَلَا تَضْرِبَنَّ، وَهَلْ تَضْرِبَنَّ، وَلَيْتَكَ تَضْرِبَنَّ، وَأَلَا تَنْزِلَنَّ بِنَا فَتُصِيبَ خَيْرًا. وَقَدْ تَدْخُلُ فِي الْقَسَمِ وُجُوبًا؛ لِوُقُوعِهِ عَلَى مَا يَكُونُ مَطْلُوبًا لِلْمُتَكَلِّمِ غَالِبًا، فَأَرَادَ أَنْ لَا يَكُونَ آخِرُ الْقَسَمِ خَالِيًا مِنْ مَعْنَى التَّأْكِيدِ، كَمَا لَا يَخْلُو أَوَّلُهُ مِنْهُ، نَحْوُ: وَاللَّهِ لَأَفْعَلَنَّ كَذَا.
text.en: It comes in the imperative, the prohibition, the question, the wish and the offer, by choice, because in each of them there is a request, as iḍribanna, wa-lā taḍribanna “and do not hit!”, wa-hal taḍribanna “and will you hit?”, wa-laytaka taḍribanna “and would that you would hit!” and wa-alā tanzilanna bi-nā fa-tuṣība khayran “and will you not stay with us, and get some good?”. It comes in the oath necessarily, because [the oath] falls mostly upon what the speaker wants; so he wanted the end of the oath not to be free of the meaning of emphasis, as its beginning is not free of it, as wa-Allāhi la-afʿalanna kadhā “by God, I shall surely do such-and-such”.

text.original: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّهُ يَجِبُ ضَمُّ مَا قَبْلَهَا فِي جَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ، نَحْوُ: اضْرِبُنَّ، لِيَدُلَّ عَلَى الْوَاوِ الْمَحْذُوفَةِ، وَكَسْرُ مَا قَبْلَهَا فِي الْمُخَاطَبَةِ، نَحْوُ: اضْرِبِنَّ، لِيَدُلَّ عَلَى الْيَاءِ الْمَحْذُوفَةِ، وَفَتْحُ مَا قَبْلَهَا فِيمَا عَدَاهُمَا؛ أَمَّا فِي الْمُفْرَدِ فَلِأَنَّهُ لَوْ ضُمَّ لَالْتَبَسَ بِجَمْعِ الْمُذَكَّرِ، وَلَوْ كُسِرَ لَالْتَبَسَ بِالْمُخَاطَبَةِ، وَأَمَّا فِي الْمُثَنَّى وَجَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ فَلِأَنَّ مَا قَبْلَهَا أَلِفٌ، نَحْوُ: اضْرِبَانِّ، وَاضْرِبْنَانِّ.
text.en: Know that the letter before it must have a ḍamma in the masculine plural, as iḍribunna, to indicate the dropped wāw; a kasra in the [feminine] addressed, as iḍribinna, to indicate the dropped yāʾ; and a fatḥa in the others: in the singular, because if it had a ḍamma it would be confused with the masculine plural, and if it had a kasra it would be confused with the [feminine] addressed; and in the dual and the feminine plural, because the letter before it is an alif, as iḍribānni and iḍribnānni.

text.original: وَزِيدَتِ الْأَلِفُ قَبْلَ النُّونِ فِي جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ لِكَرَاهَةِ اجْتِمَاعِ ثَلَاثِ نُونَاتٍ: نُونِ الضَّمِيرِ، وَنُونِ التَّأْكِيدِ. وَنُونُ الْخَفِيفَةِ لَا تَدْخُلُ فِي التَّثْنِيَةِ أَصْلًا، وَلَا فِي جَمْعِ الْمُؤَنَّثِ؛ لِأَنَّهُ لَوْ حُرِّكَتِ النُّونُ لَمْ يَبْقَ خَفِيفَةً، فَلَمْ تَكُنْ عَلَى الْأَصْلِ، وَإِنْ أَبْقَيْتَهَا سَاكِنَةً يَلْزَمُ الْتِقَاءُ السَّاكِنَيْنِ عَلَى غَيْرِ حَدِّهِ، وَهُوَ غَيْرُ جَائِزٍ.
text.en: The alif was added before the nūn in the feminine plural because of the dislike of three nūns coming together: the nūn of the pronoun and the nūn of emphasis. The light nūn never comes in the dual, nor in the feminine plural; for if the nūn were given a vowel, it would not remain light and would not be as it originally is, and if you left it unvowelled, the meeting of two unvowelled letters would follow out of its proper bounds, and that is not allowed.
